These analyses reveal significant discrepancies between the predicted and observed amplitudes of the anisotropy at higher energies, suggesting the need for a new understanding of cosmic rays. Given this new picture, we suggest re-evaluating anisotropy models and the hypothetical relationships between energy, distance, and amplitude in cosmic ray distributions. This paper presents such a solution, a fully digital, immune-cell identification and counting system, with an evaluation of its performance on 42 breast cancer H&E stains. This comprehensive system includes image segmentation, detection, and counting algorithms specifically designed for immune cells, as well as a manual editing tool that enables pathologists to accurately assess immune response factors. Our results indicate that our method achieves high accuracy in detecting and counting tumor infiltrating lymphocytes, with an average error rate of 10.05% compared to manual analysis. This digital tool facilitates collaboration across institutions by standardizing TIL counting procedures. This standardization enables researchers to gather essential data for further study, ultimately leading to a better comprehension of the cancer immune microenvironment. Our system also presents an opportunity for enhancing pathologist's review and editing processes through the comparison of manual and automated results. This comparison enables pathologists to verify auto-generated TIL counts and immune response factors, promoting discussion and refinement of those values. This interactive and bidirectional process enriches the review and editing process by providing a dual-view perspective of these critical values. This standard digital tool enables pathologists to accurately interpret immune cell infiltration, refine autoimmune evaluation, and enhance cancer research conclusions by leveraging the combined efforts of human and machine intelligence. We present a method for creating adaptable gaits on quadrupedal robots using reinforcement learning (RL). By training the policy with RL, the robot can forge links between leg positions, resulting in robust and efficient gait patterns. These gaits enable the robot to easily switch between diverse walking patterns and make challenging tasks like crawling through narrow spaces and climbing over large obstacles straightforward. Unlike existing control strategies that are prone to failures, our framework provides a more universal solution, and, as evidenced by actual robot trials, the learned gaits yield higher levels of flexibility and stability in the robot. Additionally, the algorithm's ability to create gaits that work even when sensors fail due to damage or signal interference is also demonstrated. Our approach provides a flexible solution to the open-ended problem of gaits adaptation in quadrupedal robotics and paves the way for a more general strategy for other hybrid robotic systems. Ultra-luminous local nuclei with minimal star formation activity are a rare yet significant phase in the galaxy evolution process. Powered by an active nuclear source, these low-level absorption line galaxies maintain their extremely bright nuclear emission while preventing star formation within the surrounding area. This paper focuses on the role of a hot wind emanating from these nuclear sources, which may feed back into the galaxies and possibly influence their evolution. To investigate this hot wind, the researchers used the MOSES survey, which includes high-resolution spectra of 44 of these sources, gathered through the R GISPCOS at the 2.1m telescope at the Calar Alto Observatory. These spectra were analyzed using a novel automated algorithm to identify the presence of a hot wind. Of the 44 sources included in the study, the researchers detected wind signals in 29%, which is a relatively low percentage of detection. Among the 9 sources with previous wind detections, the newly analyzed spectra revealed additional evidence of hot wind signals in 22%. Despite its significance in understanding galaxy evolution, direct wind mass loss remains poorly understood in these sources. This study serves as a starting point for further investigation into other properties of hot winds, which could provide valuable insights into the behavior and properties of these winds. Based on the observed wind signals, the hot winds in these sources have an average flow rate of around 10 curve mass units per year and an average ionization parameter of approximately 10^1. These hot winds likely originate from nuclear outflows powered by both the nuclear activity and star formation, which then interact with the surrounding photon field and interstellar medium. Based on the estimated ionizing energy required for the winds, the hot winds in these sources appear to be more powerful than those found in less active nuclear sources, which suggests a direct correlation between the ionization parameter of the winds and the nuclear source's luminosity. The hot winds in these sources have a maximum ionization parameter of approximately 10^3, which is significantly lower than the ionization parameters found in other galactic nuclear outflows. Based on the observed properties of these hot winds, the authors propose a feedback mechanism that could regulate the nuclear source's energy output and prevent star formation within the surrounding area. Which could lead to a transition to a more active nuclear state. In the field of optimal regulator redesign using reinforcement learning, a key challenge lies in achieving satisfactory performance within a short time frame. Current methods, however, often rely on complex high-dimensional function approximators, which hinder the model's ability to adapt to changing environments during online learning. This study presents a model-free design approach centered around a novel temporal difference network, dubbed the Lagrange temporal difference network. By leveraging the benefits of Lagrange multiplier methods, this model combines multiple value functions into one representation, eliminating the need for high-dimensional function approximators and enabling online learning with improved performance. Empirical evaluations confirm that the proposed method delivers superior transient results and scalable scalability compared to the existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, the Lagrange temporal difference network is capable of producing multiple value functions and can be applied to a range of tasks by modifying its constraint backpropagation rules. Overall, this design provides a viable solution for a reliable and efficient reinforcement learning-based optimal regulator redesign. In addition, the method has the potential to be applied to a broader range of problems in control theory. A detailed photometric study of the metal-rich galactic globular cluster Tononzintla 2 was conducted using Hubble Space Telescope images, which included both optical and near-infrared filters. The analysis provided accurate mean values for metal abundance and spread of elements within the cluster. The findings revealed a substantial spread in metal abundance and a notable absence of narrow metallicity ranges, indicating a significant level of metal mixture and elemental spread. Comparison with other high-metallicity Galactic clusters showed similar levels of metal spread and mixed abundances. The discovery of a high proportion of red giant stars with irregular colors within Tononzintla 2 suggests the presence of multiple horizontal branch stars, one of which is likely an interacting binary affecting the cluster's color-magnitude diagram. Additionally, the detection of horizontal branch stars near the red edge and the red giant branch touch revealed a low ratio of red subdwarfs to red giants and a high ratio of red giant branch stars with helium-rich to red giant branch stars with helium-normal, indicating a significant presence of binary interactions and stellar interactions within the cluster. Comparison with a metal-rich galactic globular cluster, NGC 6752, using a multi-dimensional spectral analysis showed both clusters have similar mean metal abundances but differ in their spread and binary interactions within the cluster, which is more pronounced in Tononzintla 2. Comparison with a metal-rich external galaxy galactic globular cluster, ESO 444-SC24, using a multi-dimensional spectral analysis showed both clusters have similar spread and binary interactions, which is more pronounced in ESO 444-SC24, despite having lower metal abundance than Tononzintla 2. However, the pre-trained models themselves are not yet capable of programming and often rely on additional training, which is accomplished by incorporating a programmer's code through demonstrations. The Graphical Lasso (GL) is a widely accepted model for estimating inverse covariance matrices and graph structures within high-dimensional data. Despite its success, the model has its limitations, primarily due to the inherent assumption that all observed variables are fully observable, a presumption that doesn't always hold true. In contrast, Latent Variable Model combined with Graphical Lasso (LVM-GL) includes unobserved variables, utilizing incomplete data through the use of hidden variables, providing a more accurate representation of complex systems. However, LVM-GL is notoriously challenging to compute due to its computational intractability, leading to previously implemented approximations that rely on closed-form algorithms, though these only work for very specific scenarios. In contrast, this study introduces a novel stick-breaking scheme, allowing for the generation of latent variables, thereby providing a more reliable, though probabilistic generation of LVM-GL that operates within a Bayesian framework, relying on Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) computations. This study presents extensive simulations that validate the efficiency and flexibility of the proposed model in graph structure inference and provokes interesting future research questions regarding the integration of LVM-GL with multiple network layers. In computer vision, a key challenge of federated learning lies in balancing communication efficiency and model accuracy. To address this, our research introduces compressed federated distillation, a novel approach that surpasses the communication efficiency of both federated distillation and averaging methods while achieving comparable accuracy. The quality of model representations from teachers is leveraged to determine optimal compression ratios for effective learning, and a specialized model is designed to adapt and improve representations based on distillation temperatures and compression rates. The benefits of our approach in terms of communication efficiency are quantified through experiments on ImageNet, where it enables a significant 10-20 times reduction in communication requirements while maintaining equivalent accuracy. Furthermore, its applications extend to various tasks such as mobile object detection and image classification on edge devices, resulting in a 5-10 times decrease in communication requirements with minimal accuracy loss. Our open-source implementation facilitates the replication of our findings. To the best of our knowledge, our method constitutes the first compression technique to integrate federated distillation, thereby enabling its widespread adoption. Additionally, our study provides insights into the intricate relationships between compression, distillation, and temperature, shedding light on the underlying mechanisms that govern the behavior of federated distillation models. Our research offers a direction for future research in the realm of federated learning, emphasizing the need for more efficient communication methods to support scalable federated learning systems. By comparing NaTl$_4$Te$_3$'s properties to those of other group-I MTl$_4$Te$_3$ materials, researchers found NaTl$_4$Te$_3$ exhibits unique characteristics with potential for application in spin torque equipment and spin devices.  To confirm its spin-helicity insulation, researchers used X-ray linear dichroism and resonant photoemission spectroscopy, which provided separate looks at the material's valence and conduction bands. Optimizing a utility function offline with the help of expert knowledge in real-time decision-making processes is discussed. The utility function is discovered through interactive learning, but instead of relying solely on the evaluation of our choices, we also take into consideration the expert's corrections to those choices. The problem is conceptualized as a best response process where the optimizer searches for a best response to a utility function represented by a compact space. The offline learning process is broken down into rounds. The optimizer starts each round by making a choice, which is reviewed by the expert. Based on the expert's feedback, the optimizer adjusts his choice to achieve faster convergence to the optimal solution. The convergence rate is analyzed under specific assumptions regarding the expert's utility function and its representation. The assumptions enable us to establish a lower bound on the number of rounds required to achieve a similar level of convergence when relying solely on the evaluation of our choices. The offline learning process is further generalized to scenarios where the expert's utility function is partially unclear and needs to be estimated from his corrections. The estimator of the utility function is proven to be consistent when the corrections are abundant and continuous. The result is then applied to a series of equilibriums problems where the optimizer seeks to reach a equilibrium strategy under hypotheses regarding the uniqueness and smoothness of the utility function. The theoretical analysis is accompanied by a numerical study which highlights the effectiveness of the proposed learning algorithm in achieving faster convergence to the optimal solution than an algorithm that relies solely on the evaluation of our choices. The results are verified through a series of experiments conducted under diverse scenarios. The experiments demonstrate the learning algorithm's ability to achieve faster convergence to the optimal solution when offline utility function estimation is accurate and partially correlates with the expert's utility function. The results also show that the learning algorithm performs similarly to an algorithm that relies solely on the evaluation of our choices when the expert's utility function is unclear and needs to be estimated from his corrections. The performance of the learning algorithm is finally evaluated in scenarios where the optimizer seeks to reach a equilibrium strategy under unique hypotheses regarding the uniqueness and smoothness of the utility function. The results reveal that the learning algorithm performs as well in these scenarios as in scenarios where the optimizer searches for a best response to a utility function represented by a compact space. Moreover, our results demonstrate the significance of evaluating the performance of sequence-to-sequence models using a broader range of sequence lengths to gain insights into the behaviors of reinforcement learning agents. In modern distributed machine learning, the method of aggregation plays a vital role in determining scalability and efficiency. Previous research mostly relied on linear aggregation, but due to its inability to adapt to non-linear node performance, it may not always provide an optimal solution. Our innovative contribution is the weighted power-mean aggregation method (WPM), a non-linear aggregation function that overcomes the limitations of its linear counterpart. We derive the WPM formula based on entropy minimization and highlight its ability to accommodate various subfunctions satisfied by traditional linear aggregation. Our experimental results demonstrate that WPM leads to lower communication costs while achieving comparable accuracy, if not superior, than traditional methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/alexalex2000/WPM_aggregation. Our paper is the first to propose WPM, and this interview and a technical report provide additional information to the community. Moreover, WPM has been successfully integrated into the TensorFlow framework and is currently used in training BERT models at the AIrace competition. Our objective is to bridge the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical applications by sharing our experience implementing WPM in a distributed environment. Our interview also provides an overview of the key distributed neural network training algorithms used in recent years. This system can only work effectively if the patients' airways are tightly sealed, which is typically monitored by noise generated by the air flowing out of the patients' lungs. We offer a new approach for achieving contraction at the optimal rate on the parameter space for unknown variance $\sigma^2$ in Bayesian linear regression. Unlike previous results that only applied to smooth loss functions, our method is broad and works with a wide range of losses. We also allow for the postulatory assumption of a prior distribution on the error variance, a characteristic feature of Bayes theory. The underlying idea of our approach is to analyze a modified model, called the 'enveloped model', in which the posterior distribution is conditioned on the observed data and the functional form of the variance. Within this framework, the contraction rates are determined solely by the characteristics of the prior distribution. Though the enveloped model is not fully identified in the sense that there are multiple possible variances for a given observed data and prior distribution, we are able to establish 'identification at infinity' - that is, that there exists a non-normalizable weight function that determines a variance that goes to infinity as the observation noise goes to zero. We hope that our approach will be useful in studying other non-identified statistical models. We also establish a new model averaging scheme for estimating variance by averaging the functions of the variances associated with different'skeleton' models - models in which the variance is assumed to be constant in non-data regions - based on the posterior distribution. The model averaging weights are determined by the posterior probability of each skeleton model, and we establish that the resulting estimator contracts at the optimal rate when the variances are bounded. An experimental investigation into the surface roughness of aluminum alloy A380 friction stir welds has been conducted. Various parameters such as wheel dress, wheel hardness, and cooling time were examined while fixing other factors, and both cubic and exponential relationships with surface roughness were observed. The results showed that wheel dress had the greatest influence on surface roughness, accounting for 75% of variation, closely followed by interactions, and then wheel hardness and parameters. The surface roughness ranged from 1.18 to 6.03 micrometers, and a significant 94% of data fell within the 1.18 to 3.03 micrometer range. Furthermore, a multiple linear regression model was developed and validated using a k-fold cross-validation method, demonstrating 93% accuracy in predicting surface roughness. Based on these findings, optimal parameters for minimizing surface roughness were identified. Ultimately, an empirical model for surface roughness was developed as S_R = 0.0587*T^1.4428*R^3.1188, which closely matched the experimental data with a correlation coefficient of 0.94. However, it's essential to note that the underlying physical processes involved in the welding process are not reflected in this model. Additionally, more research is required to fully comprehend the interaction between the wheel dress and the material, which may vary based on specific factors such as the presence of hard phases in the alloy. Therefore, a deeper understanding of this interaction is necessary for developing an accurate and reliable predictive model. As an application of this research, a second part explores how to apply and modify this model to account for the effects of parametric variations in FSW processes. Through a combination of simulation and experimental validation using a kN hybrid simulation machine, a third part confirms the model's accuracy and reliability. Consequently, a fourth part verifies the reliability of the model when subjected to increased load and simulated time, up to 10 minutes of welding time, by reapplying the kN simulation conditions. Theoretical predictions for how different particles such as $\eta$ and $\eta'$ mix together has been examined using Clark-Sarantopoulou's approach within the context of mass and flavor symmetry breaking dynamics. Our results show that the ratio of the mixing parameters for $\eta$ and $\eta'$ equals the ratio of the inverse squared masses of these two particles, provided that the strengths of the transition interactions are proportional to the flavor-braking interactions governing their masses. This prediction is in line with experimental values, and gives further impetus to recent studies on the mass and flavor dynamics of these pseudoscalar mesons. The methodology employed is in line with modern theoretical strategies in strong interactions, and is in conformity with the standards of analytical calculations in quantum field theories. Our analysis has also been used to explain various hadronic properties, and has in particular been successfully applied to understand the decay widths of the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ into photons. Additionally, existing graph machine learning methods for privacy are generally isolated from broader graph machine learning applications. To address these challenges, we present the Graph Privacy Advisor, a novel framework that leverages a conditional generative adversarial model to generate graph representations of image nodes from any given image, even those outside of the trained model's dataset. The Graph Privacy Advisor is based on an unsupervised meta-learning approach, starting with pre-trained graph models and adapting them to various privacy graphs in an efficient manner. The advantages of this method are twofold: it enhances existing graph models by simulating diverse node features, and it also enables these models to be used in a broader range of applications, including both graph and image classification tasks. This research introduces an advanced model that estimates pose using single or multiple images along with inaccurate sensor readings from an inertial measurement unit (IMU) embedded in a camera. Unlike existing methods focused solely on individual error simulations, our model incorporates a comprehensive framework for IMU-based camera pose estimation with various types of error, including translational and rotational noise, as well as correlated and uncorrelated factors. This approach is necessary since traditional methods often rely on assumptions of independent and distributed errors, which is uncommon in real-world situations. By interpolating noise parameters from activity levels or direct estimation of the error covariance matrix from historical data, our method outperforms existing techniques and achieves accurate results, even with limited training data. Furthermore, our study demonstrates the integration of real-time noise modeling into optimal control principles associated with the subject's activity level to produce effective pose estimation. Additionally, our model may also utilize intermediate activity levels that are not directly involved, thereby producing reasonable outcomes in challenging scenarios. Our method may be used in a variety of applications, such as human-robot interaction, wearable robotics, human-computer interaction, and implicit input prediction based on body language. To accelerate the generation of binary matrices, the Fisher-Yates shuffle is commonly utilized, yet research has demonstrated that a non-uniform sampling approach can be more efficient, albeit less commonly adopted. This study examines the theoretical sampling efficiency of binary matrices derived from the Fisher-Yates algorithm, both with and without a non-uniform probability distribution. Our analysis shows that when a non-uniform distribution is employed, the average number of samples required to generate a matrix is less than half the number needed when using a uniform distribution. Furthermore, we validate these findings experimentally and investigate the potential for adapting non-uniform sampling to other algorithms. Additionally, we apply an approximate Bayesian inference method to estimate the probability distribution of binary variables. This approach allows for the estimation of a large number of probabilities, outperforming the current state-of-the-art methods in terms of log-likelihood. Our analysis also reveals that the probability distribution is self-similar, possessing similar characteristics at different scales. Building on this understanding, we introduce a new scalable scheme for binary matrix sampling, leveraging the derived probability distribution. Our results indicate that this scheme can generate samples more quickly than existing methods. To facilitate the reproduction of our findings, we provide the code used in our analysis publicly. The code can be accessed via the GitHub repository: https://github.com/achittora/Binary-Matrix-Sampling. Furthermore, the repository includes modifications to the existing library (pybs) to facilitate the sampling of binary matrices and the calculation of probability distributions. https://github.com/achittora/PyBS. Nonlinear coaddition algorithms such as median and clipped-mean are widely used to produce highly accurate science images. However, they have a significant drawback: they preserve the thermal spread function (PSF) and detectability of objects unevenly, depending on their flux. This has made scientists seek alternative nonlinear coaddition methods that maintain a consistent PSF while effectively rejecting outliers. We introduce a new algorithm of weighted clipped mean (WCM) that achieves exactly this. By incorporating a weight calculation procedure based on the Laplace distribution, WCM seamlessly integrates clipped-coefficient calculation and weighted averaging. This ensures a consistent PSF for point sources and a constant detection efficiency across the entire flux range. Our results show WCM to be nearly as efficient as median coaddition in terms of noise reduction, while providing a more stable and reliable PSF. This algorithm has been successfully implemented in the SciPy image processing library. Our findings are validated through a range of synthetic and real images from the VLA radio telescope. This new algorithm will play a crucial role in maintaining a consistent PSF for future legacy surveys like the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST).} }}.

Due to the inherent complexity of cells, accurately identifying and processing them poses a substantial challenge for medical image analysis, particularly in central nervous system research using MRI or CT scans. To tackle this challenge, advanced image analysis techniques must be developed to efficiently identify and correct discrepancies in the detection of cells and their components. Motivated by the impressive performance of deep learning approaches in biomedical image analysis and the potential of generative models in creating realistic, synthetic data, we investigate the creation of synthetic cells via generative models to facilitate correction and validation of detected cells and their components. Focusing on two specific applications - cell tracking and segmentation - we generate realistic cells and track the movement of them and their components over time, as well as create multiple cells under varying conditions. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach, and we make our code and data available to facilitate further research in this area. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to leverage synthetic cells for validating and correcting cell lineage information. Our code and data can be accessed at https://github.com/zhkozak/synthetic_cells. Additionally, the paper provides more detailed information about the used code and data. Alternatively, you can contact the corresponding author at z.kozak@ucl.ac.uk to request access. Despite their effectiveness, there has been limited exploration into the internal dynamics of RNNs in the context of RL.  Previous studies suggested that feature persistence influences task performance in geometric tasks.  However, there is a lack of understanding about how persistence affects subtasks within a single goal-oriented task.  This study aims to investigate the relationship between task performance and feature persistence in multi-objective tasks.  We observed that feature persistence correlates with task performance in our test cases.  Notably, there were instances where optimizing this relationship resulted in efficient task completion.  This led us to speculate that feature persistence serves as a task-relevant intrinsic reward signal.  This hypothesis is further supported by the existence of subtasks that are sensitive to persistence and can learn from associated rewards.  To validate our findings, we analyzed the learned policies and confirmed that they are indeed influenced by the persistence of features.  This research highlights the significant role of feature persistence in multi-objective tasks and suggests its potential as a task-relevant intrinsic reward signal.  Additionally, our study demonstrates the variety of ways persistence impacts task performance and suggests exploring more complex dynamic task designs to fully utilize its potential as a intrinsic reward signal.  Finally, our work emphasizes the importance of investigating the internal dynamics of RNNs through a deeper analysis of learned policies.  This knowledge can be utilized to design high-performance tasks that leverage the dynamic properties of RNNs.  To further our understanding of RNNs, we propose a framework that generates a-biotic tasks optimized for RNN performance, allowing us to explore and confirm our findings in a larger set of experiments.  This framework is based on Geometric Search, a method of searching the task space for the most challenging tasks that extract the full potential of RNNs.  This process is guided by statistical analysis of over 800 RNN configurations and their associated performance profiles. This variant addresses dynamical arrest in semi-implicit models and eliminates unconditioned updates. Building upon previous work, Newtonian ECMC now incorporates a choice of maximum eccentricity tolerance. We enhance this method by integrating optimal orientation rules for eccentric jumps to minimize eccentricity acceptance rates and assess its efficiency through computational costs. These enhancements are likely applicable to other multi-site jump algorithms. We further extend Newtonial ECMC to three-dimensional dipolar models, a complex system characterized by long-range spatial correlations and multi-scale complexity. Despite these challenges, Newtonian ECMC effectively navigates complex energy landscapes, achieving a 10-fold speedup over its predecessor while accurately estimating equilibrium averages and providing a detailed picture of the model's equilibrium state. Specifically, we confirm the existence of quasi-equilibrium distributions corresponding to the initial, extremely slow, and long-ranged correlations at high temperatures. We also demonstrate the accuracy of Newtonian ECMC at simulating long-lasting equilibration trajectories when starting from such quasi-equilibrium configurations, a process that would be impractically time-consuming for event-driven methods. We validate the reliability of Newtonian ECMC by comparing equilibrium autocorrelation functions with analytical predictions. Notably, Newtonian ECMC enables the simulation of a quasi-static trajectory for three-dimensional dipolar models on an extremely long time scale (tens of thousands of hours) and provides a precise prediction of the dynamics of individual particles within the system. Secondly, the method allows for the accurate estimation of long-range spatial correlations in the system by leveraging a combination of quasi-static and equipartition conditions applied to distinct frequency ranges of the dipolar model's fluctuations. Data augmentation has gained significant attention in recent years from researchers working on sound event detection as a means to boost performance without resorting to additional training data. In our study, we take a closer look at the impact of various data augmentation methods used in conjunction with deep learning models. To achieve this, we employed several complex models and evaluated their effectiveness on the DCASE 2019 task 03 dataset, a benchmark for polyphonic sound event detection. Our results indicate that certain combinations of data augmentation methods can enhance model performance, with significant improvements observed in certain instances. Notably, the effectiveness of data augmentation methods appears to be influenced by the architecture of the deep learning model. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the fact that data augmentation methods have a varying effect on different classes within the sound event detection task. This phenomenon was confirmed through the calculation of class-specific false positive rates. The outcomes of this study suggest that data augmentation methods should be carefully selected on a per-class basis. Lastly, the results of our experiment reveal that data augmentation can either enhance or hinder model performance, with a maximum improvement of nearly 8% compared to a baseline model without data augmentation observed in one of the classes. Based on these findings, it is clear that the effect of data augmentation methods on sound event detection tasks is highly class-dependent and potentially dependent on the specific architecture used. This insight can aid researchers in developing effective data augmentation strategies for their particular classification tasks within the sound event detection domain. Additionally, our study provides a comprehensive reference for researchers working in the area of data augmentation for machine listening applications. This article examines the essential characteristics of superposition coding, emphasizing its utility in capturing complex relationships and constraints. In particular, we explore the role of superposition coding in relation to various broadcast channel models, and highlight its potential to enable innovative solutions for complex applications, rather than simply serving as a necessary tool for achieving optimal performance. By understanding the essential properties of superposition coding, we aim to reveal its broader implications and enableings, leading to more efficient and generalized designs. Leveraging this insight, we can apply superposition coding in more straightforward ways, even in cases where more complex structures are not necessary for achieving the best results. By analyzing cluster stability, we develop a set of criteria to determine whether two clusters are stable individually and do not interfere with each other. Utilizing this approach, we successfully determine the number of synchronized clusters in the Mackey-Glass system, a chaotic circuit known for its difficulty in clustering. Moreover, we outline a general framework for other nonlinear systems and provide evidence of the algorithm's robustness against parameter variations. Additionally, we explore the relationship between cluster partitions, demonstrating that different partitions often yield distinct insights into the system's dynamics. Ultimately, we showcase the potential of our method to reveal the underlying structure of complex systems and its applicability to various nonlinear systems. Further study is recommended to establish the computational efficiency of the algorithm. Developed mathematical theory is contrasted with an alternative approach using delay embedding techniques. Our approach is uniquely positioned to analyze coupled complex systems, its effectiveness verified in this context with the case of coupled chaotic oscillators. Lastly, we outline promising avenues for further research. We firmly believe that our method will facilitate the discovery of cluster structures in complex systems and enhance our understanding of their underlying behavioral patterns. The information engine concept has gained significant attention in the quantum community for its potential to harness missing information as a source of energy. Currently, most information engine studies rely on weak measurement techniques despite the fact that continuous measurement is more prevalent in everyday life and can be modeled in quantum systems. This study aims to bridge this gap by exploring the continuous measurement approach as a means of information driving an engine. Specifically, we examine the quantum harmonic oscillator and consider a continuous measurement process that is positive semidefinite, where both its spectrum and duration can be adjusted. Our analysis focuses on the information binomial ME model, which allows for easy calculation of key statistics such as entropy production and current. This model also enables us to examine the speed of information extraction and its influence on energy generation in relation to the stability of the system. Furthermore, we compare its performance with the standard weak drive setup used in prior studies and find that, although it may not outperform them in all situations, continuous measurement can offer a more practical and feasible solution in certain contexts. This research highlights the importance of considering the underlying measurement process in the information engine design for real-world applications. Moreover, the information binomial ME model provides a valuable mathematical tool for handling continuous measurement in quantum systems. Given its straightforward calculations, this model can serve as a bridge for connecting continuous measurement approaches, such as continuous and weak measurement, and may find use in the quantum simulation of mesoscopic systems. Lastly, the continuous measurement scheme proposed here could potentially be emulated in future experiments using ultra-cold atoms. This would not only facilitate the evaluation of our theoretical findings but also enable the implementation of the information engine in the quantum regime. Specifically, we demonstrate the outcome of emulating a positive semidefinite measurement spectrum using a 1D Gaussian potential with a width of $ eta=0.1P$, where $P$ denotes the Planck mass. This particular potential leads to a significant increase in the information extraction rate in comparison with the standard weak drive setup. Importantly, the generated power can exceed the thermodynamic limit by approximately three orders of magnitude. This research investigates the jamming transition in a space constrained by two parallel walls, where disks of varying weights are placed alternately and randomly. Weighted disks were chosen to introduce asymmetry into the system, while alternate placement ensured symmetry in the confining environment. Through extensive simulations, we gathered data on the system's properties near the jamming point, focusing particularly on how weight disparities affect its behavior. Our findings reveal that, contrary to expectations, the system's properties near jamming do not exhibit symmetry breaking, despite the weight disparities. Instead, we discovered that the jamming transition is influenced primarily by disk size, not weight. Our results are consistent with previous theories on the subject, offering a deeper understanding of the system's dynamics. Furthermore, we explored and confirmed the predicted state near jamming, as described in the literature. Lastly, we examined the system's behavior during unjamming and found that the most densely packed structures undergo a transition to less densely packed states through the removal of disks from the system's center. This behavior is observed regardless of the weight of the disks. Our research provides a comprehensive insight into the jamming transition in an asymmetric system, shedding light on its complex and intriguing phenomena. Our findings are relevant and applicable to various processes where jamming occurs, including granular materials and self-assembly processes. Our work opens the door for further research into the unjamming process, aiming to control and manipulate jammed structures and their transition to less densely packed states. This knowledge can be utilized to develop methods for undoing jamming and exploiting its associated instability. This capability has the potential to improve current techniques for controlling jammed structures and may lead to new applications in material science and self-assembly technologies. This research can be extended by analyzing and characterizing the force networks in jammed structures composed of disks of different weights and sizes, placed alternately or randomly. Our previous work has demonstrated that, for identical disks, the jamming transition is accompanied by a significant change in the system's force distribution, leading to a drastic reduction in jammed structure's rigidity with weight. Our current findings suggest that, for weight disparities, this trend may not be present, thus requiring a thorough examination of force networks in asymmetric systems. By studying this system with a combination of theoretical calculations and experimental techniques that measure the behavior of the system at different energies, the properties of the system in its normal and excited states can be determined.

Furthermore, the system can be controlled to exhibit either weak or strong correlations of the electrons through adjusting parameters that affect the energies of the electrons in the system. 

These findings are important because the same system can exhibit two different behaviors, and the transition between these behaviors can be controlled by adjusting the parameters of the system, rather than the parameters of a more complex underlying lattice structure. Instead, the variations in the energies of different orbital states play a key role in determining the system's behavior and its potential for hosting correlated matter. 

In the end, the system can be considered a model for the study of correlated matter, and the behavior of the system can be controlled through adjusting parameters that affect the energies of the electrons in the system, rather than more complex underlying lattice structures. This paper outlines a statistical model-building method that incorporates physical principles, using data from wildfires including smoke and soot, to simulate the scattering of optical signals. The model aims to fill a critical gap in signal distortion modeling, where traditional methods rely on precise wildfire data, including the size, depth, and composition of fires, to accurately predict signal attenuation. Our approach uses data-driven regression analysis to develop an empirical formula for estimating the optical signal's attenuation coefficient, at specific wavelengths, based on smoke and soot particle properties. By comparing the proposed model with a more detailed fire environment simulation, this paper evaluates the accuracy of the statistical model in estimating AOD and AODstar for different smoke and soot compositions. The results indicate the statistical model's average error in estimating AOD and AODstar is around 0.05, with a maximum error of approximately 0.25 in both cases. Our study further demonstrates the statistical model's capability in providing rapid estimates of AOD and AODstar for various smoke and soot combinations, with processing times under a second. Overall, this paper highlights the potential of the statistical model as a suitable alternative to more computationally expensive methods for a wide range of remote sensing applications involving wildfire-related signal attenuation. This study examines how inter-site variability affects the propagation of differences in brain networks across groups. We analyzed a large, $n=1,246$ subject dataset from the Human Connectome Project with fMRI data and estimated functional brain networks. These networks were compared across individual subjects and we adjusted for age, sex, and handedness. Our analysis reveals that although we could reliably detect group differences in network properties for many nodes, there was significant variability between HCP scanning sessions. We found that sites with high inter-site variability or small propagation spreads were less reliable in detecting group differences and often showed distorted individual brain network connectivity patterns. These findings suggest that considering inter-site variability is essential for accurate detection of differences in brain networks and consistent results. We have provided open-source code to replicate our study's results. Our data analysis framework can be used to investigate the reliability of brain connectivity patterns in large datasets and we have applied it to the study of brain networks. Our study's findings emphasize the need to consider inter-site variability for consistent conclusions in the analysis of large datasets. In evolutionary studies, researchers often focus on the average impact of gene replacements or substitutions on overall fitness or characteristics.  This average value is typically insufficient for determining a comprehensive understanding of those changes.  Using only mean values fails to provide information about the distribution of effects and whether certain gene substitutions have a greater impact than others.  Although this limitation has been acknowledged, a more in-depth examination of higher-order moments is needed to address it.  We conducted an exhaustive analysis of the various moments of effect distributions and found that the structure of evolutionary data along selective gradients can give insight into how selection influences the evolution of traits and the rate of substitutions over time.  We applied our findings to widely used data sets and observed unique patterns in the distribution of effects for different types of genes, including those associated with gene expression levels, discrete traits, and non-coding regions.  We also developed new statistical methods that combine information across different moments to identify artificial intelligence models and uncover underlying patterns in data.  Through our comprehensive analysis, we found that the distribution of effects is more extensive and varied than previously estimated and provided more precise and accurate information about the evolution of traits and selection pressures compared to earlier studies that relied solely on mean values.  These novel approaches can be applied to various genomic data sets to uncover additional insights into how selection influences the rate and distribution of gene substitutions.  Ultimately, our research highlights the untapped potential for analyzing higher-order moments in evolutionary studies and suggests new directions for investigations into the mechanics of evolution and the distribution of effects. A crucial aspect of bipedal locomotion is the periodic nature of movement, which allows large strides to be achieved while maintaining stability. The complexity arises from the initial and final points of the step being different, making it challenging to capitalize on the energy generated during each stride. Our solution involves leveraging feedback loops in the gait patterns of bipedal robots, enabling them to utilize the energy produced during each step and transfer it into the subsequent one. The effectiveness of this approach has been simulated using a model developed in Modo and validated through experiments conducted both in simulation and physically with a specialized robot called Redrobot. The results demonstrate that this method leads to a more efficient and sustainable walking pattern for bipedal robots. The associated code can be accessed at: https://github.com/mcms-eth/BipedalRobot_Gait_Synchronization. Our research outlines a novel technique to optimize bipedal locomotion, aiming to resolve the challenge of catapult-like gait patterns and facilitate more realistic and sustainable movements in bipedal robots. The proposed strategy relies on closed-loop feedback to transform the energy produced during each step into the subsequent ones. Initially tested through a simplified model and validated both physically and numerically, this approach has shown promising results and can be accessed via the associated code at: https://github.com/mcms-eth/BipedalRobot_Gait_Synchronization. Future plans include integrating this technique into Redrobot's existing gait controllers and exploring its applicability across multiple gaits. The expected outcome is that Redrobot will be capable of generating more realistic movements, as evident in human locomotion. The proposed technique has the potential to improve current bipedal robots, enabling them to achieve greater stability and efficiency in their gait patterns. The integration of this novel strategy is expected to significantly enhance the performance of Redrobot, enabling it to generate more realistic movements, akin to human locomotion. In this study, we explore the limitations of the independent learning model in the decentralized setting under the control of parameter and data mechanisms. We identify that the model relies heavily on assumptions regarding network connectivity and data distribution among nodes, assumptions regarding the number of rounds and data available, and is highly susceptible to interference from external factors. In response to these concerns, we introduce a semi-supervised and client-personalized approach to the federated learning process. Our approach ensures that each node receives tailored weights and data labels, breaking the dependency on network connectivity and data distribution. Our results demonstrate that the new framework surpasses the independent learning model in both efficiency and performance, with reductions of up to $80\%$ in communication costs and increased classification accuracy of up to $12\%$ in relevant datasets. Our approach also outperforms other existing decentralized learning models by at least $26\%$ in terms of communication costs and achieves higher accuracy in $80\%$ of local datasets with only $20\%$ of the independent learning rounds. Our key contribution lies in developing a personalized semi-supervised learning model and thoroughly evaluating its effectiveness and performance in comparison to independent learning. Emergency departments are facing significant pressures with high volumes of patients and short treatment times, leading to increased referrals for further treatment. Studies have examined the impact of treating patients for a longer period on ED return visits and readmissions within thirty days, revealing that extending treatment by half an hour or one hour does not substantially influence these outcomes. However, the optimal duration of treatment is not yet clear. To address this, a study was conducted using over 1.5 million patient visits and 2,500 treating physicians in the United States, aiming to provide insights into how treatment duration affects ED returns and readmissions within thirty days. By incorporating a key variation where increasing treatment time by thirty minutes resulted in lower 30-day revisit and readmission rates, controlling for patient symptoms and medical necessities, providing policymakers and healthcare professionals with a practical reference point for optimizing treatment lengths and improving patient outcomes. In cooperative systems, agents often make decisions based on their current task load and the benefits they can still gain from working. A key factor influencing these decisions is how challenging their current tasks are. To explore this, we created a simulator where agents voluntarily take on new tasks of varying difficulties, aiming to contribute up to a maximum amount to their community. Tasks have a limited lifespan and require a certain amount of work from the agents who've taken them. Those who complete their tasks efficiently can still work on new ones, while those who've struggled might focus on finishing their existing tasks. We found that a mixture of easy and hard tasks among the agents led to a balance where each took on new tasks at the right pace, resulting in a community where everyone worked at an optimal rate in the long term, regardless of their previous performance. This phenomenon persists even with large numbers of agents and varied task distributions. It suggests that a natural, self-regulating system can develop its own set of rules and achieve a collective good. We've confirmed our simulation's results through statistical tests and shared the code to allow for further exploration and validation. This research offers a new twist on a well-studied problem, contributing to our understanding of how complex systems behave and how their components can work together towards a common goal. It may also help scientists and practitioners studying and observing similar phenomena in the natural world. However, sharing network traffic data with sensitive information poses significant security risks, necessitating innovative solutions. A potential answer lies in the federated learning framework that combines AI-powered intrusion detection and privacy protection. Nonetheless, the federated learning framework's efficiency can be hindered by several challenges. To address these limitations, we developed FL-Intrusion, the first federated learning-based solution for network intrusion detection, allowing organizations to collaborate securely. Moreover, we established a collaborative framework for testing and training, enabling the development of scalable, distributed systems capable of handling a large volume of network traffic. Through comprehensive evaluation using three intrusion detection datasets, we validated the effectiveness of FL-Intrusion in delivering accurate intrusion detection and improving model robustness, despite data privacy preservation. Notably, our results showed that FL-Intrusion excelled over traditional learning approaches, achieving higher AUC scores on the NSLKDD dataset and comparable performance on larger scale datasets, including ImpliedMemory and UNSW-NB15. Furthermore, the research contributions from this work have potential applications in other network-based learning tasks, such as network traffic classification. In addition to its technical significance, our work has valuable implications for real-world implementation, highlighting the potential of federated learning to revolutionize the development of scalable, private intrusion detection systems, and showcasing a viable technology for organizations to collaborate securely and drive industry innovation, thereby paving the way for the broader adoption of federated learning in real-world applications. Ultimately, the architectural framework of FL-Intrusion can be tailored to other network-based learning tasks by adjusting the types of local and central models, selection methods, and evaluation metrics, as demonstrated by the ImpliedMemory evaluation example. The performance of semiconductor devices is heavily influenced by the materials used in the gate, and achieving optimal results often necessitates experimenting with various gate materials.  However, investigating the effects of gate materials in the absence of device modifications has been impractical, until the advent of 3D nanoelectromechanical systems.  We have introduced an innovative method to study gate materials without altering the underlying device architecture.  Utilizing a three-dimensional nanomanufacturing technique, we have developed a system comprising a planar gate and a suspended gate on a field effect transistor.  An electrostatic force enables the adjustment of both transducer and gate a distance above the device surface.  Experimental findings indicate that increasing the transducer gap height reduces the threshold voltage and optimal voltage, and these effects are most pronounced when using air as the gate material.  Numerical simulations reveal that these observations are attributed to reduced tunneling resistance and capacitance in the presence of air.  Notably, air yields better results than alternative gate materials like metal or graphene, and we attribute this to the interplay between resistance and capacitance.  The discovery highlights the potential for improving semiconductor performance through gate material optimization.  Furthermore, this study contributes to the development of a more detailed tunneling model by incorporating quantum confinement, tunneling, and dielectric leakage.  The proposed tunneling model is found to be in excellent agreement with experimental results, and it may be utilized to gauge the existing surface passivation in operational devices.  The underlying technology has the potential to enable material parameter optimization, and its applications extend beyond gate materials to the study of alternative channel materials and surface treatments.  The novel 3D NEMS gate material transducer has been found to be durable against mechanical stresses, and it may be employed in the investigation of material stresses, surface roughness, and adhesion forces.  The evidence presented suggests a new level of understanding of the electrostatic force, and it may be utilized in the development of sensitive force sensors, surface force measurement systems, and variable couplings in micromechanical niches.  The findings of this study indicate that the gate material transducer can be operated at both low-frequency and high-frequency conditions to investigate various surface phenomena, and it may be deployed in the measurement of surface charges, surface potential, and chemical etching.  The evidence suggests the potential of this transducer in measuring the chemical properties of surface materials, and it may be utilized in the detection of molecular imbalances, chemical field effects, and chemical binding forces.

We investigate how group synchronization in networks of oscillators is affected by minor system deviations and the presence of antagonistic dynamics. In many synchronized groups, a single oscillator stands out as a leader. When we introduce small variations in system parameters and examine the stability of group synchronization, our results show that the outcome depends on the relationship between this leader oscillator and the rest of the group. If the leader interacts extensively with other oscillators, even slight deviations will eventually cause the group to unsynchronize. Conversely, if the leader has minimal interactions with other oscillators, group synchronization will remain stable even with considerable parameter fluctuations. To illustrate these findings, we focus on a specific model of coupled oscillators representing the dynamics of a laser system. We then explore the broader implications of our findings for understanding how synchronized groups function and maintain stability. Lastly, we examine the opposite scenario in which a synchronized group undergoes antagonistic dynamics; interestingly, this can give rise to innovative and stable phenomena. For example, in a laser system, we demonstrate how two synchronized lasers can be maintained even with opposing dynamics by introducing a small deviation in one of the lasers. Conversely, if the deviation is introduced into both lasers, group synchronization will eventually collapse, leading them out of sync. Building on this example, we hypothesize that this phenomenon may occur widely across different types of oscillator networks. To delve deeper into this hypothesis, we conducted additional experiments involving different types of oscillator networks and found that it holds true for at least one more case, as seen in a group of van der Pol oscillators. To summarize, our findings indicate the following. Firstly, group synchronization will remain stable with minor system deviations and extensive interactions between a key leader oscillator and the rest of the group. Secondly, if the leader oscillator has minimal interactions with other oscillators, group synchronization will remain stable even with considerable parameter fluctuations. Lastly, group stability can also be achieved through antagonistic dynamics, resulting in innovative and stable phenomena in the group, as exemplified by our studies on laser and oscillator networks. To further explore this hypothesis, we propose a broader investigation into its applicability across different types of oscillator systems and encourage researchers to continue examining this intriguing phenomenon. To facilitate this effort, we provide a simple and reliable method for inducing the synchronized group to undergo antagonistic dynamics and encourage the exploration of additional examples and applications of this phenomenon. Ultimately, our long-term goal is to understand how the synchronized groups of oscillators achieve and maintain stability, relying on inherent mechanisms of interaction and communication between the oscillators and their components. for video distributors, particularly in view of emerging alternatives like Yandex Video.

Under various levels of delay, from instantaneous to significantly lag behind, we examine how the network converges to a singular time. Semi-supervised node classification in graph neural networks is a crucial task that has seen considerable progress with the integration of pseudo-labeling techniques. These methods have allowed limited training data to be expanded into a larger, fully-labeled set of nodes, leading to improved performance. Pseudo-labeling methods achieve this by estimating node labels without relying on ground truth, which can sometimes result in inaccurate labels influencing the model's training and decreasing its effectiveness. In this study, we examine how pseudo-labeling methods impact GNNs and propose a novel method called Node Confidence-based Pseudo-Labeling (NCPL). NCPL adjusts the model's training by incorporating node confidence into pseudo-label assignment, thereby mitigating previous issues. Our results show NCPL outperforms traditional pseudo-labeling techniques and serve as a foundation for enhancing GNN-based node classification methods. Our code is accessible on GitHub at the address https://github.com/QianStudy/NCPL. Additionally, the employed GraphNN models can be found in the nearby repository https://github.com/QianStudy/GraphNN-Node-Classification. Our analysis led to two notable outcomes: Firstly, it yielded an analytical expression for the multi-point, multi-time distribution, expressed as a sum of products of positive Fourier coefficients. Furthermore, it demonstrated how initial conditions influence this distribution, resulting in distinct forms for positive and negative coefficients. Notably, when the initial conditions are entirely positive or entirely negative, many of these coefficients become zero, simplifying the distribution. Consequently, under completely positive or completely negative initial conditions, we derived a closed-form expression for the multi-point, multi-time distribution, thereby extending the findings of [Bertini, Giacomin, Olla, and Velfre, 2019]. The field of view of its distance sensor is limited, which causes it to only detect the wall within a certain range and not beyond that point. Previous studies have tested the reliability of proof generation by comparing human-created proofs with artificially generated ones, yet there is no established review process for verifying the correctness of a larger-scale proof. This paper proposes a scaleable review process that leverages advanced natural language processing techniques to evaluate the accuracy of a systematically minimized and linguistically normalized proof. By applying machine learning and semantic analysis to extracted phrases and their contextual connections, we have developed a classification system that effectively distinguishes correct from incorrect reasoning processes. We have demonstrated the efficacy of our approach through an experiment involving both a human-based evaluation of 50 proofs and an automated assessment of a dataset of 1,111 artificially generated proofs. Ultimately, the accuracy of the machine-learning classifier matched that of human reviewers, suggesting that our proposed method offers a practical solution for verifying the reliability of generated proofs and paving the way for the trustworthy deployment of AI-driven automated reasoning. In the future, we intend to expand our technique to cover a broader range of mathematical content and scale up the complexity of the proof structures. This article introduces Proto-Quipper-M, a higher-order functional programming language designed for quantum circuit-based quantum computing. The cloning, deleting, and mixing of quantum states are prohibited in Proto-Quipper-M to ensure its quantum embeddedness. The absence of cloning is enforced through type inference, while a novel technique based on passive property preservation is used to ensure the absence of deleting and mixing. We investigate the rank lasso problem in high dimensions and introduce an efficient algorithm that reframes rank lasso as a series of smaller problems through adaptive sieving. This approach reduces computational complexity from $O(p^3)$ to $O(p^2)$ in the worst case, while maintaining the ability to handle up to $p$ blocks of features. Each iteration involves selecting a block, solving a smaller rank lasso problem for that block, and assessing its relevance through a transitivity test driven by our new block-best orthogonal approximation property. We further derive bounds on the number of iterations required to reach an optimal solution within an acceptable tolerance. Empirical evidence supports our theoretical findings, demonstrating the algorithm's superior performance over existing methods in both speed and accuracy. Notably, when all blocks are included, our algorithm converges to the optimal solution, according to our analysis. We develop a faster first-order interior-point method to optimize the reduced problems and propose several strategies to accelerate the sieving process. We also introduce a randomized version of our algorithm for further performance enhancements. We conduct extensive experiments on artificial and real-world datasets, comparing our approach to existing methods such as block-wise coordinate descent, block-nuclear norm non-convex optimization, and the original rank lasso algorithm. The numerical results confirm our theoretical predictions and highlight the adaptive-sieving-based algorithm's superior scalability and efficiency. Based on these findings, we propose a heuristic that combines our algorithm with block-wise coordinate descent to potentially achieve better trade-offs between computational speed and solution quality. We validate this heuristic through experiments and observe improvements in both its speed and solution quality. We estimate that our heuristic yields an average reduction of $8.8\%$ in processing time over block-wise coordinate descent. We also evaluate the heuristic on the problems of multiblock multi-antenna bidirectional networks and joint rank lasso, utilizing real-world datasets and modifying these problems to incorporate the block-best orthogonal approximation property. The results demonstrate the heuristic's ability to reach an optimal solution within an acceptable tolerance for the multiblock multi-antenna bidirectional networks problem, while yielding a solution that meets the required criteria for joint rank lasso. We anticipate our work to serve as a foundation for future research in this domain and hope the numerical evidence to support our theoretical analysis will aid researchers in enhancing the performance of rank lasso algorithms. We intend to pursue the following avenues for further research: developing a faster first-order method to optimize the reduced problems; creating new optimization techniques by combining our algorithm with existing rank lasso methods

As Artificial Intelligence becomes increasingly ubiquitous in daily life and business, its environmental footprint is growing and warrants examination. Although prior studies have studied the environmental impact of AI, they often lack a comprehensive framework that considers the entire lifecycle of AI systems, including production, use, and disposal. In this study, a novel method based on Life Cycle Assessment is proposed to evaluate the environmental effects of AI services. The development of a comprehensive inventory analysis model, dubbed the Artificial Intelligence LCA model, is presented. Then, the methodology is demonstrated in a case study of conventional Photo Sketching AI services. The results show that AI services' environmental impacts stem primarily from the production stage, where the generation of methane and carbon dioxide are of particular concern. The findings of this research can be utilized to develop strategies for minimizing the environmental impact of AI services. Based on the analysis, recommendations are provided to mitigate the environmental impact of PSB, PS, and Face Sketching AI services. These recommendations involve implementing process-level improvements to reduce green energy usage, optimize resource allocation, and enhance model quality. Ultimately, the life cycle perspective is advocated for AI service design to facilitate the development of more sustainable AI systems. Furthermore, the proposed methodology is versatile and can be applied to various AI services with merely a substitution of inventory analysis data. The expected outcomes are (i) enhanced sustainability features for AI services, (ii) a decrease in AI-related greenhouse gas emissions, (iii) accelerated adoption of more energy-efficient AI technologies, and (iv) a reduction in AI-related e-waste through improved design. The next steps for this research involve evaluating various AI applications and comparing their environmental impacts using the proposed LCA model. Then, the findings will be utilized to recommend areas for LCA improvement and open-source AI libraries that promote environmental sustainability. The primary goal of process monitoring is to provide early warning signals for potential issues and prevent problems. While many studies have explored predictive methods, there is a notable lack of research on verifying their effectiveness in real-world settings. This study addresses this gap by examining the practical application of two predictive methods for process monitoring: (1) predictive control based on predictive models and (2) real-time predictive modeling. We selected and modified these methods according to common practices in the literature, then tested them on actual process data from a production planning case study. To evaluate their performance, we used multiple metrics and varied the modeling parameters. Our results indicate that both methods can facilitate early identification of deviations from standard behavior and protect against unnecessary interventions associated with false positives. Nonetheless, a real-time predictive model exhibited better performance in several aspects, including better deviation detection, fewer false positives, and easier adaptation for decision-support systems. This case study offers practical insights for process monitoring and highlights potential areas for improving predictive control methods. Moreover, this research demonstrates how predictive modeling can be utilized for process monitoring and highlights its potential for supporting decision-making in the specific production planning scenario. Based on these findings, we propose future research directions. We also provide an open-source implementation of the method to facilitate replication and further investigation. Additionally, we present several opportunities for additional contributions that could help apply prescriptive process monitoring methods in various contexts and domains. We encourage researchers to utilize our study as a benchmark for comparing novel approaches to process monitoring, and we offer our knowledge and experience to aid in the development of effective methods for identifying and resolving process issues. We intend for this research to serve as a foundation for future studies and evaluations, and we hope it to be a useful reference for both theoretical and practical assessments of process monitoring methods. We plan to continue working on this topic by exploring predictive control methods based on machine learning, such as multi-class classification, feature extraction, and regression, with the aim of improving current process monitoring techniques, adapting them to fit practical applications, and incorporating them into a decision-support system for managing and interpreting process data. We look forward to contributing to the process community's ongoing efforts to apply theoretical methods in real-world settings and promoting the effective use of process monitoring methods in actual processes. The process of converting transcribed DNA into functional mRNA involves a complex interplay of delays, transportation times, and processing times along the RNA chain. A new model, built from fundamental principles of DNA transcription, AT-rich regions in gene bodies, and RNA processing patterns in budding yeast, reveals how various delays and times contribute to the development of mature mRNA. The model shows that the length of a gene significantly influences the time between transcription completion and mature mRNA production, largely due to the effects of delays on RNA maturation increasing with gene length. Moreover, analysis of multiple factors indicates that changes in transcription and RNA production are closely linked across different genes and show a strong correlation with delays and times. The integrated framework offers a straightforward method for examining the temporal dynamics of RNA processing and transcription across entire gene sets, revealing previously unseen relationships, such as the positive correlation between delays related to RNA processing and the frequency of specific RNA processing elements within genes. The framework also enables the exploration of possible mechanisms underlying RNA processing and the investigation of how factors influencing delays and times are linked to alterations in RNA production and transcription. As such, it can be applied to the examination of RNA processing in other species by means of homology to budding yeast. We investigate how Bucket Elimination, a dynamic programming method, can be applied to graphical models with arbitrary variables. By integrating Bucket Elimination into existing algorithms, such as Belief Propagation and Maximum a Posteriori, we develop enhanced versions: Belief Propagation with Bucket Elimination and Maximum a Posteriori with Bucket Elimination. The former technique accelerates each iteration by leveraging local approximations and cutting knowledge, while the latter adds a optimization layer after finding a temporary solution. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of these methods in both simulated and real-world scenarios, frequently outperforming the standard versions. The analysis suggests that Belief Propagation with Bucket Elimination tends to speed up the process, often achieving a constant factor speedup, and may also provide a regular path for subsequent layers, facilitating higher average performance. In contrast, Maximum a Posteriori with Bucket Elimination typically achieves a significant speedup in some instances, occasionally resulting in lower overall performance due to the temporary nature of the approximations. The research aims to provide a foundation for further applications of Bucket Elimination in graphical models. The proposed methods are implemented in the open-source C++ package BMEst: https://github.com/ivanlele/BMEst. We demonstrate the empirical effectiveness of Belief Propagation with Bucket Elimination and Maximum a Posteriori with Bucket Elimination, which can be potentially applied in realistic scenarios, specifically on treewidth-three graphs, which commonly model realistic problems efficiently. We also present a preliminary analysis on general graphical models, suggesting possible speedups, which could be achieved by introducing minor adjustments. The key restriction of Belief Propagation with Bucket Elimination is the need for narrow local functions, which can be overcome, as shown in the experimental results, by using an alternative model. For Maximum a Posteriori with Bucket Elimination, the challenge of narrow local functions is more fundamental and difficult to overcome, suggesting the requirement of a more in-depth reformulation. The concepts of isotropic jamming and shear jamming cover a broad range of systems that experience a sudden transition from fluid to solid behavior. However, research so far has indicated that the characteristics of these transitions differ in terms of their critical properties. Building on earlier work, our research introduces a theoretical framework that explains the varying exponents in both types of jamming transitions through a dependence on a specific parameter representing friction. By applying this framework to spherical particles in both two-dimensional and three-dimensional systems, our analysis shows that a particular combination of exponents is universal for frictionless jamming, whereas a different combination is universal for shear jamming with friction. When these predictions are compared with existing numerical simulations, our results are found to be in agreement with previous findings. Furthermore, our study provides Jamming Theorems for both types of jamming transitions, and suggests potential directions for future research. Ultimately, our work offers a deeper understanding of the underlying causes of the distinct critical properties observed in isotropic and shear jamming transitions. Additionally, our study also provides a link between the concept of jamming and the broader applicability of phase transitions in material science. It integrates an AR(4) autoregressive component with two latent variables to capture dynamic patterns and outliers across four-hour time intervals. By doing so, this model surpasses the performance of the standard AR(4) model in both forecasting and outlier detection tasks, as evidenced by US3hr and WADE datasets tests. Furthermore, the advantages of MS(2)-AR(4) are most evident when analyzing times series with straightforward dynamics and minimal signal complexity. Public sector professionals require knowledge of potential algorithmic biases present in Web search results to ensure fairness in their decisions.
