A key challenge in radiation therapy is accurately delivering X-ray beams in line with the disease's shape and position each day. Daily image-guided radiation therapy uses imaging data to adjust X-ray beam positions, yet this process is time-consuming due to the necessity of aligning beams in straight lines. We propose an approach for optimizing X-ray beam positions and weights to enhance treatment efficiency without compromising accuracy. Our technique aims to minimize the total treatment time by allowing multiple X-ray beams to be directed from the same position at specific angles, which can be calculated using cone beam radiation therapy planning algorithms. To demonstrate the potential benefits, we compared standard linear X-ray beam treatment with our approach using cone beam radiation therapy for patients undergoing treatment. Our results indicate a significant reduction in treatment time can be achieved without compromising tumor coverage, which will be verified clinically through a randomized controlled trial. We also provide an open-source treatment planning software for other researchers to validate our findings. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to various radiation therapy modalities beyond X-ray, such as proton therapy, to improve treatment flexibility and reduce patient discomfort. By potentially reducing treatment time from several minutes to a few seconds, our technique has the potential to make a significant clinical impact on over 1 million patients treated with radiation therapy each year in the United States. Ultimately, the goal is to improve patient quality of life by minimizing their daily visit to the treatment center. Our approach can potentially reduce the required number of visits from 29 to 5 days, which is a promising development. Our study's findings demonstrate the feasibility and efficiency of our treatment planning method, which will be validated clinically through a randomized controlled trial. In the context of option learning models, where agents navigate multiple states to achieve goals, we investigate a scenario with multiple interacting components. We demonstrate that a well-designed memory system enables agents to effectively track unobserved states and make accurate predictions from partial observations. Furthermore, our findings reveal that dynamic memory systems offer advantages over static systems, enabling agents to adapt to changing conditions. We develop a specific memory architecture and a corresponding loss function to maximize reward returns, as well as evaluating its performance in comparison to alternative methods. Our study is based on a sequence prediction task from the field of molecular simulation, where agents need to track the behavior of multiple molecular interactions to predict their future states. The cognitive diversity of cognitive batteries is tested using a range of tasks 
that challenge various aspects of brain function, and its results can be used to 
predict genetic and phenotypic information. Existing cognitive batteries are 
limited by the type of tasks they include, which are primarily easy to solve 
and require basic knowledge of computer science. To expand the potential 
of these batteries in identifying hidden biologic signals, we introduce a set 
of more complex tasks, known as Mod-Cog, which are designed to solve moderate 
problems using moderate techniques. The diversity of Mod-Cog tasks is greater 
than that of existing batteries by an order of magnitude, and its performance 
can be predicted with high accuracy using artificial neural networks. To verify 
the effectiveness of Mod-Cog, we studied the performance of individual and 
group solvers, and found that both human and machine problem-solvers, working 
alone or together, can demonstrate significant cognitive abilities, such as 
attention, that are difficult to fake. Notably, these complex cognitive 
characteristics are often associated with serious psychiatric and cognitive 
conditions, and our study highlights the potential of these batteries in 
identifying pathologic signs and predicting the impact of treatment. The 
availability of Mod-Cog tasks, code, and data enables the replication of our 
results and the development of new, advanced cognitive tasks. The ongoing 
cognitive race between humans and machines will soon be taking a new turn, 
where the distinction between humans and machines will no longer be clear-cut, 
and our study invites participants to take part in this exciting new chapter 
in the history of cognitive tasks. To join the fun, visit our website at https://modcog.com. 
Our mission is to make cognitive tasks more diverse, accessible, and interesting 
for everyone, and to use them to improve people's lives around the world. To 
achieve this goal, we are launching a call for action to our community, and to 
all solvers, to take part in developing new, complex tasks, and to help us 
identify the cognitive and phenotypic characteristics embedded in their solutions. 
Together, we can create a rich collection of cognitive tasks that will drive 
significant scientific progress, and will make a meaningful difference in people's 
lives, while setting a new standard for what it means to be intelligent.

This paper delves into a novel proposal for large-scale jet formation in Minkowski jets originating from BL Lacertae objects. It suggests that inverse Compton interactions between relativistic electrons and background photons could provide the necessary energy to produce high-energy radiation observed in these jets on large scales. Our theoretical framework is based on a collisionless process, not dynamic jet interactions, offering a new, persistent mechanism for continuous energy feedback into Minkowski jets. We propose that this energy feedback, steady and persistent, could be responsible for the illumination of large-scale jets and may also contribute to the acceleration of relativistic particles within these jets, in addition to powering the infra-red and sub-mm emission observed in some Minkowski jets. However, not all large-scale jets exhibit this emission, implying that another mechanism must be at play to account for the dust emission in many Minkowski jets, consistent with a broader phenomenon observed in larger-scale structures within and around galaxies. We hypothesize that the Inverse Compton process could also be the primary driver of this phenomenon, which we will investigate further in a future study. We note that our proposal is compatible with existing theories of BL Lacertae objects and jet formation, specifically the "rocket theory", "ballistic motion", and magnetohydrodynamic equations. We do, however, argue that our inverse Compton model offers a more straightforward and stable solution to large-scale jet formation, as it eliminates the need to explain the global pressure and dynamic interactions of jet feedback. We conclude that large-scale jet formation remains an enigmatic phenomenon, perhaps requiring multiple mechanisms to explain its complexity. We acknowledge some ambiguities in our analysis and welcome further comments and insights from colleagues. We also emphasize that our study is intended to contribute to our understanding of large-scale jet formation, rather than provide a comprehensive explanation for Minkowski jets and related astrophysical phenomena. We look forward to continuing our investigation of large-scale jet formation in future studies. We intend to examine particle acceleration more closely in a future future study, where we will investigate the role of relativistic particles in large-scale jet formation. We will examine the theoretical framework of our inverse Compton model more closely in a future paper, where we will delve into the technical details of our analysis. The SIFT algorithm identifies distinctive features in probe and reference images, while CPD uses complex data representations to capture complex relationships between images. In our approach, SIFT features are combined with CPD to ensure a thorough understanding of image features and their interconnections. The effectiveness of SIFT-CPD is demonstrated through registration of CT, MRI, and histology images, which shows improved results over existing state-of-the-art techniques. Specifically, SIFT-CPD outperforms existing methods in registering images with distinct structures and intensity levels. The proposed algorithm successfully handles diverse medical images and showcases its potential in computer vision and medical imaging applications. Developing deep learning models for analyzing complex time-series data is difficult, primarily because there's a severe lack of accurately labeled training data. Existing solutions often rely on over-simplified representations, but these models struggle with new, unseen data. To address this challenge, we've created TCube, a novel system that combines a diverse set of artificial data generations with a specialized neural network capable of identifying rare classes. TCube enhances the quality of generated data and improves the robustness of classification models by emulating various aspects of real data distribution. Additionally, TCube incorporates an innovative data augmentation technique that mimics the effects of domain experts' manual modifications. Our experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate TCube's ability to significantly boost the performance of baseline classification models. Furthermore, our study highlights the benefits of artificial data and data augmentation in time-series analysis, and shows that TCube can effectively replace traditional data augmentation methods. This research investigates solutions to hyperbolic equations in a smooth manifold's phase space, equipped with a metric that's not necessarily smooth. The study also considers how solutions to these equations decay as time approaches infinity, especially in cases where initial conditions have restricted support. The analysis involves constructing a suitable Hamiltonian operator whose symbolic properties align with those of a symbol associated with the equation's principal symbol. The work also explores the impact of the phase space's singularity on the loss of solution smoothness. One of the key findings is that for certain non-smooth metrics, solutions can exhibit singularities, even when initial conditions have compact support within a bounded domain. The result is that solutions may become discontinuous, even in relatively controlled environments. This study examines the effectiveness of LSTM in enhancing Japanese word segmentation using basic models, aiming to replace traditional HMM-based methods. Our results indicate that LSTM outperforms HMM in Japanese word segmentation, as supported by multiple evaluation metrics. Furthermore, to minimize computational costs, we implemented a compressed LSTM model, incorporating a unit representation with a reduced size of 64, while maintaining comparable performance. Our findings demonstrate that this compressed LSTM model yields high accuracy in Japanese word segmentation, suggesting its potential as a mobile application for real-time Japanese word recognition and segmentation. Specifically, our test on 10,000 Japanese characters revealed an average processing speed of 13.4 milliseconds per character. Therefore, we propose that the compressed LSTM model be utilized in Japanese word segmentation systems, particularly for mobile platforms where processing speed is a crucial consideration. In addition to its potential for mobile applications, we believe this model can be employed in speech recognition and synthesis for Japanese language. However, due to the limitations of model size and computational complexity, its applications in certain Natural Language Processing tasks remain doubtful. Ultimately, our study contributes the compressed LSTM model, an advanced Japanese word segmentation technique, with the hope of inspiring further enhancements. Specifically, we anticipate that the leverage of character-level linguistic information and the incorporation of sentence-level linguistic information in Japanese, akin to that available for English, could lead to improved modeling efficiency and enhanced performance in Japanese word segmentation. If successful, this could pave the way for the application of LSTM in HMM-based models. Conversely, this boost in performance may result in significantly increased computational costs and larger model sizes, necessitating further refinement to balance linguistic information and system resource constraints. Nonetheless, we maintain that exploring sentence-level linguistic information in Japanese using LSTM models remains a promising area of research and development. Our study offers a comprehensive comparison of the HMM and LSTM approaches in Japanese word segmentation, highlighting their respective advantages and limitations. Notably, our results suggest that the basic LSTM model, devoid of any sentence-level linguistic information, already surpasses the performance of HMM, an observation deserving of further scrutiny in the context of related works. To mitigate the risk of overfitting, we employed regularization techniques, including dropout and a modified LSTM model with reduced depth, thereby confirming the robustness of our findings. Furthermore, our study confirms the effectiveness of character-level linguistic information in Japanese, a notion previously reported by Nakagawa et al. We now extend their work, demonstrating that the integration of sentence-level linguistic information in Japanese can yield enhanced word segmentation accuracy, a phenomenon not previously reported

Despite the vast knowledge stored in Stack Overflow, users repeatedly share the same external resources to answer questions, rather than creating new answers or asking for existing ones. To understand why this happens, we analyzed 1.5 million valid edits from high-reputation users on Stack Overflow and found that links to coding tutorials and libraries were the most frequently shared external resources. However, due to concerns about maintenance and copyright issues, these links often become outdated or invalid. We aim to address this problem by identifying the patterns in the metadata of the shared resources, including title patterns, and demonstrating how these patterns can be used to establish resource relationships, even when URLs change. We also developed an approach to detect and handle cases where resource metadata changes over time. The findings represent a crucial first step towards developing automatic mechanisms for maintaining and updating broken links on Stack Overflow and similar knowledge-sharing platforms. To further explore this area, we plan to look into creating a systematic process for validating the metadata of shared resources, comparing different methods of extracting and analyzing the metadata, and investigating how to effectively communicate changes to resource metadata to users. Additionally, we plan to examine the potential of integrating Stack Overflow with services such as GitHub and GitLab to leverage their API-powered maintenance capabilities. To identify symptoms in medical images accurately, the same class label can be assigned to similar symptom categories. This shared-labeling approach facilitates training machine learning models that generalize well across domains. Furthermore, using domain generalization techniques enhances the model's robustness to unforeseen domains. In our research, we leverage domain generalization to enhance symptom extraction in medical images. To achieve this, we propose an innovative architecture that integrates an attention mechanism within the ResNet model. The attention mechanism allows the model to focus on relevant features globally, and then local attention is applied to extract local characteristics. The combined features are then fed into a classification layer. Experiments were conducted on the iDOS dataset and our SymSym dataset. The results reveal that our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on both datasets. Moreover, by incorporating domain generalization techniques, our method demonstrates enhanced performance compared to conventional transfer learning methods. Consequently, our approach demonstrates significant potential in extracting symptoms from medical images accurately and reliably. Autonomous driving systems rely heavily on Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to navigate partially observable environments by making informed decisions based on past experiences and current inputs. Despite their effectiveness, RRLs are prone to overfitting in systems similar to Atari games, where raw pixel data is used as input. To address this, extensive data must be collected, which can be costly and impractical for autonomous driving. To overcome these challenges, we developed AutoFocus, an innovative training method that maintains the strengths of RRLs while mitigating overfitting through targeted focus shifts within the visualization space. AutoFocus employs an attention mechanism and a Focus Network to identify relevant past experiences for each decision. The focus shift strategy is then learned through a predictive process called FocusPursuit. In our experiments, AutoFocus consistently outperformed RRLs and Focus Deterninistic RRLs (FRRLs) on a diverse range of autonomous driving tasks and systems. Moreover, we observed that our method explores the visualization space more efficiently than other methods, such as Q-learning, thereby outperforming them by a significant margin. To facilitate further research, we made our code available at https://github.com/alexrame/AutoFocus. Additionally, our results can be found on https://www.alexrame.fr/autofocus. Finally, our vision for our work can be found at https://www.alexrame.fr/autofocus/#vision.

Our study confirms that two-layer ANNs are robust, which could lead to further research into network architectures with altered structures. Personal devices are increasingly performing computational tasks, such as training neural networks, which can be time-consuming. By utilizing a network of devices, called a Pando cluster, these tasks can now be efficiently completed in a fraction of the time, even when a single device isn't available. Our system stands out from other distributed computing frameworks because it dynamically adjusts the size and composition of the Pando cluster in real-time based on the requirements of each task. Once a computation is complete, the Pando cluster instantly disbands. Our system's performance in training neural networks was remarkable, with speeds up to five times faster than using a single device, and even outpacing top competitors in certain tasks. Furthermore, because Pando clusters are transient and don't persist, there's no need to worry about ongoing costs or complex cluster management. Our research demonstrates that a distributed computing system with adaptive, on-demand infrastructure can effectively tackle complex computational challenges. To facilitate this, we're making the Pando system available in open-source form. Our paper delves deeper into the benefits and mechanics of Pando, as well as experimental results showing its performance in comparison to other systems. Our long-term goal is to make Pando the standard for collaborative, distributed computing that works seamlessly in everyday life. Our current focus is on demonstrating Pando's potential by applying it to neural network training, but we're excited to see its uses expanding to a broader range of computations in the future. Our main contributions are as follows: Our system automatically assembles and dissolves Pando clusters in response to incoming computations, unlike other frameworks that maintain persistent clusters. Our framework dynamically adjusts the size and composition of the Pando cluster based on the requirements of each computation, unlike other frameworks that rely on pre-configured setups. Our system uses networked personal devices in a way that minimizes overhead and makes the computing process efficient, unlike other frameworks that prioritize raw processing power over practicality. Our research shows that gradual, distributed training methods that work well with large, persistent clusters also perform well with the transient schedules of personal devices. Our system uses intermediate checkpoints to facilitate restarting computations and ensure reliability, as well as providing a flexible way to configure the Pando cluster for confidence intervals and hyperparameter tuning. Our open-source implementation allows users to define custom scheduling strategies and adapt the Pando cluster to various hardware configurations and computational tasks. In the context of approximating eigenvalues and eigenfunctions, several numerical methods rely on a quasi-arithmetic mean that serves as a dynamic target for sampling. By incorporating an adaptive sampling strategy along with this mean, we can increase the efficiency of these methods. This sampling method allows for resource allocation to be adapted according to the varying complexity of the approximation at hand. Utilizing a specific example involving Hermite-Gaussian modes, we demonstrate that our adaptive sampling scheme enhances the accuracy and computational speed of the approximation. This approach is particularly beneficial for scenarios where certain eigenvalues or modes are of greater significance than others. Furthermore, the adaptation can be customized to prioritize specific modes or regions of interest. This adaptive technique is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of problems, including electromagnetic imaging and spectroscopy. Additionally, the inherent stability and convergence properties of the method enable seamless integration with regularization strategies. This integration is essential for handling ill-posed problems and potential noise or statistical uncertainties that may arise during data collection. This paper showcases the adaptive sampling method's efficacy in a series of numerical experiments and introduces a corresponding open-source code for reproduction of the results. This open-source code is part of the PyFR code library. This software is continuously maintained by an extended team of researchers and developers. We actively encourage users to partake in the ongoing development of the software by contributing their knowledge and expertise to the GitHub repository, which is accessible via the provided link. We examine $SO(N_{c})$ gauge theories containing an excess of flavor quarks, in addition to an appropriate number of massless quark fields. Our investigation focuses on the behavior of these theories in the large $N_{F}$ limit. In this regime, we discover that an $SU(N_{F})$ chiral symmetry is eroded due to the effects of quark bilinear operators, and the resulting effective theory is an $SO(N_{c})$ sigma model with a specific $SO(N_{c}+N_{F})$ chiral symmetry. A vertex operator algebra is utilized to derive the sigma model action, which aligns with a previous proposal by Armoni, Correa, and Shalom. Our findings further indicate that in the large $N_{c}$ limit, the sigma model exhibits a non-perturbative beta function that can be matched to existing literature. In the multi-color regime, we observe that a set of massive sigma models, stemming from the rank symmetry breakdown, interact in a coupled manner. We apply renormalization group techniques to the effective coupling of each massive sigma model, which enables us to construct a unified flow diagram across the entire flavor quark mass spectrum. In the large $N_{c}$ limit, the distribution of Landau poles for various couplings is free of singularity. Our work suggests that an enhanced rank symmetry $SO(N_{c}+N_{F})$ chiral protection persists until the occurrence of Landau poles at larger scales compared to theories lacking this symmetry. We verify the existence of enhanced chiral protection in multiple examples, including quark-seagull interactions and effective theories derived from QCD with valence quarks and various twisted mass configurations. Our investigation demonstrates that an adequate number of flavor quarks can render an $SO(N_{c})$ gauge theory perturbative up to the occurrence of Landau poles. Interpreting the predictions of machine learning models, particularly in time series forecasting, has gained significant interest in recent years. In this research, we introduce a novel approach, Disentangled Attribution Curves (DAC), which reveals the impact of each predictor on the model's predictions in a dynamic manner. By applying DAC to a bike-sharing dataset, we uncover noteworthy insights that have practical implications for bike-sharing services and their stakeholders. Our analysis also compares the performance of DAC with existing model interpretability techniques, demonstrating that DAC outperforms the alternatives in one aspect: its seamless integration with time-series data. Furthermore, DAC enables us to identify the optimal model selection for our use case through a systematic evaluation. Our findings are made available in a dedicated repository, allowing our approach to be reproduced by others. Finally, DAC is designed to be adaptable to a wide scope of machine learning models, thereby enabling its application to a diverse range of forecasting tasks. A significant challenge in developing private machine learning models lies in maintaining data privacy beyond what traditional approaches can achieve. Existing methods in federated learning have limitations, such as assuming the threat actor has minimal knowledge, assuming all data records contain the same type of sensitive information, and relying on parameters and gradients that can be computationally expensive to transfer. To address these issues, this paper presents a new approach called L$^3$FL, which is designed to be robust, efficient, and adaptable. L$^3$FL is built on three main components: 1) a novel privacy metric called RuiVal, which quantifies data privacy based on record valuations; 2) a lightweight protocol for secure multi-party computation called SCVAP, which facilitates secure data sharing among participants; and 3) a new federated learning technique called VGG, which enables the efficient training of convolutional neural networks on small datasets. Our experiments demonstrate that L$^3$FL can achieve state-of-the-art performance while reducing the communication cost up to 47% compared to other federated learning algorithms. Additionally, the RuiVal metric offers more precise privacy guarantees than other approaches, offering 1-2 orders of magnitude greater privacy resilience in certain scenarios. Our open-source implementation of L$^3$FL can be accessed at https://github.com/jiashai-lyu/L3FL. This research paper outlines a proposed solution for a driver testing framework, allowing programmers to run and evaluate driver code on small microcontroller devices, such as those used in the Raspberry Pi Pico. Our solution consists of three key components: a driver testing API, a test framework, and a compiler plugin. The driver testing API and test framework are developed in C, while the compiler plugin is created using LLVM. Our approach starts by having programmers write and implement driver code using the specified API, following best practices, and compile this code using our modified LLVM compiler. Additionally, developers test the compiled code on a microcontroller device using our custom test framework. Our solution enables efficient testing of drivers on microcontroller devices, including the Raspberry Pi Pico, by running a variety of automated tests. These tests cover both functional and performance assessments of the drivers, including real-world applications and benchmarking tools. We estimate that with this framework, the time required for testing drivers can be significantly reduced from current manual processes, which take around one to two days, to just a few hours. Our solution also saves programmers the effort of navigating complex compiler tools and testing software, by providing a comprehensive compiler and test framework that supports a wide range of operating systems. Filtering system calls and managing memory can be challenging, especially for applications written in interpreted languages. To overcome these issues, we introduce an innovative component called Timeloops. This module, which has a minor performance overhead, can effectively control system calls and block malicious code for websites built with PHP and Python. Additionally, Timeloops provides a straightforward way to isolate vulnerable applications at the application level, making it easier to deploy and manage memory sharing. This module serves as a universal guardian, monitoring user interactions and blocking potentially harmful scripts. This protection comes without compromising the seamless sharing of memory. Besides its core system call filtering capabilities, Timeloops offers a range of advanced features. For instance, it can block specific system calls, impose temporary memory limits, cloak sensitive fields like keyboard and sound records, share memory only with approved applications, or disable potentially hazardous scripts on user command. A stochastic Model Predictive Control strategy was implemented to tackle a tractability issue related to optimization under a unique measure. The solution involves treating the optimal trajectory as a random variable, whose expected value is computed using Monte Carlo simulation in conjunction with a dynamic programming algorithm. However, the process becomes infeasible due to its high computational complexity for large systems. We mitigate this limitation by leveraging properties of the measure and its potential non-uniqueness, allowing us to conduct simulation and optimize smaller systems in a divide-and-conquer manner. The approach is verified by comparing its performance with an alternative method based on convex optimization for a representative example. The results indicate that our method achieves comparable performance with significantly shorter computation times. The proposed framework exhibits potential for treating uncertainty as well as handling large systems with complex trajectories. Moreover, it offers an advantage in solving efficient convex optimization problems by incorporating a stochastic trajectory. The study demonstrates the versatility of stochastic Model Predictive Control in handling various system conditions. This study investigates the principles of information behind compressed sensing and independent component analysis, and incorporates them into two new algorithms that combine the efficiency of compressive sensing with the component purity of ICA. We develop two algorithms based on this idea: a first one that directly aims for low-dimensional signals in a linear subspace, and a second one that incorporates a learning phase to better handle non-linear data. This work marks the first instance of algorithms that merge compressive sensing and ICA, and paves the way for new research in this field. Experiments using synthetic and real-world data reveal that these algorithms outperform traditional ICA methods while requiring significantly less memory and providing more reliable results. Notably, they can run on devices with limited processing capabilities such as microcontrollers or tiny computers. Their potential applications include analyzing data from embedded systems, such as neural signals or image capture, that are unable to handle large datasets due to hardware constraints. In particular, they show promising results for the analysis of neural signals recorded by electrodes or imaging systems. This research demonstrates the strong connection between sensing and separation techniques, and opens up new avenues for research in this area. In particular, it would be interesting to incorporate other sensing techniques such as multi-sensor data, or new optimization strategies such as regularized models. A possible future direction could also be the development of new sensing techniques tailored specifically to the characteristics of the data being analyzed. This could be achieved by incorporating prior knowledge of the signals into the sensing process, or customizing the sensing matrices to best extract the desired components. Yet another potential future research area could be the incorporation of time-related data into the algorithm, either by using time-dependent models or incorporating time-stamps into the sensing process. This could be particularly significant in applications such as image analysis or neural signal analysis where temporal correlations between different components are common. A final possible future research area could be the development of new algorithms for non-linearly compressed signals, either by using prior knowledge of the signals or incorporating other relevant factors such as smoothness or sparsity constraints. This could potentially lead to new theoretical results and insights into the characteristics of the signals themselves. Ultimately, the long-term goal of this research is to develop new and efficient algorithms for analyzing data in scenarios where resources are limited, and to provide a broader understanding of the principles involved through theoretical results. This could be achieved by further combining sensing and separation techniques, and potentially leading to new and improved algorithms in a wide range of application areas including neural signal analysis, image capture, and microcontroller-based data analysis.

We analyzed the voter model with species-specific and independent noise to understand how two species compete in an asymmetric environment. Our studies revealed that the probability of coexistence is extremely low, and the long-term outcome is mostly the dominance of one species. However, in cases where coexistence is possible, the system often switches between the two species's dominant periods. Notably, the system's behavior resembles a random walk in both its overall dynamics and the probability of one species becoming the exclusive winner. The random walk model also allowed us to calculate the exact probability of the slower species dominating, which confirms a previous approximation made by Cucurux et al. Our findings offer insights into how species interact and compete in diverse environments. Our models can be applied to analyze the complex dynamics of multiple species in various ecological systems. Our investigation centers around von Neumann algebras generated by the local subalgebras $L_R$, corresponding to the unions of subalgebras $I_F$, derived from the many-body wave functions of the Minimally Entanging States, within the Hilbert space of a one-dimensional system with local interactions. We prove that these von Neumann algebras are type II_1 and contain no non-trivial finite dimensional inclusions, and their central series ends within a certain number of generations, dependent on the number of interactions. We show that, for ground states that are frustration-free, the local algebras $L_R$ are classified in terms to simple higher semi-commutative von Neumann algebras. We apply these results to quantum spin chains and lattice systems of finite size, and examine the properties and structure of the algebras $L_R$. We find that, for some systems with local interactions, the algebras $L_R$ are type I, specifically of the type I_∞ or type I_∞ with a matrix, depending on the number of particles. We examine how initial coherence and the presence of a regulatory feedback influence ground state entanglement in the context of a two-qubit system subjected to random diamond-shaped fluctuations. When the system's dynamics is governed solely by its Hamiltonian, certain boundary conditions generate maximal entanglement due to the conservation of phase. Nevertheless, this phase-related coherence is disrupted by the diamond-shaped fluctuations. Nevertheless, in systems analogous to those found in cavity optomechanics, we discover that the presence of a regulatory feedback loop enhances the robustness of ground state entanglement against thermal effects, thereby exceeding traditional Hamiltonian-boundary-condition-generated entanglement. Furthermore, we illustrate the need for accurate tracking of the system's density matrix diagonal and off-diagonal components in order to quantify entanglement using a thermodynamic uncertainty principle. This proves advantageous over conventional methods that solely analyze the main diagonal of the density matrix. Our study offers a unified quantitative measure of robustness against thermal effects for entangled states governed by a Hamiltonian and illustrates a series of non-trivial, highly controlled, and realistic two-qubit quantum states. This research has the potential to open doors to new applications in quantum information sciences. Furthermore, we outline a straightforward method for experimentally generating these quantum states and demonstrate that the regulatory feedback loop can be achieved experimentally through the interaction of one qubit with a larger mechanical oscillator. This is made possible by integrating the mechanical oscillator into a larger optical cavity in order to facilitate the use of advanced techniques such as heterodyne laser measurement. Our research also highlights the benefits of incorporating a laser field capable of cooling and modulating the mechanical oscillator on a microscale in order to implement the necessary regulatory feedback loop. This research has the potential to open doors to new applications in quantum information sciences. This paper outlines a citizen science initiative aimed at gathering and publishing comprehensive information on sundials across Indonesia. Undue emphasis has been given to European sundials in the past, resulting in limited recognition of historic sundials within Indonesian cultures. To rectify this, our project aims to collect detailed data on sundials in Indonesia through community involvement, ensuring accurate documentation of these timekeepers from diverse Asian backgrounds. Current knowledge of Indonesian sundials is restricted to approximately 30 documented examples, spanning from old temples to modern building designs. To facilitate widespread participation, a mobile app has been developed for both Android and iOS platforms, enabling anyone to register and share information on sundials. Each sundial entry in the app includes essential details such as location, photo, and time recorded, along with a built-in mechanism for validating newly added entries against a predefined set of criteria. All collected data will be displayed on a web map for easy reference and is currently being stored in a local database due to data security concerns. Our goal is to crowdsource significant information on Indonesian sundials, fostering a community of co-researchers and providing a platform for ongoing research and development. In the near future, we plan to integrate a ranking system that allows experts to verify and prioritize the collected data, ultimately leading to the publication of a comprehensive guide to Indonesian sundials. If you're interested in participating, please download the app from app.sundial.io and start contributing to the world of Indonesian sundials! In a multi-user DED2D system, the TFIET scheme ensures that data and energy are transferred to users in an iterative process by allocating resources and determining transmission power in each step. Assuming that channels are randomly generated from a fixed distribution and satisfy a specific condition, we prove that the TFIET algorithm achieves optimal performance in multi-user DED2D networks, and provide mathematical bounds on the gap to optimality. Unlike previous research, our work doesn't rely on specific channel distributions and requires significantly fewer assumptions about the problem setting. Additionally, we propose a modified version of the TFIET algorithm that converges more rapidly by reducing the number of iterations in each step. Our analysis using the Weibull distribution shows that the bounded suboptimal performance of TFIET can be precisely determined. To further improve performance, we developed several variants of TFIET, including a iterative algorithm that combines TFIET and zero-forcing beamforming, and a variant that minimizes transmit power while meeting users' information and energy requirements in multi-user DED2D networks. Our results confirm that the TFIET algorithm is near-optimal and effective in a range of wireless communication systems. To verify our theoretical analysis, we conducted numerous simulations under diverse channel conditions, and found that the rapid version of TFIET achieved results comparable to the best known algorithms, and in some cases outperformed them in terms of sum-rate and transmit power. This research addresses Asser's conjecture regarding the class of spectra, specifically a narrower scope. We examine how the broader class interacts with undirected bipartite graphs. The goal is to understand whether there are any graph-theoretic conditions that ensure a spectrum's broader class is equivalent to its narrower scope. We look at specific spectrum properties and their relationships to graph features like graph distance, eigenvalues, and graph rank. We also explore the connections between these graph theory elements and the mathematical concept of measure theory. Ultimately, we discuss the challenges and obstacles within the research area, along with some counterexamples that highlight unusual properties and behaviors. These examples serve as a foundation for a new project, where researchers can contribute to the understanding of a spectrum's class by analyzing specific graphs. This initiative allows individual researchers to determine whether a given graph falls within the spectrum's broader or narrower class, with data available online. By gathering data on this website, we aim to verify or refute the conjecture proposed by Asser. The project also includes an algorithm that evaluates the class of a spectrum for individual graphs. This tool is accessible online for users to calculate and compare the class of a spectrum for various graphs. In addition to the website, we provide an open-source software implementation of the algorithm used to determine the class of a spectrum. This implementation allows researchers to contribute their findings to the project. Our study involves over 200 graph-theoretic conditions that determine the class of a spectrum. We present these conditions along with their corresponding status - whether they solve, refine, or fail to solve Asser's conjecture, along with some failed attempts that might serve as a foundation for future research. We also discuss potential future research areas, along with some interesting observations and open-ended questions that require further investigation. The ultimate goal of this research is to provide meaningful insights into the relationships between graph theory elements and the mathematical concept of measure theory, along with Asser's conjecture. The project serves as a source of information on the class of a spectrum for over 200 individual graphs. This knowledge can be used to tackle the conjecture proposed by Asser. In various electron microscopy techniques like scanning electron microscopes and image shift microscopes, a fundamental component is the electrostatic phase plate, which serves to focus a beam of electrons. The design of these plates has been studied in relation to the properties of the electrons that interact with them. This research examines how changes in fill-factor and pixel patterns impact the size and intensity of the electron probe. The findings show that filling-factor affects the probe size, while pixel patterns have a negligible influence. Despite widespread consensus among scientists, climate change denial continues to circulate widely on social media platforms. A multi-million post climate change conspiracy theory network has been identified on Twitter, controlled by a specific group. Our analysis reveals that each second, over 100 new tweets emerge claiming climate change is a hoax. To combat this, we have developed a system that incorporates human intelligence, employing workers to assess the impact of accounts suspensions on climate change conspiracy theory-related content. Our findings show that account suspension has limited effect, with replacement accounts appearing within an average of 10 minutes. Our research also demonstrates that a small group of users contributes significantly to the dissemination of these conspiracy theories. Conversely, retweets from influencer accounts have a negative impact, with their engagement often validating users' beliefs and reducing the likelihood of users exiting the network. Furthermore, we have found that climate change-related tweets from self-identified scientists are largely ignored by users, whereas similar tweets from other self-identified experts can receive significant engagement. Our study reveals that counter-messaging can backfire, and that a more effective strategy involves sharing personal stories or experiences related to climate change. Our analysis indicates that this type of content is more likely to receive engagement, on average doubling the likelihood compared to tweets from self-identified experts. Our ultimate goal is to contribute to the development of strategies that can mitigate the spread of climate change conspiracy theories on social media platforms. Our findings emphasize the need for targeted interventions focused on influencer accounts, suspension policies that address network effects, and the importance of engaging expert endorsement. This study provides a detailed analysis of earning potential in Norway and Denmark in relation to higher education choices. Our investigation reveals significant disparities in the advantages of various fields of study between the two countries. While many fields in Norway yield relatively comparable earning potential, the results in Denmark show considerable variations, with certain fields such as primary and secondary education being significantly disadvantaged. Our findings also suggest that Danish students are largely unaware of the substantial earnings disadvantages associated with certain academic majors, which may be attributed to the lack of transparent information about the advantages of different fields of study in Denmark. In contrast, Norwegian students have more accessible information about the labor market outcomes associated with their chosen majors. Based on these findings, we propose that the Norwegian model of informing higher education choices be adopted in Denmark. Additionally, we recommend that Danish high school students be explicitly informed about the potential earning disadvantages of primary and secondary education when making their higher education decisions. Our research suggests that adopting these measures could increase the proportion of Danish students choosing more lucrative majors, which would result in a significant increase in the country's GDP per capita. Similar benefits could also be achieved in Norway, and we speculate that the same effect could be produced in other countries with comparable systems for informing higher education choices and linking academic majors to labor market outcomes. Ultimately, our analysis highlights the significance of both these factors in shaping the allocation of students across different major fields of study. We also verify that our results are robust in the face of several alternative assumptions concerning the decision-making behaviors of high school students in Denmark. The minimax principle can be seen as a way to establish the existence of solutions for various variational problems by ensuring the existence of a minimum and maximum value between two function sets. This paper applies the minimax principle to demonstrate the existence of solutions for two equilibrium problems and the regular displacement problem in the context of nonlinear elastic solids following the non-smooth geometry of Mateos, Munoz, and Romero in 2018. To achieve this, we rephrase these problems as fixed point problems for mappings that satisfy conditions equivalent to those established by that research. As a result, we leverage the property that a minimax function achieves both its minimum and maximum values when evaluated on specific sets, which in this case are the fixed points of the mappings in question. We also extend the existence of solutions to problems involving differential and integral equations with discontinuous operators by drawing comparisons with the original problems of nonlinear elasticity. Ultimately, we establish the existence of solutions for the regular displacement problem even when the material's energy predicate is not convex, which marks a distinction from prior studies in the field. In addition to the existence of solutions, we also explore the regularity of the displacements and derive the key result that discontinuous problems can be reformulated as smooth variational problems through the introduction of a smooth approximation of the material's energy predicate. Consequently, we are able to obtain the desired regularity of the displacements for the original problem of nonlinear elasticity. We believe the approach adopted in this research offers a more straightforward and versatile method for establishing the existence of solutions to a broader range of equilibrium problems compared to earlier techniques in the field. Ultimately, we are able to establish the existence of multiple solutions to problems of differential and integral equations with discontinuous operators, which marks a departure from the field's traditional focus on a single solution. We hope this research will serve as a more comprehensive treatment of the subject. To facilitate the understanding of the methods presented, we have adopted an approach that emphasizes the clarity and simplicity of the proofs, often at the expense of presenting more general results. We look forward to the opportunity to present a more detailed account of the research in a future study. This paper is organized into seven sections, with Section 1 providing an overview of the problem, Section 2 establishing a key result for fixed point problems, Section 3 addressing equilibrium problems, Section 4 examining differential and integral equations with discontinuous operators, and finally, the regular displacement problem in Section 5 and the regular displacement problem with the positive line in Section 6. Highly mobile wireless channels create significant challenges for channel estimation and performance monitoring. Consequently, channel estimation, which is a critical process in various wireless systems including MIMO-OFDM systems, becomes increasingly difficult with rising mobility levels. By leveraging the adaptive properties of LSTM neural networks that allow them to learn from their environment and adjust expectations accordingly, we propose an innovative solution to mitigate the limitations imposed by high mobility. The proposed LSTM-AE approach aims to improve the precision of channel estimation in such scenarios. The proposed method utilizes multiple LSTM deep neural networks to predict channel state information for various path delays and individual antenna pairs, resulting in notably improved channel estimation accuracy compared to conventional non-adaptive methods. Furthermore, the proposed method enables the simulation of ideal pilot signal conditions by leveraging its memory mechanism to effectively integrate past observations and current data for enhanced performance. The results show that LSTM-AE achieves significant improvements in channel estimation accuracy with decreasing pilot signal lengths, and is particularly effective in scenarios with high mobility and long pilot signal intervals. The proposed method is non-recurrent and can be applied to various MIMO-OFMD systems with an arbitrary number of co-located antennas. The research is primarily centered on LTE-like single-user MIMO-OFMD systems with two co-located antennas and five antenna pairs. The proposed method is highly pertinent to a wide range of modern wireless system applications including MIMO-OFMD, millimeter wave, and future MIMO-OFMD frequency bands. The results indicate that deep learning methods are essential for channel estimation and optimization in various MIMO-OFMD frequency bands and future MIMO-OFMD systems with high mobility and long pilot signal intervals. We introduce a system for improving low-quality astronomical images captured by the ZTF (Zooming Time Facility). These images are often impaired by imaging distortions and irregular shapes due to the unique telescope design. We tackle the issue of image improvement in two stages. Firstly, we utilize a registration technique to align images taken at different epochs. Since the telescope's field of view is not fixed, these images are often non-uniform and cannot be directly aligned using conventional registration methods. We develop a new approach that leverages a pre-defined template image to facilitate accurate image registration. Once the images are aligned, we apply a restoration technique to enhance their overall quality. Since the ZTF images are characterized by a limited field of view and coherent pixel values, we frame this as a spatio-temporal image restoration problem and propose a novel model based on the transport equation and filtered back projection methods. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our system in improving image quality, specifically in terms of shape regularization and noise reduction. This is evident from our comparison with state-of-the-art image improvement techniques. We also conduct a performance analysis and showcase our results on actual ZTF images for validation. Our method for image improvement can be adapted to a range of astronomical image improvement tasks, including those related to the selection of active galaxy nuclei. To facilitate seamless and efficient human-robot collaborations, a new interactive learning framework has been devised by combining Federated Learning with Imitation Learning. This innovative approach tackles four key problems often encountered in robotic learning: collision avoidance, path planning, goal recognition, and dialogue management. Our framework enables multiple robots to learn from human interactions within localized datasets, reducing communication requirements to aggregate models and thus overcoming common communication challenges. The proposed system consists of a centralized knowledge base, disseminated to the robots through a scalable communication strategy, from which the robots can learn through interaction with humans, while simultaneously updating their imitation learning models to align with the overall knowledge base. A distributed imitation learning algorithm was developed to tackle this challenge, along with a new architecture for recognizing human goals in robotics. This new system recognizes human intentions as atomic actions within a pre-defined set of goals using a cutting-edge atomic action recognition approach. Furthermore, the framework is completed by a dialogue management system for effective human-robot interaction, as demonstrated in a recently published journal on the integration of Federated Learning with Imitation Learning. Experimental results for goal recognition and dialogue management are presented, highlighting the advantages of the proposed framework in terms of communication efficiency and the scalability of learning components. The benefits of the Federated Learning framework in multi-robot, multi-human collaborations have been empirically validated through various applications. One such experiment involved a human interacting with two robots to identify objects, as shown in Figure 11. The results showed improved performance in object identification, reduced communication requirements, and better learning scalability. Specifically, the number of communicated bits was found to be in the order of thousands, making the proposed framework highly communicative efficient. This research introduces a new estimator that achieves two critical goals: it has the most accurate bias reduction possible and is highly resistant to model irregularities. By initially developing an expression for the bias of the traditional average treatment effect estimator, our analysis reveals that standard practices for reducing bias often rely on implicit assumptions about model smoothness. To overcome this limitation, we provide an alternative estimator with bias reduction capabilities, while explicitly accommodating scenarios of non-smoothness and infinite-dimensional models. Additionally, our proposal is based on a novel variant of the linear projection technique and is highly computationally efficient. We further demonstrate its efficacy in high-dimensional settings by applying it to the estimation of causal effects in experiments with multiple arms. Through a simulation study and real-world data analysis, our results show that the proposed estimator effectively resists the effects of model smoothness and often outperforms established benchmarks in terms of accuracy and resistance to false positives. Knowledge graph link prediction is an essential task in knowledge graph completion that uses established fact-tripping to forecast missing connections between entities within a knowledge graph. Current KGP methods either ignore the details provided by relation extraction or utilize them in a confined way, missing the broader picture. Conversely, we propose RelEx-GNP, an innovative GNP model that fully leverages the information extracted through relation extraction and incorporates it into the knowledge graph, enabling the connection between entities to be predicted with even greater accuracy. To achieve this, we extend the conventional GNP framework by incorporating extracted relations, enabling the model to distinguish between correct and incorrect connections based on enhanced contextual information. Our model's efficacy is demonstrated through empirical evaluation on multiple datasets, yielding significant enhancements in accuracy and the quality of predicted links. Furthermore, we analyze the behavior of our model in relation to existing explanations in the field. Ultimately, the code for our proposed RelEx-GNP model is made available at the following repository address: https://github.com/adoss/RelEx-GNP. The paper evaluates fairing and Debye mass types for a color fluid with multiple Debye lengths, formulated based on a mean-field approximation that incorporates magnetic and chemical potentials.  Analyzing fairing and Debye mass types in various approximations reveals that introducing a chemical potential shifts the types from concave and convex to convex and concave respectively.  Additionally, the paper compares these types with types derived from perturbation theory and Landau theory, highlighting their resemblance in certain approximations.  The study also demonstrates that fairing and Debye mass types can serve as indicators of phase transitions and instabilities in the model.  Specifically, the results show that fairing and Debye mass types coincide in determining both the deconfinement and the QCD critical point as well as the onset of plasma and the QCD critical end point.  Finally, the paper finds that fairing and Debye mass types can differ in their evaluation of the Higgs mode in the color fluid and the QCD critical point.  The results show a fourth-order instability at the QCD critical point, in contrast to the second-order instability indicated by fairing and Debye mass types.  The free energy surface also exhibits a saddle-point structure for the fairing and Debye mass types, in contrast to the mean-field theory scenario of a free energy surface with a cusp.  The results for the Higgs mode in the color fluid suggest a possibility of a first-order deconfinement transition, in contrast to the QCD specification of a second-order deconfinement transition. Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 are known for their unusual magnetic arrangements and the presence of a rare transition between incommensurate magnetic phase and commensurate magnetic phase that depends on the ratio of the two different Ru ions. This paper explores the electronic and magnetic properties of these two compounds using a model that incorporates strong correlations, and investigates the effects of rotation symmetry of the Spuehdev triangle on their phase diagrams. Unlike previous studies, our calculations show that this symmetry has a significant impact, and we explain the observed magnetic arrangements and the incommensurate-commensurate transition in terms of this effect. Additionally, we examine the magnetic arrangements of other elements in the Spuehdev triangle and discuss possible future research into these compounds. Lastly, we compare and contrast the electronic and magnetic properties of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7, and demonstrate that the observed similarities and differences are consistent with the presence of a Spuehdev triangle ground state. This research was conducted under the assumption that the compounds have d1 symmetry; however, we suggest that the presence of a unique triangle ground state is not dependent on this particular symmetry configuration. Finally, we propose potential future research into the magnetic arrangements of other elements in the Spuehdev triangle and the effect of various perturbations on the compounds' electronic and magnetic properties. Some of the calculations presented in the paper are ongoing and have not yet been completed. In order to identify and assess interventions, studying the relationships between variables is crucial in both social and natural sciences.  Although structural equation models (SEMs) effectively determine interventions for specific variables, they fall short in addressing two essential aspects:  the interdependence of variables is limited to linear relationships and the specified variables often fail to account for missing factors.  In response, we introduce a new class of models known as semi-generative models (SGMs) which integrate aspects of both generative and discriminative models of probabilistic graphical models.  By distinguishing between causal factors and effects using latent variables, SGMs retain the ability to determine interventions while accounting for the interdependence of variables in a more comprehensive manner than traditional SEMs.  In this study, we propose a new class of Gaussian SGMs and investigate their representational and relational capabilities through the lens of intervention and representation policies.  Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of Gaussian SGMs by applying them to the analysis of synthetic and real-world data sets.  Ultimately, the analysis reveals that Gaussian SGMs offer a new class of models that achieves a dynamic balance between the integrative properties of generative models and the predictive versatility of discriminative models.  This research has important implications for the practical application of SGMs in both theoretical and empirical domains.  In particular, we demonstrate the utility of Gaussian SGMs by applying them to the analysis of a synthetic data set and an actual study on the effect of college education on earnings.  The outcomes of this research position Gaussian SGMs as a new class of models that maintains a harmonious equilibrium between the integrative qualities of generative models and the predictive capabilities of discriminative models. Consider a cubic field $K$ obtained by attaching a ramified $3$-isomorphism to $\mathbb{Q}$, and let $\mathcal{O}_K$ denote its ring of integers. For any $\beta \in \mathcal{O}_K$ with $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\beta)$ equal to $3$, the set of lattice minima in $(\mathcal{O}_K^3)^{\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{A}_K/\sigma_3)\rightarrow\mathrm{Aut}}$ is investigated. Specifically, it is proven that the number of lattice minima remains the same when $\beta$ is replaced by $\sigma_2(\beta)$ or $\sigma_3(\beta)$. Furthermore, conditions on the field $K$ and $\beta$ are established to ensure that the number of lattice minima in $(\mathcal{O}_K^3)^{\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{A}_K/\sigma_3)\rightarrow\mathrm{Aut}}$ is accurately calculated. In particular, it is shown that for many cubic fields, the number of lattice minima in $(\mathcal{O}_K^3)^{\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{A}_K/\sigma_3)\rightarrow\mathrm{Aut}}$ can be determined by computing a sum involving specific $K$-isomorphisms and their associated heights, which can be compared with established upper bounds. We also provide alternative proofs of recent findings by deveney-motley-payne that relate the distribution of lattice minima in cubic fields and their associated hasse-minima. Moreover, it is proven that there are infinitely many cubic fields without hasse-minima. Finally, the results are generalized to degree-$3$ covers of functions fields, and new approaches are developed to investigate lattice minima in such scenarios. For example, it is shown that there are infinitely many cubic functions fields without hasse-minima. Additionally, conditions on the fields and parameters are established under which the number of lattice minima in degree-$3$ covers of functions fields can and cannot be calculated. These theories and examples provide crucial insights into the study of lattice minima in cubic fields and their generalization to degree-$3$ covers of functions fields. They also reveal connections with previous research on cubic fields, function fields, and the associated problems of finding elements with specific heights or heights less than a specified constant. In spite of extensive research over the past ten years, a comprehensive, universally applicable explanation or interpretation of these networks has yet to be found. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework in facilitating the interpretation of the networks' behavior at two levels: firstly, we show that our framework reveals the local properties of each layer in a deep neural network, and secondly, we discuss how these revelations can be used to understand high-level decisions made by the networks. Although the two models are equivalent at any fixed RG flow, our calculations reveal distinct properties in terms of conservation and crossing symmetry. Specifically, the Hamiltonian-derived model amplitude fails conservation and crossing symmetry at low orders of perturbation theory, in contrast to the standard parquet amplitude, which satisfies these symmetries exactly. However, our analysis also demonstrates that the Hamiltonian-derived model achieves conservation and crossing symmetry at higher orders of perturbation theory. We demonstrate how this notion is in line with existing concepts in proof theory and then focus on deriving methodological benefits from its distinction between containment and converse relationships. We show that using proof-theoretic containment yields more reliable results in comparisons between alternative systems for intuitionistic and classical logic. A prominent paradigm in reinforcement learning incorporates human feedback to overcome difficulties in reward design. Typically, each state-action pair from a dataset is evaluated by humans, providing an expensive and time-consuming process. We aim to optimize this process within the reinforcement learning system by incorporating human feedback in batches, rather than one pair at a time. By utilizing a self-paced learning method, where comparisons are grouped into batches on the fly based on current performance, our approach achieves multiple benefits. First, it allows the system to learn from suboptimal batches without wasting time, while also adapting to potential changes in the humans' interpretation of the comparisons, should their understanding evolve during the process. Moreover, batch comparisons can be selected more efficiently, as they are based on more reliable estimates achieved through cumulative human feedback. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through a practical application in an inventory management setting, where our method outperforms real-time and offline baseline strategies. Our code can be found at: https://github.com/alevazquez/batch-reward-learning. Our paper further discusses the details behind this batch reward learning technique. A video illustrating the process can be found at: https://youtu.be/5V4O1EILF_Y. In addition, an extended version of our paper, including more thorough evaluation results, can be found at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.10310. We hope this batch reward learning technique can be applied broadly across a variety of environments, not just the simple ones we tested. Our long-term goal is to allow agents to learn from diverse domains, providing rich and context-dependent state and action representations that can be effectively generalized from human feedback. We plan to achieve this by first applying batch learning in environments similar to the inventory management setting, and then expanding its use to more complex applications, such as the robotic manipulation of objects. Ultimately, we hope to develop agents capable of learning from multiple sources of human feedback in a variety of practical settings. Within a rotating, fluid-filled annulus, researchers have found that it can often settle into a state characterized by ongoing baroclinic circulation. This circulation exhibits various characteristics that are generally similar across different setups, such as the formation of anticyclonic vortices near the inner edge and cyclonic vortices near the outer edge. To better comprehend and control this behavior, researchers have developed methods to diagnose and analyze surface flow patterns using PIV techniques and surface flux measurements. This has enabled them to investigate how the baroclinic circulation affects mixing within the annulus, specifically its impact on vertical mixing and how it compares to situations where baroclinic circulation does not develop. Additionally, researchers have studied how adjusting various parameters affects the behavior of the system, including the strength of the background rotation and the width of the annulus relative to its depth. By manipulating these parameters, researchers have entered states characterized by different types of flow behavior, including ones where strong, wavy surface flows coexist with minimal vertical mixing. Ultimately, researchers have used their findings to develop a parameterization for vertical mixing that is conditional on the presence of baroclinic circulation. This parameterization can be incorporated into global circulation and chemical modeling frameworks, allowing these models to more accurately account for baroclinic circulation's effects when those models are applied to stratified systems with similar characteristics to the ones studied here. We examine the challenge of enhancing fairness in reinforcement learning when there's an opportunity to manipulate reward functions. Assuming a corruption coefficient epsilon is known in advance, we develop an approach that achieves near-optimal performance and ensures fairness by finding the closest set of reward functions to those provided by multiple experts. The new algorithm guarantees fairness by minimizing the loss due to adversarial corruption, enabling fair learning and allowing for quick recovery when such corruption occurs. Additionally, we investigate the impact of unknown corruption coefficients and propose a solution with dynamic and adaptive exploration. We test these algorithms using synthetic data and find they perform efficiently in scenarios with varying levels of corruption. Notably, our approach exhibits robustness when the corruption coefficient is approximately 0.5, but may collapse in cases of extremely high corruption, requiring further modification to improve its fairness and efficiency in such scenarios. We also successfully apply these algorithms to a real-world task of training agents to play the game of Matrix Bandit fairly. For instance, when using corruption coefficient 0.5, our approach allows us to achieve a 30% better outcome compared to an algorithm that doesn't consider corruption. We observe that the new algorithm performs similarly to the optimal solution in scenarios with low levels of corruption. Moreover, the technique of using corruption-aware exploration proves beneficial, as it yields an 8% improvement over the optimal solution in scenarios with moderate levels of corruption. This study investigates the exact controllability of the impulsive heat equation. Our analysis shows that impulse approximate controllability is achievable using a single control force distributed over the entire domain. Moreover, we find the minimal cost of impulse control to be proportional to a positive power of the finite impulsive times. Notably, we demonstrate that a significant portion of the optimal impulsive control arises early in the control sequence. Specifically, we reveal that the optimal impulsive energy is concentrated in the first impulsive time, and the number of required impulsive controls can be estimated as the power of the optimal impulsive time itself. Our findings are supported by the resolution of a quadratic optimization problem. We also extend these results to multi-dimensional impulsive heat equations and examine the asymptotic behavior of the control function as the optimal impulsive times become arbitrarily sparse. Notably, our analysis shows that the control sequence exhibits persistent features and oscillations, and we can approximate the optimal control of the standard heat equation through a limiting process of the optimized impulsive controls. To achieve these results, we developed a novel combination of deep learning and bounded optimal control techniques that enables the approximation of exact controllability at finite impulsive times and supports the existence of minimal controls even in cases where classical asymptotic controllability is unattainable. Our numerical simulations illustrate the efficiency of the proposed algorithm in recovering the exact impulsive control and the remarkable sparsity of the optimal control sequence at finite impulsive times. Moreover, we observed that the support of the optimal control at twice the impulsive frequency is quite prevalent and that oscillating controls are necessary to achieve a continuous approximation of the standard heat equation. We hope that our study and algorithms will facilitate future research on bounded optimal control and spatio-temporal finite impulsive control applications. We present a deep learning approach to optimize finite impulsive controls and demonstrate its efficiency in recovering the exact impulsive control for various two-dimensional and three-dimensional spatial domains, even at the minimum possible impulsive times. Our results are consistent with theoretical analysis and show the sparsity and oscillatory nature of the optimal control sequence, revealing a fundamental role of support at twice the impulsive frequency. We also successfully apply the proposed algorithm to solve a bounded optimal control problem of the standard heat equation, achieving a continuous approximation of its solution through a limiting process of the optimized impulsive controls. Out-of-distribution detection is a crucial problem in machine learning that helps to identify data points that do not fit in predicted categories. Traditional methods for out-of-distribution detection have been primarily tested on controlled, pseudo-out-of-distribution data and have shown strong performance in these cases. However, these methods begin to struggle and lose accuracy on more realistic, semi-synthetic, semi-supervised, and unsupervised data. Moreover, these methods can easily be manipulated by an adversary who has control over the data distribution. In response to these issues, we propose a new method for out-of-distribution detection that is more robust and less susceptible to adversarial influences. Our method is based on testing the consistency of predictions from multiple models with varying levels of confidence. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method by showing that it outperforms existing methods of out-of-distribution detection on a range of challenging data sets. In particular, our method exhibits stronger performance when tested on semi-supervised data and when subjected to adversarial manipulations. In addition, our method offers several valuable insights into the nature of out-of-distribution detection and could be used as a tool for validating the accuracy of other detection methods. Our method can be used as a reference implementation at the following URL: https://github.com/alexeydp/voting-ccd. Our code for generating the challenging data sets can also be accessed at the following URL: https://github.com/alexeydp/challenging-data. Our method represents a new approach to out-of-distribution detection that is more robust, less susceptible to adversarial influences, and can be used as a validation reference for other detection methods. Our code can be used as a source of inspiration for future research in this area by being easily customizable and adaptable to a range of different scenarios. Our study highlights the importance of testing detection methods on a range of different distributions and can be used as a guide for generating challenging data sets in other domains. In addition, our study highlights the need for more transparent and interpretable detection methods in critical applications. Nature's engines, powered by chemical energy, move molecules along themselves according to specific directions dictated by specific binding sites. Similarly, in particle and condensed matter physics, motorized particles are driven by physical forces, offering a versatile means of transporting items. We have developed a model where a microscopic arm is used to transport molecules with the help of a magnetic field and chemical energy. Our proposal utilizes a head-and-tail structure of magnetic arm segments that bind to specific parts of a walking protein. As a result of a magnetic field, the arm turns in a specific direction, pushed by its free magnetic particles, and can therefore be synchronized with a walking protein to move along a track in a specific direction. This mechanism can also be applied to other types of motors, either protein-based or dye-driven, to achieve similar results. Additionally, we have calculated the energy efficiency of this system, comparing it to nature's energy efficiency, which has led to the development of several possible implementations using artificial DNA, motor proteins extracted from nature, and artificial tiny motors. Our study concludes by discussing the future applications and challenges of this system. Our code is available at https://git.io/LLM. We would be happy to hear any suggestions or proposals.
