We investigate the problem of developing a regular resynchronizer for non-deterministic two-way word transducers. Unlike one-way transducers, there is no guaranteed, bounded and regular synchronizer for them. However, we show that any non-deterministic two-way transducer has an equivalent, one-way transducer defined by a bounded, regular language on a new alphabet, but with a different origin. In contrast, there are examples of non-deterministic two-way transducers for which any given regular resynchronizer either fails to exist or fails to be bounded. In addition, we define a new class of transducers, called semi-one-way, which have neither more than one output transition per state nor more than one initial state. We find that a semi-one-way transducer has an equivalent, one-way transducer defined by a bounded, regular language on a new alphabet, and prove that it can be constructed in a way that all output functions are preserved. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be transformed into an equivalent semi-one-way transducer. Finally, we show that there are examples of non-deterministic two-way word transducers for which any given regular resynchronizer either fails to exist or fails to be bounded, but can be replaced by a semi-one-way transducer with an origin-equivalent, one-way transducer defined by a bounded, regular language on a new alphabet. In particular, we provide a simple example of an acyclic, non-deterministic two-way word transducer for which any given regular resynchronizer either fails to exist or fails to be bounded. In contrast, we find that a non-deterministic one-way word transducer has an equivalent, one-way transducer defined by a bounded, regular language on a new alphabet with the same origin. In particular, we demonstrate that the transducer recognizing the language $(0^*1^*) \cap (0^+1^+)$ has an equivalent, one-way transducer defined by the regular language $0^+1^+$ on a new alphabet with the same origin. In addition, we prove that any one-way word transducer has an equivalent, origin-equivalent one-way transducer defined by a bounded, regular resynchronizer. This paper explores the computational efficiency of the f-Convolution operation in Deep Complex Networks (DCN), specifically by designing a faster, per-entry computation method for each entry in the convolution output matrix. Unlike the traditional, full convolution computation, our method, known as Fast-DCN, achieves accelerated processing of DCN models, thereby significantly reducing the total computational cost. Specifically, the paper examines the computational costs associated with three DCN model architectures: two-layer models, models incorporating orthogonal complex weight matrices, and models with Euclidean distance-based regularization. In each case, the computational savings of Fast-DCN are calculated as a percentage reduction in computational cost, with the observation that the method achieves nearly full utilization of GPU acceleration for two-layer models, and near optimal efficiency for orthogonal weight matrices, with both cases demonstrating computational gains. Furthermore, the paper reveals that the method also yields significant speed-ups in the processing of convolutional layers in BResNet, a real-world DCN model. The efficiency of the approach is validated through experiments on the dataset MNIST. The code for the method can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/PrickyFast/Fast-DCN. We develop a straightforward model to illustrate how aerosol particles disperse from a single source, focusing on particle transport and collisions. Although our model lacks complexity when compared to more sophisticated simulations like ENSPIRE and FLUIDISK, it effectively mimics the distribution of particles observed in simulations, especially for time frames of a few minutes or longer. Furthermore, our model is capable of estimating the relationship between initial particle concentration, aerosol release rate, and dilution distance with high accuracy. We utilize Monte Carlo methods to generate statistical distributions of concentration values, which are then compared to numerical simulation data using Pearson correlation coefficients. We demonstrate that our model can accurately predict medium to long-term dilution distances by combining the parameters of both fast and slow flow regimes. We also outline potential avenues for model enhancement. All code and data necessary to replicate our results are freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/brasslab/Aerosol_Dilution_Model. Our aim in creating this model is to contribute a fundamental, yet understandable representation of aerosol dynamics, which can be utilized for task-specific applications or as a pedagogical tool. Such a model could be particularly valuable in training and validating more sophisticated models, evaluating specific assumptions or representing a particular physical process in detail. For example, this type of model could be used to validate and verify complex simulation tools like ENSPIRE and FLUIDISK by comparing and contrasting results. We discuss a hypothetical scenario in which our model could be employed to estimate the relationship between aerosol concentration and dilution distance using only camera footage, demonstrating its potential as an open-source, engineering-level tool. We conclude by highlighting the benefits of utilizing this type of simplified model in reducing the computational requirements for more complex models, effectively performing "physics-based learning rate adjustment." We outline a strategy in which a simplified model is initially trained to generate reliable statistics, which are then utilized to train a more complex model using these statistical values rather than attempting to model the physics directly. This approach, inspired by the physics-by-example method, can be viewed as a variant of physics-based learning rate adjustment. We refer to this methodology as "physics-by-statistics." In a future study, we will investigate the prospect of utilizing this simplified model as a forward solver to generate precise time- and spatially-dependent aerosol concentration data, which can then be employed as a boundary condition for more complex modeling techniques in reverse simulation studies. To evaluate the effectiveness of various chess openings, a cluster analysis of games played on the Lichess platform using the Economic Fitness and Complexity algorithm has been employed. This method recognizes areas of similarity within the game tree and assigns a fitness score to node representations. Through a dynamic approach, the fitness scores are adjusted in accordance with recent achievements in chess. The outcomes show that certain openings are linked to specific player skill levels and that even minor variations in openings are associated with distinct levels of proficiency. Consequently, a more precise assessment of chess players' abilities is possible by taking their opening strategies into account. Furthermore, a more comprehensive evaluation of chess openings can be achieved by considering how they interact with the platform's players. A ranking system for 35 popular openings has been developed, taking into account their associated player skills and how they contribute to success on the Lichess platform. The findings show that even the most aggressive opening strategies are not linked to improved skills and that more modest approaches may be beneficial for novice players. This research provides a basis for further investigations into the relationship between chess strategies and player skills. Additionally, the analysis highlights potential issues with the Lichess platform's rating system and opens discussions on how to use the GFC to identify novel strategies for chess players. The evolution of close binary stars can lead to the formation of an unusually massive neutron star born from a stellar collapse that has grown larger than its companion, typically a less massive star. As the companion star interacts with the neutron star over time, it may lose mass, fueling the growth of the neutron star through a process known as accretion-induced collapse. This chapter will provide detailed information about the accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs and neutron stars, including the signs and effects of such events, the representation of such processes in binary star models, and proposed methods for identifying and studying accretion-induced collapse events. Additionally, we will cover the potential impact of such events on pulsar surveys and the study of supernovae, as well as how to further improve existing methods for identifying and studying such events, making it possible to utilize large astrophysical datasets to study compact binary evolution. Specifically, we will explore recent findings including the discovery of the second confirmed compact birth from an accretion-induced collapse, the discovery of the pulsar J1418-2523, and how this finding offers further evidence of such events. Overall, we will provide an in-depth overview of the state of knowledge on such events, highlighting both established facts and areas for further research and study. Ultimately, we will outline the opportunities and challenges presented by deep all-sky pulsar surveys such as the Gaia survey, the Pan-STARRS experiment, and the LSST project, and how these changing research landscape will impact our understanding of such events in the future. In particular, we will cover how these new sources will provide access to: existing data sets that could be re-analyzed for possible events, the potential for discovering pulsars with characteristics of such events, and new tools and methods for identifying and studying such events. Additionally, we will explore at what point future advances in the study of such events will necessitate the involvement of other research specializations, such as gravitational wave research, in order to make progress in this field. The exoplanet HD80606b undergoes a substantial temperature shift as it orbits its parent star, exhibiting a notable rise of up to 1000K in effective temperature as it moves from its unilluminated to fully illuminated positions.  Although previous studies suggested the presence of a thermal equilibrium state in HD80606b's transits, our research presents a new thermal model that accurately captures the planet's varying temperatures and phases.  We propose a two-layer model, incorporating a thick atmosphere and inner core, to account for HD80606b's unique thermal properties and observations of its transit phases, and also to analyze its thermal evolution over 100 million years of orbital motion.  Our thermal model is in close agreement with the planet's observed temperatures and shapes of its transits, and successfully recreates the distinct temperature and luminosity variations observed in HD80606b's longest periods of orbital motion.  Our study further reveals the effects of the planet's atmospheric expansion and vertical mixing on its thermal dynamics, and proposes interior and atmospheric composition scenarios that could maintain a thermal equilibrium state in HD80606b's transit phases.  Our models indicate that HD80606b's internal temperature and structure remain relatively constant over a 100 million-year period of orbital motion, and rule out the possibility of the planet's atmospheric expansion being primarily driven by irradiation alone.  Our study demonstrates the ability of the planet's thermal dynamics to provide insights into its internal composition, and suggests the need for further observations of HD80606b's long orbital periods to refine our thermal models and improve our understanding of the planet's internal structure and composition. Current best practices in autonomous navigation involve employing local cost functions that forecast environmental changes along a planned path. However, this approach can lead to suboptimal outcomes in complex environments where the path may not be followed as intended. In this study, we introduce a novel model called MemoNav that capitalizes on memory-based shortcuts to bypass obstacles, augmenting the traditional local cost function with a memory cost term that estimates the scenario's persistence along different routes. MemoNav's memory cost term is learned through a convolutional neural network that maps beam angles to a memory map, which is then forecast over a rolling window of past sensor readings. During navigation, the model compares forecasted scenes to the originally encountered ones, calculating the memory cost which guides optimal steering. In our assessment, MemoNav achieves better performance than an approach using a global map and a constant steering threshold, resulting in a significant reduction in steering adjustments and more efficient path planning. Traditional information theory typically assumes that past data can be fully accessed in order to understand a communication channel's characteristics, limitations, and performance potential. However, in reality, many systems, such as digital signals and biological pathways, experience a delay between when information is received and when it can be used, causing past data to be partially or fully inaccessible. This delay, which we'll refer to as causalization time, has significant implications for the performance of memory-limited systems and can significantly impact channel capacity when causal state information is available. To better understand the effects of this availability, we develop a mathematical model that measures a channel's capacity under various causalization times and observe that this capacity can be both positively and negatively affected. Interestingly, we find that there are specific ranges of causalization times within which the capacity remains consistent, much like how certain frequencies are not affected by causality in physical systems. To optimize communication in such systems, we devise simple, low-complexity encoding and decoding methods that achieve these optimal performance levels. Finally, we test our models and strategies in scenarios involving mixed channels, which combine deterministic and random effects, and discover new applications and challenges in such systems. Overall, our study highlights the significant impact of causality on system performance and reveals previously unrecognized connections between information theory and the inherent delays in physical systems. Additionally, our work also addresses outstanding issues in the current literature on information theory and state collecting. In iron-based superconductors, the combination of spin-orbit coupling and superconductivity yields a unique symmetry that protects a topological superconducting phase from perturbations. Although this phenomenon has been extensively studied theoretically, there has been limited experimental verification. This study presents experimental findings on the proximal superconductor/ferromagnet interface, demonstrating that the superconducting leading order tunneling density of states exhibits a notable increase of approximately 20% due to spin-orbit coupling. This interface can be treated as a three-terminal spin valve, whose tunneling properties are highly responsive to external magnetic fields. Isolated spin-orbit effects are distinguished from magnetic effects through comparative analysis of tunneling spectra obtained from different iron-based superconductors with varying spontaneous magnetic fields. Ultimately, this study offers a new method for detecting superconducting topological order at a macroscopic scale. Additionally, this research may contribute to the development of topological superconducting nanowires and the discovery of topological superconducting materials. Based on the experimental findings, it is speculated that the superconducting topological order in FeTe1-xFex can be enhanced by adjusting its chemical composition via stoichiometry. This prediction is consistent with previous experimental observations of the material. Lastly, this study presents a theoretical calculation of the superconducting topological order in FeTe1-xFex as a function of chemical composition, which confirms the experimental predictions made earlier. This study provides a new approach for detecting superconducting topological order in materials, which can be extended to other superconducting systems as well. Ultimately, this research offers a new method for evaluating the superconducting phase of any material that features a combination of spin-orbit coupling and superconductivity. As a result, this study has significant implications for the broader field of condensed matter physics. \\ \\ --- Abstract in Russian ---

The steady-state flow equation in an anisotropic, vertically-stratified aquifer was reworked into a single second-order partial differential equation with changing properties across layers. By assuming the hydraulic conductivity changes linearly within each layer, the partial differential equation was further simplified and combined into a first-order equation with a coefficient that accounts for the entire layer. Two scenarios were considered: (i) constant porosity across all layers and (ii) variable porosity across all layers, and both cases were further analyzed using the method of characteristics. Nonetheless, specific solutions using the method of variation of parameters and integration by parts were only presented for the case of variable porosity. The resulting expression for the specific discharge includes integration with layer thickness and a logarithmic term, and when applied to two-layer systems, the derived expression matched the standard solution for such systems. Furthermore, numerical examples were conducted to validate the derived formulas. The derived expression for specific discharge was found to be more feasible to apply numerically than the original partial differential equation. The study confirms that the steady-state flow can be efficiently determined across entire layers by integrating specific discharge across each layer. The derived equations may be useful in determining steady-state flow in two- and three-layer systems. The approach is expected to be applicable to multi-layer systems with similar properties. The conjugate gradient method and the finite element method are suggested as potential methods for solving partial differential equations in future studies. Additionally, the study emphasizes the importance of accurately determining hydraulic conductivity and thickness of each layer for accurate steady-state flow determination. The accuracy of the results is significantly influenced by these parameters, especially for two-layer systems. The derived equations provide a useful framework for future studies on transient flow in such systems. The non-zero non-homogeneous term in the partial differential equation may be an appropriate representation of natural or anthropogenic sources or sinks in the aquifer. The derivation of the steady-state flow equation in such systems could be extended to include the effect of surface water. The approach could also be applied to cooperative flow between layered systems with highly conducting and low-conducting layers. The derived equations may also be applicable to saltwater intrusion in such systems in the future. This study investigates the sulfur dioxide elimination performance in an oxidative reactor using ozone and ultraviolet light. The reactor's response to various influent sulfur dioxide concentrations is examined through both modeling and experimental methods. The models developed accurately predict the reactor's performance for different conditions, including different sizes and flow rates, as well as the effects of oxygen and ozone dosages. The results show that increasing reactor size or residence time leads to higher sulfur dioxide removal rates, but the actual removal rate peaks at a specific residence time and then declines. A mathematical equation is also formulated to optimize sulfur dioxide removal, taking into account various influent concentrations, ozone dosage, and other factors. The optimal conditions for maximum removal rates occur at lower ozone dosages and flow rates, and the model shows a high degree of accuracy in predicting the reactor's performance for a range of concentrations and residence times. The application of this model to a specific industrial flue gas treatment process confirms its practical usefulness. The study further examines the effects of turbulent mixing on the reactor's performance, using two different parameters to model the ozone-sulfur dioxide reaction. The results show that different models yield similar predictions for high sulfur dioxide concentrations, but the actual removal rates differ significantly at lower concentrations. Finally, the potential for an oxidative reactor to remove sulfur dioxide in flue gases is evaluated, considering both the reactor's capacity and energy requirements. The results indicate that such a reactor could not meet the federal regulations set for sulfur dioxide emissions in the United States, either in terms of the reactor's capacity or the energy expended. Therefore, an alternative approach using an in-line scrubber is recommended for sulfur dioxide removal in flue gases. The study confirms the effectiveness and applicability of the models developed for an oxidative reactor using ozone and ultraviolet light. The results show that such a reactor has the potential to remove sulfur dioxide very effectively, with high removal rates and low energy requirements. Specifically, at a residence time of ten seconds, the reactor can achieve nearly ninety-nine percent removal rates for concentrations as high as two hundred micrograms per cubic meter. The study further confirms the robustness of the models by examining a wide range of variables, including different oxygen and sulfur dioxide concentrations, water content, temperature, and particle loads. The results show that the reactor's performance remains unchanged even under conditions of very high particle loads, where the particle-coil removal mechanism dominates the sulfur dioxide removal rates. The increase in energy efficiency achieved by neuromorphic accelerators through binary neural networks comes with its own limitations - the need for significant memory bandwidth and data transmission between cores. As a result, the architecture of how the virtual platform is segmented can greatly impact performance, yet researching this aspect is hindered by the high development time of custom HW-SW interfaces for FPGAs. With the growing interest in customizable computing, there's a corresponding need for an automated tool to generate HW-SW interfaces for various platform architectures, enabling fast design space exploration. The proposal of NeoTile marks a significant breakthrough in hardware acceleration, but its dual-memory architecture poses challenges in achieving high transmission speeds comparable to through-silicon interconnects. The presented tool generates hardware for communicating between cores, including data transmitters, receivers, and management units, using VHDL and a unified interface for digital signals. The tool enables a platform with multiple memory banks and supports various packet-based protocols, including a novel one specifically designed to reduce data transmission between cores. The tool's performance was validated by implementing a binary CNN on the V1G2 Pynq board, resulting in a significant speedup of 22.4 times over software-based implementations on CPU and a substantial reduction of 5.6 times in memory usage compared to a single memory bank architecture. We introduce Indecision Trees, a novel model of computationally efficient decision-making models called Networks, where each node represents a question or action, and is either a decision made by a question, or an action taken without further inquiry. By balancing the need for detailed inquiry and the urgency of action, Indecision Trees achieve a balance between the generality of Network specifications and the speed of inference processes. In turn, this allows Indecision Trees to be generated efficiently in polynomial time, and to yield significant computational benefits for conventional machine learning tasks such as classification. In particular, we demonstrate Indecision Trees' capacity to accelerate key inference processes like Belief Updating and Counterfactual Reasoning, which are crucial for applications like Natural Language Processing and Program Verification, respectively. Our mathematical analysis reveals that Indecision Trees scale more efficiently than conventional decision trees and networks, and often yield significant performance gains. For instance, in settings like Graph-Based Text Classification, we observe average inference speeds of up to 58% faster than conventional models, while still achieving similar accuracy. Our empirical findings are further substantiated by a theoretical proof of near-equal performance capabilities, establishing Indecision Trees as a viable and efficient alternative to traditional models. This research is a significant enhancement to previous work on decision-making models, and paves the way for new applications in areas like Symmetric Program Verification and Quantum Circuit Learning. Moreover, the conceptual novelty of Indecision Trees itself offers fresh avenues for investigation in Quantum Computing, like the potential for reducing the number of qubits required to solve problems efficiently. Additionally, the INDICE algorithm for constructing Indecision Trees presents a novel approach to solving the long-standing Open Problem of Efficient Decision Tree Construction, and yields polynomial time bounds that surpass previous state-of-the-art results. Consequently, the time complexity of INDICE matches the existing lower bounds for this problem, making it the first known algorithm for constructing decision trees in linear time. In terms of scalability, we observe that the size of Indecision Trees constructed by INDICE grows linearly with the number of attributes, and scales sublinearly with the number of classes, which facilitates the construction of highly efficient Indecision Trees, especially when the number of classes is relatively low. For instance, in settings like Graph-Based Text Classification with many classes, we observe a size growth of at most 12 times, which is a manageable upper limit. This study and data collection framework addresses a pressing need in evaluating automatic grading systems for introductory programming courses. These systems are particularly crucial in ensuring the fair assessment of large student cohorts teaching such courses. We developed a framework that integrates existing tools for measuring code quality and automatic grading. We conducted an experiment with approximately 800 students whose programming skills ranged from introductory to semi-proficient, submitting 16 diverse tasks over a period of two academic sessions. Our experiment examined two aspects: the impact of providing feedback on test cases and code quality, and the effect of assigning multiple tasks on grading performance. We collected data on code quality, performance on individual and multi-task assignments, and the correlation between these metrics. Our results indicate that providing feedback on test cases enhances code quality but not grading performance. Conversely, feedback on code quality and multi-task assignments simultaneously lead to higher grades. We discovered a positive, moderate correlation between code quality and performance on multi-task assignments. These findings suggest that the same feedback can benefit students' code quality and grading performance, and that leveraging multiple assessment metrics can yield stronger predictive outcomes. We anticipate these results to inspire and guide research in the field of automatic grading, while also highlighting potential practical applications for instructors and grading systems. Advancements in machine learning have led to the widespread use of black-box classifiers, despite their lack of transparency in showing the impact of input features on their decisions. To address this, symbolic surrogate models have been developed to generate simple, interpretable models imitating complex, black-box ones. Nonetheless, current research using symbolic surrogates has primarily focused on understanding the global structure of these classifiers, without delving into how features affect the classifiers' output. To uncover such relationships, we propose a new approach that employs program synthesis to develop symbolic models. We then validate our method by comparing it to a variable-based method in an analysis of a breast cancer dataset, revealing the former discovers more meaningful feature interactions as identified in multiple studies. Furthermore, we reveal new, statistically significant feature combinations contributing to the classifiers' output, unforeseen by the variable-based method or human domain experts. Ultimately, our approach provides a deeper, more intricate insight into the decision-making processes of black-box classifiers. We intend to enable researchers to leverage this greater complexity in classification models, uncovering novel, data-driven insights that can drive further analysis and inform domain experts. In the future, we aim to expand our technique to allow for the discovery of more complex feature combinations by using more sophisticated forms of logic to guide the search for possible models. In addition to machine learning, our method can be applied to other areas of study where understanding how input variables interact is crucial for developing informative models. For instance, we could analyze how genetic variables impact the risk of developing a disease. In a different direction, we could examine the effect of environmental factors on a disease risk to better understand non-genetic inherited risks. In all these scenarios, our goal is to identify the underlying interactions that inform public policies and public awareness while also respecting privacy concerns. Based on these findings, we develop Algorithms for Mitigating Over-smoothing with practical applications, and our empirical results on real-world datasets showcase the efficacy of our approach in reducing over-smoothing compared to existing methods. Our analysis also highlights the interplay between these factors, which provides new insights for developers in the field of graph convolutional networks. We introduce BFKL equations incorporating an additional type of motion, beyond longitudinal and transverse movement, which affects the positions of partons within hadrons, particularly in the context of small-$x$ scattering. To incorporate this into the BFKL equation, we modify both the kernel and single-scale parameters according to the impact of this new motion. Utilizing a potential $V(x)$ for internal parton motion, we formulate this modified kernel and demonstrate that it maintains the integrability of the BFKL equation. Furthermore, we analyze potential corrections at the next-to-leading order (NLO) and observe that the new motion introduces an additional factor into reggeization compared to leading-order (LO) case. On the other hand, at NLO, the constraint under consideration, which affects the kernel, can be removed due to the presence of two reggeization parameters. Internet Service Providers, such as Metro Ethernet, have a content delivery market where they compete with each other by investing in infrastructure to benefit multiple Content Providers. We focus on a specific market structure where Metro Ethernet Service Providers invest in delivering popular content to geographically dispersed users and develop a cooperative strategy to manage their investments, aiming to maximize combined earnings and achieve better results compared to a non-cooperative approach. Our analysis shows that cooperation yields higher payoffs for Content Providers and more profitable investments for Service Providers, exceeding the payoffs achieved through individual investment efforts. We present an innovative cooperative solution, along with the corresponding nonnegative scalar multiplier problems, to establish the optimality conditions for both Content Providers and Service Providers. Our study examines how the number of Service Providers affects investments, revealing that cooperation leads to increased investments from each Service Provider when there are two or more of them, whereas investments remain the same when there is only one Service Provider. We also explore how cooperation affects investments by Service Providers when there are two Content Providers, discovering that each Service Provider reduces investment when the other increases it. We conduct numerical case studies to illustrate our model's behavior and confirm through sensitivity analysis that our model's results are versatile and applicable to a wide range of parameter settings. Our investigation is relevant to the current market dynamics of Metro Ethernet Service Providers, such as CenturyLink and Comporium, and our analysis sheds light on the potential impact of changes in user location and content popularity on investment strategies. Our model also offers a valuable tool for Service Providers to determine their optimal investment in response to changes in market conditions, such as increased traffic or competition, by comparing the current and modified scenarios using our cooperative and non-cooperative approaches. Our study confirms that cooperation has a positive effect on investment decisions, resulting in better outcomes for both Service Providers and Content Providers. We conclude by highlighting the challenges and opportunities presented by changes in user behavior, content distribution across Metro Ethernet networks, and the potential for Service Providers to expand their infrastructure and compete in other market segments. Our analysis suggests numerous avenues for further research and contributes to the ongoing discussions in the communications industry about investments in Metro Ethernet networks. Our study demonstrates that cooperation among Service Providers yields more efficient investment decisions, benefiting both Service Providers and Content Providers, and provides an actionable guide for Service Providers and network administrators to make informed investment decisions in response to changes in market conditions and network developments. Our findings offer practical insights and policy recommendations for Service Providers and network policymakers, emphasizing the need to address ongoing transformations in user behavior, content offerings, and network developments across Metro Ethernet

This research paper studies twists in finite group actions on a torus through the lens of equivariant cohomology, building upon ideas from 'twisted' topological theories as explored in string theory. We demonstrate that by incorporating twisted equivariant cohomology, twists can be captured by a group action orbit. Additionally, we develop an algorithm to compute twisted equivariant cohomology with a torus as the base space, applying this method to the torus's own twisted action. The findings reveal an interesting connection between twisted and unrestrained equivariant cohomology within torus scenarios. Furthermore, we connect these concepts to both the unrestrained case and the Braids' signed cohomology from Menichi's work. Building on Kiems' premise that equivariant differential forms can be used to develop an orientation for the equivariant sphere, we show this construction satisfies all of Borel's and Moore and Smith's criteria for an orientation. Finally, we link this equivariant sphere with Kostant's tangent spaces on orbit spaces, calculating the cohomology of these spaces in both the unrestrained and restricted cases. This research serves as the foundation for examining twists in actions on more complex manifolds and further exploring the connections between equivariant cohomology and the Borel-equivariant Dolbeault cohomology of complex manifolds. It also explores at length the twisted action on one-dimensional complexes, examining a case involving six generators and a specific twist. Furthermore, this document includes an investigation of the twisted action on the torus by its three generators, 1, r, and r^2, using techniques similar to those applied in the one-dimensional scenario. We investigate how sellers behave in non-credible second-price auctions by employing an extensive-game model. Our research indicates that sellers fail to generate maximum revenue when they participate in such auctions and frequently refrain from revealing their true values, even in situations where it would be beneficial to do so. Our findings suggest that two main factors contribute to this non-compliance: (1) the difficulty in obtaining high revenue in auctions with multiple bidders, which necessitates submitting authentic values, and (2) the tendency for bidders to place higher bids when prices are high, which creates an incentive for sellers to deceive other participants. Our model is applicable to a broad range of auctions beyond the second-price variety. Additionally, its insights are not limited to auctions; they also have implications for other settings where actors make strategic decisions in multiple situations. Our study focuses on the effects of changes in bidders' characteristics and market conditions on the amount of revenue generated in auctions. Our findings show that in situations where bidders' characteristics and market conditions change, the revenue gained from non-credible auctions often decreases, which indicates that non-compliance may result in a loss of revenue. Our research also examines how the participation of multiple sellers in auctions impacts the strategies employed and reveals that non-compliance is more likely in situations where sellers participate in small numbers and when bids related to the seller's item have a significant connection with other auctions. Our analysis further highlights the challenge in developing methods that enable participants to identify whether an auction is credible or not. Our evaluation shows that the highest level of uncertainty regarding an auction's credibility occurs when the participation of multiple sellers is involved and when bids related to the seller's item have a significant connection with other auctions. Our study confirms a previous discovery made by Brown and Hassid (2015) that in credible second-price auctions the strategies employed by sellers involve revealing their true values in situations where it would be beneficial to do so and not maximizing their revenue when they participate in such auctions. This paper introduces an innovative approach to generating brushstrokes for paintings by leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks, specifically tailored for continuous, high-dimensional data. Our method generates brushstrokes as dynamic trajectories in three-dimensional space, influenced by prior brushstrokes and artistic intentions. To create realistic brushstrokes, we develop brush models that mimic real brushes, using prior brushstrokes to inform future brushstrokes. Our system enables the creation of brushstrokes at multiple scales, from fine details to broad strokes. To achieve this, we develop a simple yet effective algorithm for learning brushstrokes, combining prior work on graph neural networks and adversarial training. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of our method in producing natural-looking brushstrokes, brush tips, and painting scales. Our approach enables the creation of brushstrokes with varying thickness and colors, similar to those found in actual paintings. To compare the performance of our method, we created a dataset of brushstrokes using a traditional technique, specific to the Rembrandt course at the Utrecht University of Art and Design. Our study indicates that our generative model outperforms the existing method in terms of generating brushstrokes. Additionally, our analysis reveals unique characteristics of the brushstrokes generated by our method, which were not present in the traditional dataset. To reproduce our results, you can visit our website at https:// brushstrokes.in.uu.nl. Our generative model is designed to run on standard GPUs, and our source code, as well as the brushstroke dataset, is available at https:// brushstrokes.in.uu.nl, our Facebook page at @brushstrokes, or by contacting the main author at [johan.thammer@gmail.com]. The fast instability emerges at the interface of a hydrogen-rich ejecta layer and the expanding shockwave in a type II supernova. Ejecta density is critical to the development of this instability, yet the density profile is uncertain. Studies suggest the density increases gradually within the ejecta layer, whereas 1D hydrodynamics simulations often reveal a complex and unpredictable shockwave structure, making it difficult to pinpoint the location where the instability arises. Consequently, researchers previously assumed the instability occurred at the outer edge of the ejecta layer. We performed the first comprehensive 3D study of the fast instability, using pre-calculated supernova ejecta and simulating the early supernova explosion. Our model began with an outer shockwave perturbation consisting of both radial and axial variations, creating a complex structure that facilitated the development of the instability. Pulsation modes arose due to variations in density, causing the shockwave to modify its shape and move inward. As the shockwave receded, regions of high curvature led to the formation of self-gravitating cavities. Notably, our model revealed the instability failed to occur at lower energy levels, but succeeded at higher energy levels, marking a significant shift from previous studies. At higher energy levels, our model revealed the creation of a low-density bubble behind the shockwave, accompanied by the development of the instability. Our model suggests the probability of the instability occurring depends on the efficiency of the supernova explosion, with a greater probability at higher explosion energies. Our findings also highlight the disparity between 1D hydrodynamics simulations and 3D numerical simulations, emphasizing the importance of fully understanding the early supernova explosion. Our model has paved the way for further studies of the instability's impact on the structure and chemical composition of the ejecta layer. Our study demonstrates the complexity of the fast instability, emphasizing the need for additional simulations to better understand its development and effects. Our model reveals the potential for the instability to significantly impact the structure and chemical composition of the ejecta layer, leading to a greater yield of nitrogen and its final location near the outer edge of the ejecta layer. Our study marks a significant advancement in the understanding of the instability and its effects on the structure and chemical composition of the ejecta layer. Our model invites further additional simulations to better understand the role of the instability in supernova explosion. Our research tackles this challenge by developing a novel algorithm that chooses optimal primer pairs for each partition by minimizing overlapping and allowing data distribution flexibility. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method through realistic simulations, which show significant performance improvements over existing approaches. The speed of waves produced by an oscillator in a given environment is of significant interest in active matter research. Although the linear approximation yields the expected speed, deviations from linearity affect this process, and their impact remains understudied. By placing an active particle within a dynamic medium that follows the Alexei-Vicsek protocol, our research observes wave speed variations in response to changes in environmental activity levels, particle size, and wave frequency. Through both numerical and analytical means, our findings reveal that speed changes result from interactions between the oscillator and the surrounding wave system, and our analysis provides a framework for predicting these interactions and their effects on wave speed. Furthermore, our results validate the conventional assumption that the speed of waves in an active system is independent of the frequency of the oscillator. However, we discovered a rare situation in which this assumption is broken, and the role of the oscillator frequency in determining wave speed becomes evident. The effectiveness of machine learning models in solving real-world problems depends heavily on the credibility of their underlying assumptions and the quality of their training data. For medical image classification tasks, supplying models with additional clinical characteristics enhances their reliability, but supplementing training data becomes a more feasible option. We explored how data augmentation methods with and without clinical features affect the reliability of models predicting patient symptoms and examined how these methods compare to model training with clinical features. Our analysis reveals that model reliance on clinical features lessens as the symptoms have broader applications and are more closely associated with specific diseases. A novel quantum algorithm for clustering is proposed, based on a quantum version of the K-means method. This algorithm leverages quantum computers to process data points and their centroids, treating them as quantum states. Specifically, it employs two operations: the unitary rotation of data points based on centroids, and the application of an inverse phase shift to separate clusters. Due to its quantum nature, the algorithm's running time is significantly reduced, at an O(n^2) complexity, which is an improvement over classical methods at the expense of several assumptions. particularly, it assumes data points can be perfectly categorized after each iteration, which may not always be the case in practice. Furthermore, a hybrid approach is developed to facilitate the implementation of this quantum algorithm on near-term quantum devices without a quantum compiler. This allows for the creation of a quantum network architecture for clustering, which can be efficiently run on near-term devices. Finally, the proposed quantum clustering algorithm is tested on synthetic datasets, and the results show it outperforms classical methods in terms of data separation for two-gaussian datasets. however, for more diverse datasets, classical methods remain competitive. potentially, improvements could be achieved through a quantum version of data preprocessing. We suggest an approach for shadow computation that draws upon triangle
approximations and retains accuracy within a pre-defined error margin. This
method leverages and extends the parallel ray-triangle intersection algorithm.
By using a shadow mapping technique with triangle centers as key factors, we
generate certified shadow maps that ensure precise results. We propose the
Minimally Expansive Cone of Uncertainty (MEC) framework for establishing
shadow regions and outlining confidence intervals. Moreover, we extend traditional
ray tracing techniques with uncertainty quantification through the adoption
of our shadow computation method. We compare the performance of our shadow
computation method with that of prior approaches and establish that our technique
is both faster and more accurate. Additionally, we showcase the application of
our shadow computation method to generating measurably correct images and for
performing robust rendering operations. Since our shadow computation method can
be decoupled from the rendering pipeline, it may also be utilized for other tasks. We
demonstrate the implementation of our method through a test suite consisting of
renderers built using modern graphics APIs such as Vulkan and Direct X, and
provide the associated source code for evaluation purposes. Experimental
evaluations were conducted across a variety of scenes, ranging from simple objects
to 3D models like human bodies and cars. Our method has been found to be both
accurate and efficient with a frame rate exceeding 60 frames per second for
complex scenes. We store the test data and source code for our method on an
external website for reference purposes. Further details can be accessed at the
website indicated in the reference list at the end of this document. \par

In probabilistic origin-destination demand modeling, the probabilistic Wardrop equilibrium (PWE) is a widely recognized concept. With an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm, PWE can be efficiently estimated. However, AMP faces the issue of accurately estimating the covariance matrix, which is used to compute the demand matrix. Unfortunately, the zero-mean assumption, necessary for AMP to work, does not account for the off-diagonal structures resulting from statistical relationships and road connections. Previous studies resolved this problem by employing a structured sparsity approach with a block-wise diagonal regularization. However, such methods have limitations in practice due to the need for prior knowledge of the structure. In an attempt to overcome this limitation, the study presents a new approach based on lasso regularization, aiming to enhance the accuracy of the covariance matrix and extend the application to various networks. The study demonstrates the improved lasso method's effectiveness in scenarios with and without known network structures, leading to more reliable results in both cases. Furthermore, the proposed approach allows for the incorporation of probabilistic link demands, thus providing a more comprehensive O-D demand estimation. The improved lasso method outperforms traditional and structured sparsity approaches in terms of covariance matrix accuracy and overall generalization. The study's findings are significant, as they promote the use of lasso regularization in probabilistic O-D demand modeling and pave the way for its extension to more complex network settings. We've examined the stability of phase-locked states in networks of nonlinear oscillators, where the frequency dispersion is weak but widespread. Unlike the stronger dispersion often studied, where it splits into quasi-localized patterns, we've found that weak dispersion stabilizes localized patterns and allows for a wider range of synchronization frequencies. Through both mathematical and numerical analyses, we've demonstrated how localized patterns and fixed points emerge and transition in networks of coupled oscillators, where small changes in the system can lead to significant pattern and network dynamics shifts. These stability features are consistent across various coupling mechanisms and can be attributed to the localized nature of the weak dispersion itself. These findings are relevant to numerous systems involving synchronized oscillators, including biological networks and electrical communication systems. A more efficient hybrid method is developed for creating uniform spanning trees (UST) through a combination of both exact and approximate techniques. While the exact algorithm generates full detail trees, the approximate method produces USTs with a high degree of accuracy, with the difference in size ranging from 0.01% to 0.4% based on the type of graph. The proposed hybrid algorithm starts with the approximate method and uses the exact method only to generate precise trees when the approximate method's error threshold is exceeded. With the approximate method accounting for the majority of UST generations, the hybrid method significantly outperforms the exact algorithm, resulting in a substantial speedup of 100 to 500 times. Furthermore, the hybrid method offers an efficient alternative to the approximate method alone, providing full precision trees in scenarios where the additional error is unacceptable. Labeled linear dot notation is used to express the generation process of all trees, enabling the efficient creation of full precision trees. The performance of both the approximate and hybrid methods is demonstrated through the generation of USTs for randomly permuted trees. The hybrid method is also applied to the study of protein folding proteins, resulting in the rapid generation of precise USTs for a wide range of proteins, including the 1S5Y and 6O9J structures. The precise USTs obtained provide a valuable framework for the development of algorithms and testing the accuracy of various folding algorithms. This paper presents a multi-agent framework called FollowMe, designed for autonomous driving. It enables a lead vehicle to guide a platoon of cars with varying follower speeds, using a pre-built library of motion patterns. The leader can be either a human or another automated vehicle. To create smooth, continuous trajectories, FollowMe employs motion planning algorithms paired with a simplified model of the vehicles' dynamics. The implementation makes minimal assumptions about the interaction between vehicles, allowing it to operate effectively in turbulent environments. The approach has been successfully tested using simulation tools and compared with a strategy that does not account for the dynamics of follower vehicles. The results show that FollowMe outperforms a previously proposed method known as CarFollowing, especially in scenarios where followers have varied speeds and reactions. The largest improvement was observed in a 'dagger' scenario, where FollowMe performed 33% better than CarFollowing in maintaining a constant distance between the leader and closest follower. The approach has also been compared with another automated driving method and shown to be more adaptable and robust in various scenarios. The proposed framework has many potential applications, including human-robot interaction, racing simulations, and managing traffic flows. We have investigated binomial mixtures consisting of $s$ species each consisting of $N$ identical particles, where one species acts as an activator and the others as inhibitors, under two different non-interactive dynamics: the Bernoulli mixing and the binomial mixing. Our analyses show that, despite the absence of interactions, these mixtures can exhibit rich and complex behavior, forming numerous stable states. In particular, we found that the maximum number of distinct stable states in the Bernoulli mixing is equal to the number of species in the mixture, while for larger systems, we established an upper limit on the number of stable states in the binomial mixing, which approaches half the number of species as the system size grows. Our numerical results confirm these predictions, validating our analytical findings. Our study provides a framework for understanding more complex systems consisting of multiple species interacting through weak forces, and its implications, along with difficulties in establishing the presence of stable states in such systems, are discussed. Our analysis also offers insights into the emergence of complex phenomena in non-interactive systems. Our results may be of interest in the study of mixtures consisting of active and inactive species, including systems observed in cell biology where the presence or absence of signaling molecules determines their behavior and response to external stimuli. Ultimately, our investigation offers a better understanding of one type of complex system, which can be generalized to mixtures of multiple species interacting through weak forces. Our study may be relevant in fields such as biomedicine, population dynamics, and geological processes where similar types of systems are studied. To our knowledge, our finding the maximum number of stable states in the Bernoulli mixing, along with our bound on the number of stable states in the binomial mixing, has never been reported before. Our analytical results are corroborated by numerical investigations, which are in agreement with simulations of systems consisting of up to 10,000 particles. Our study offers a starting point for examining the critical behavior and phase transitions in systems consisting of multiple species interacting through weak forces, which may be explored in future research. Our results could be compared with experiments on mixtures of active and inactive species, such as systems studied in cell biology where the presence or absence of signaling molecules determines their behavior and response to external stimuli, their behavior parallels that of ferromagnetic and ferroelectric systems, including spontaneous symmetry breaking and switchability. Our discovery may inspire new experiments on ferromagnetic and ferroelectric systems that examine the presence or absence of signaling molecules, their behavior, and their response to external stimuli

Observations of sunspots have detected sudden changes, known as magnetic waves or flares, traveling across the surface of the Sun at high speeds of up to 2000 km per second, originating from solar flares and other explosive events. Similar phenomena have been discovered in the context of exoplanets, particularly super-Earths, which exhibit rapid magnetic changes in their star-disc systems or when passing in front of stars in transit observations. We present initial evidence of a magnetic wave on a super-Earth, known as K2-27 b, based on data from the Multi-color Optical Lever technique used in transit observations, revealing a magnetic fluctuation traveling at 1000 km per second across the star-disc system. We attribute the source of this phenomenon to explosive events on the star or one of two existing giant planets present. We calculated the frequency of these magnetic waves and found it matches predictions of celestial bodies of varying sizes, ranging from stars to super-Earths and planets. This finding could be the first of its kind to document a magnetic wave on a super-Earth and opens up the potential for further research into similar phenomena in celestial bodies of this size and others. The Madsen-Weiss theorem can be seen as a connection between several concepts: the b-principle, stability theorems, and a new class of morphisms that preserve mapping classes. This influence can be seen in different areas: the application of the b-principle in homology planes, the proof of a stability theorem in the Picard group of the Torelli group, and the unique characteristic of the Madsen-Weiss morphism that arises from the combination of the b-principle and stability theorems. Furthermore, the proof relies on a new class of morphisms that combine the features of the Madsen-Weiss morphism and the morphisms obtained from the combination of the b-principle and stability theorems. Although the Madsen-Weiss morphism is distinct in this sense, it becomes apparent that the difference is only significant at a finite level of skeletons when comparing the two morphisms. Consequently, the Madsen-Weiss morphism is shown to be a particular example of the morphisms that emerge from the combination of the b-principle and stability theorems. Additionally, this analysis leads to a new class of morphisms that reflect the combination of the features of the Madsen-Weiss morphism and the morphisms obtained from the combination of the b-principle and stability theorems. This new class of morphisms is characterized as strictly discrete and has compact boundaries, and can be seen as a more refined version of the morphisms that arise from the combination of the b-principle and stability theorems, which are themselves a more general form of the Madsen-Weiss morphism. Furthermore, an inspection of the underlying graphs of these morphisms suggests the presence of an interesting geometric pattern, and it can be strongly conjectured that the graphs of both morphisms are equivalent and share a specific universal mapping class group action. This conjectured equivalence is the basis for a proposed program of research called the b-principle program, which aims to analyze and study the combination of the b-principle and stability theorems within the context of Madsen-Weiss morphisms. This program offers an exciting new direction for research in the field and offers promising prospects for further advancement. At present, the program is self-contained and does not rely on any external scientific evidence or findings, however it is expected to have significant scientific repercussions in the future. This work offers algebraic and element-wise interpretations of the Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) method for finite element problems, and examines their similarities and differences. A specific BDDC algorithm is applied to a range of problems with various balancing parameters, and the resulting preconditioners are compared in terms of energy norm. The study demonstrates that the performance level achieved is dependent on several factors, including the problem's irregularity, solver quality, and accepting criteria. Consequently, there is no universal choice of balancing parameter that is suitable for all problems. Nevertheless, the research yields useful insights that can help inform the selection of balancing parameters in practical applications. The findings are substantiated through a range of numerical experiments. The study also provides a theoretical foundation for further enhancing the BDDC method. The results can be utilized to develop an adaptive balancing parameter strategy, in addition to other potential improvements. An initial implementation of this approach is presented, and tested on a range of problems to yield promising outcomes. The technique is insensitive to the following challenges: non-matching subdomain meshes, irregular elements within each subdomain, and an imperfect initial solution. The algorithm is resilient to variations in the following parameters: a non-uniform coarse problem on the global grid, differing acceptability thresholds, and an inexact solver. The research shows that the BDDC method can be effectively applied to problems with significant irregularities, and that an adaptive balancing parameter strategy can lead to considerable time savings in comparisons to fixed parameter approaches. Consequently, the proposed technique presents a practical solution for a wide range of real-world problems. The algorithm is particularly beneficial in situations where the problem's irregularity cannot be eliminated by refining the mesh. The presented results provide a thorough understanding of the BDDC method's behavior, and offer practical guidance for applying the technique in practical applications. The research is grounded in extensive numerical experiments, and the associated computer code is available for review. The study offers a range of opportunities for further research in this domain. The most promising areas of inquiry include the generalization of the algebraic BDDC method to a broader class of preconditioners, the theoretical analysis of the BDDC method in the context of finite element spaces, and the development of an adaptive balancing parameter strategy that is optimized for specific problems. The generalization of the BDDC method to algebraic preconditioners presents a manageable challenge, whereas the second challenge is more substantial in nature. The third challenge is the most formidable of the three, as the current code can be utilized for practical applications

Systems involving user-generated tags possess distinct characteristics that differentiate them from traditional tagging systems, such as user-generated content being rated and commented upon. To address these system needs, we develop and test a model that integrates user-generated content data into a probabilistic clustering framework, utilizing tag meanings and shared user behavior patterns. This approach is particularly useful for system designers and administrators, enabling them to identify underlying latent structures within tagged data and inform decisions on system functionality and performance. Through analysis of system properties and user behavior, we uncover opportunities for improving existing system features and develop insights to guide the development of new mechanisms for content management. The efficacy of our method is demonstrated in a practical case study involving content hosted on Wikipedia's media wiki platform. Our findings reveal promising new features for enhancing system performance and user experience. Ultimately, this research seeks to stimulate further investigation into the behavioral aspects of tagging systems and their potential for improving system design. We hope to spur a more systematic research agenda focused on leveraging system-generated data to inform theoretical and practical knowledge of tagging system properties and user behavior. Our data and analysis methods are freely accessible at https://osf.io/m3g4c/, under the license CC-BY-4.0. We present our methodology and results at the 10th International Workshop on Tagging and Language Modelling at NAACL 2021. We also make our code and data available at https://osf.io/m3g4c/, under the license CC-BY-4.0. We plan to continue working on this project and appreciate any feedback or contributions that could enhance our approach. Additional resources can be found at https://osf.io/m3g4c/. We look to collaborate with system designers and administrators, encouraging them to adapt our methodology to their specific system needs and user behavior patterns. We are exploring new research avenues focused on leveraging system-generated data to inform theoretical and practical knowledge of tagging system properties and user behavior. We are seeking feedback on our work and look to continue working on this project. We are seeking to spur new ideas and insights that could benefit system designers and administrators, informing decisions on system functionality and performance. We are now examining new research questions focused on the role of user-generated content in tagging systems and will continue to share our findings on system properties and user behavior. Up until now, this balance has been the subject of debate due to discrepancies in the literature regarding the significance of thermoviscous effects in these systems. In order to resolve this issue, numerical experiments were conducted using a zero-order acoustic sensor, and the results showed that thermoviscous effects are indeed crucial for its operation at microscale distances. In fact, the signal strength was dramatically improved by taking these effects into consideration. Consequently, a simplified model was developed to accurately predict the sensor's performance across a range of temperatures and viscosities. The efficacy of the model was verified through comparisons with numerical simulations, and the results show promising potential for applications in heat management at the microscale. Additionally, the study's findings highlight the importance of considering thermoviscous effects in the context of Brownian acoustic sensors. In a broader sense, the research underscores the need for a unified framework for designing thermal energy harvesting devices. Such framework could capitalize on the inherent thermoviscous instability at the microscale to convert thermal fluctuations into usable acoustic signals. Future work will focus on enhancing the sensor's performance through the incorporation of surface roughness and geometric non-uniformities. By exploring novel methods for thermoviscous energy conversion, the goal is to contribute positively to the ongoing debate in this field and bring microscale acoustic metamaterials design one step closer to reality. Moreover, the study's findings can be extended to the realm of light in order to investigate the microscale acoustic-optical coupling phenomenon and its potential applications in light trapping and radiance control applications. This study examines the FENE dumbbell model's low-frequency solutions below the critical frequency within the Besov space and demonstrates that it meets a unique partial differential equation (PDE) which characterizes a low-frequency condition. Consequently, it applies to all dumbbell models that meet this condition, including the NENE and SLLOCC models. Our analysis shows that the low-frequency solutions of the FENE model satisfy the same characteristics as those of the GLEBER model. Additionally, we extend the model by removing the low-frequency restriction, proving that it reaches a steady state within the $L^{\infty}$ space. Our findings are consistent with existing research on the subject. To achieve these results, we used innovative methods, including an approach that reveals the connection between the FENE model and a non-Newtonian fluid characterized by a Charlesworth-Peterlin closure. Our analysis also leads to the observation of a unique singular phenomenon in the context of the model. Ultimately, we prove the stability of the model under certain external influences and leverage its stability to derive bounds on the model's solutions in the high-frequency regime. To do so, we successfully applied the Fourier restriction estimate, an innovation in this research. Additionally, we use the time-frequency paradigm and time-scale analysis to investigate various applications of the model, including dilute solutions and the absorption-dominated regime. Our results in the high-frequency regime are comparable to those obtained by using the Dyson-Benoit approach. Furthermore, we extend the application of the model to include complex polydisperse solutions, a result that reflects recent observations in the context of polymerization reactions. Our analysis indicates the emergence of singularities in this context. To validate the model, we compare its predictions with experimental data on the polymerization of a solution composed of two types of polymers: those with double stars and those with free ends. Our results indicate the model's accuracy up to a frequency threshold of approximately $0.7\times10^{-14}$s$^{-1}$. Our analysis indicates the model's potential for application in the study of various phenomena, including the study of emulsions, biopolymers, and the behavior of bird's tail feathers. Our results are consistent with observations of this natural process. This paper develops an integrated access and backhaul network mIAB to efficiently serve a density of $K$ users traveling together, by integrating ring-shaped mobility patterns and group user data rates. The mIAB network optimizes power supply to base stations and backhaul links, ensuring a minimum power level and maximum backhaul connectivity. The problem is initially treated as a mixed-integer optimization task and later transformed into an equivalent convex optimization problem. We resolve the convex optimization problem through an efficient algorithm and propose two decomposition methods for real-time implementation. The first involves successive convex approximation and the second a heuristic lookup table method. The results show that mIAB outperforms conventional MIMO technology in terms of energy efficiency and connectivity, with minimal computational complexity. Furthermore, mIAB exhibits adaptability in handling large numbers of users and can be easily extended for use in single-user scenarios. Overall, mIAB presents a practical solution that can effectively serve a significant number of users in group settings. The findings suggest that mIAB can enhance connectivity by approximately 100% and boost energy efficiency by around 35% compared to MIMO technology for 30 users. The advantages of mIAB become more pronounced as the number of users exceeds 40. The proposed optimization techniques for power supply and connectivity achieve an average reduction in DOPF instances of around 60% and often lower in single-user scenarios. The look-up table decomposition method demonstrates better computational efficiency than successive convex approximation. Furthermore, the heuristic lookup table method exhibits better performance and faster execution times, with lower complexity and fewer optimization steps. The complexity of decomposition methods increases with the number of base stations, but remains efficient even at high densities. Specifically, the heuristic lookup table method shows minimal complexity in comparison to successive convex approximation, at a density of $K=40$ users. The execution times of both methods increased roughly sixfold at $K=120$ users, but remained under 10 ms. Therefore, the mIAB network and associated optimization techniques present a realistic solution for real-time implementation. The success of decomposition methods encourages the integration of mIAB with other optimization techniques for hybrid networks, promoting further research into this direction. The numerical outcomes confirm the superiority of mIAB over MIMO technology in terms of connectivity and energy efficiency. The efficiency and adaptability of mIAB networks also create opportunities for extending this approach to single-user scenarios, thereby widening its practical applications. This work investigates the link between hyperparameter interaction and algorithm stability in the context of deep neural networks trained with stochastic gradient descent. We illustrate how each training step's hyperparameters - learning rate, batch size, momentum, and random data sampling - interact to affect algorithm stability. In examining the hyperparameter range, we find that learning rates have an exponential impact on the algorithm's stability, whereas the effects of batch size, momentum, and data sampling vary linearly. Notably, the stability of our model can be accurately predicted across a broad spectrum of hyperparameters through analysis of its final performance on a testing set. This finding aligns with the concept of algorithmic stability in algorithm theory and suggests a potential shortcut for determining stable hyperparameters by evaluating the algorithm's performance in an early training phase. We verify the applicability and versatility of our method in three different computer vision tasks and further demonstrate its application as a metric for evaluating the stability of ensemble deep neural networks. In particular, we observe that the performance of ResNets and Ensembles with ResNets can be maximized by adjusting the size of their networks in accordance with our stability analysis. We also use this method to develop robust, highly accurate hyperparameter sets for image classification and object detection tasks. Our method has the further benefit of allowing the detection of unstable components within deep neural networks, which can hinder the performance of the training algorithm and the validity of the maximum margin principle in classification tasks, and of identifying the unstable effects of data sampling. Our research on unstable components has the potential to facilitate the development of training algorithms that make efficient use of the available data. We have made the associated code available at https://github.com/qsub/qsub. Our paper details the method in greater depth and from a theoretical perspective at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.07644. From a practical perspective, the paper may be found at https://100daysds.com/2021/03/02/stability-analysis-of-deep-neural-networks-via-proximity-to-phase-transition.html. The related video can be accessed at https://youtube.com/watch/ watch?v=7VHC3Lv3L3I. Our method, known as stability analysis via proximity to phase transition (STAPLE), can be used to determine the stability of the deep neural networks by counting the number of neurons in the near critical states. This count serves as a reliable predictor of the network's performance in the entire hyperparameter space and can be used for the early evaluation of the algorithm's performance

The quantization of electromagnetic field energy has been validated by comparing its predicted values with observed data from the Balmer series of hydrogen emissions. This includes calculating energy levels using the quantum rule $E_n = R \frac{1}{n^2-1}$ for $n$ ranging from 3 to 30, where $R$ is the energy constant, and comparing these with corresponding energy levels derived from $E_{balmer}(n) = R \frac{2^2}{n^2}-E_0$. These two expressions yield different energy level predictions, with the signs of the denominators reversed in the second expression. When we apply the quantum hypothesis that only certain energy levels are occupied, discrete emissions are predicted, matching the 7 distinct wavelengths observed in the Balmer series. These correspond to $n$ values of 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10 in the first expression and their corresponding negatives in the second expression. The small residual energy levels, calculated as the square root of the product of the negative and higher energy level, suggest the presence of additional, unseen energy levels. Current assessments of reinforcement learning algorithms are limited to specific environments, yet curricula allow for adaptation to multiple scenarios. We propose adapting reinforcement learning algorithms to seamlessly navigate shifting curricula, prompting us to investigate whether established evaluation methods accurately capture their capabilities. By analyzing a renowned dataset with diverse curricula, our study reveals that leading RL algorithms are actually exploiting free rewards in many cases, influencing our assessment of their performance. To guarantee fair evaluations, we suggest introducing structured, sequential tasks within curricula, providing a benchmark dataset, and examining the impact of varying curriculum complexity. Moreover, we investigate whether advanced RL methods are better equipped to handle changing curricula, contrasting their capabilities with simple learning approaches like local self-play. The outcomes of this investigation may prompt a reevaluation of Evaluation Methods in RL. The designed curricula and corresponding data are available at https://github.com/arkhsharma/evaluating_rl_for_curriculum_learning.
