This research introduces a class of continuous-stage Runge-Kutta methods tailored to address Hamiltonian differential problems. We demonstrate that these methods conform to the variable-coefficients variational integrator class, and further, their underlying configurations are rooted in Dirac and constraint-manifesting formulations of classical mechanics. We subsequently establish the construction of continuous-stage Runge-Kutta methods for constrained systems, and in doing so, derive the existing Gear-Garretson method and the newer Delaunay method. To evaluate the performance of these methods, extensive numerical tests are conducted across various test cases. Our findings reveal that the Delaunay method stands out due to its superior adaptability and robustness. We then apply this method to the Hamiltonian formulation of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, allowing for the numerical integration of this problem which had previously been challenging. Our numerical tests yield accurate results and verify the conservation of the equation's intrinsic invariances. The method's efficacy is also validated through the accurate prediction of oscillatory states and the examination of its robustness in the presence of increasing step sizes. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and LSTMs are prominent architectures in
computer vision and sequence analysis, respectively. Many researchers believe that
local critic training (LCT) enhances the learning process for these models, though
there's limited evidence to support this claim. Furthermore, no studies exist that
determine which aspects of CNNs and LSTMs are most affected by LCT. This study
investigates the impact of LCT on various neural network components, and our results
reveal that LCT has a significant and positive effect on the learning of convolutional
filters, convolutional layer types, and LSTM cells. To validate our findings and
inform the development of more efficient neural network training methods, we propose
a novel information-theoretic framework that measures the influence of training
strategies on specific network components. Our analysis also discloses an
unintended advantage of LCT, namely the optimization of network parameters at a
higher rate than raw data updates. Additionally, our framework enables the
identification of a novel regularization technique that can facilitate more effective
network component training in a data-limited environment. To verify our findings,
we conducted comprehensive experiments supporting our analysis and demonstrating
the significance of our proposed framework. Our study's conclusions encourage the
community to adopt a more component-centric approach to neural network training. 
Based on our analysis, we introduce an optimized version of local critic training (oLCT)
and evaluate its performance compared to the standard local critic training (LCT) and
stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Our comparison shows that replacing SGD with
oLCT results in significantly improved classification accuracy across multiple datasets. Moreover, our results indicate that integrating oLCT with local critic training (LCT) yields superior outcomes compared to implementing LCT alone. To facilitate the replication of our studies, our code is freely accessible on the GitHub platform at the following link: https://github.com/hpquantum/ComponentOptimization. Investigating the response of nearly extremal and extremal black holes to scalar field collisions has provided clear distinctions between the final states of these black holes and other gravity duals. In the case of nearly extremal black holes, the response shows the development of a thermal state with characteristics mirroring that of hydrodynamic plasma, whereas extremal black holes exhibit a mirror-smooth boundary regardless of the duration or intensity of the collision. In an effort to simplify the analysis and better understand the black hole response, our study replaces the compact radial potential with a more manageable linear one. In the process, we've identified a new exchange rate constant and have determined the long-term black hole state to be an isothermal one at the temperature corresponding to the mass of the black hole. Nonetheless, the modified potential still yields a thermal black hole state in the long term, albeit with a temperature lower than its mass. In contrast to previous conclusions, our findings suggest that the change in temperature is not a scaling one and that the temperature is not dependent on the rate constant. In the event that the potential is linear, we've found that the thermal black hole state is maintained both in the short and long terms and that the temperature remains constant throughout. In the process, we've also determined the energy density of the thermal state and have found it to be significantly lower than the energy density typically found in the thermal states of plasma. This innovative approach enables researchers to interact with star formation models, navigate through turbulent flows, and gain a deeper understanding of the underlying physics, thus providing a more intuitive and immersive experience for participants. In situations where the underlying probability distribution is not directly known, its entropy must be estimated, which can be a complicated task. This work focuses on finding accurate approximation methods for calculating Shannon and Kullback-Leibler entropies from limited functional information about the probability distribution. We employ a Bayesian approach to develop high-accuracy approximations of the probability distribution, which are then used to estimate its entropies. In addition, this method also allows us to estimate the uncertainty in these entropy estimates. We thoroughly analyze the proposed estimators and demonstrate their application in two realistic scenarios: simulating quantum system measurement outcomes and approximating the source code entropy of a secret coding scheme. Our results show that our method yields precise entropy estimates with minimal uncertainty, even when the probability distribution is poorly known. We observe that these estimators are robust in situations where the probability distribution is poorly known, and their accuracy can be further improved by increasing the number of functional information points. We also find that the approximations of Shannon and Kullback-Leibler entropies are closely related, which can be a useful finding in applications where the former is computationally costly to estimate. We anticipate that this method will contribute to the development of entropy estimators in the future. \\ \\ Note. Analytical derivations in this study assume standard definition for entropy and are applicable to any dimension. The numerical implementation of our method is independent of the dimensionality and does not rely on any dimension-specific parameters. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/asharoom/hybrid_entropy/tree/asharoom-hybrid-entropy. First draft posted as arXiv 2202.11581. Our method was initially presented in ISIT22. Neural networks are widely utilized in cybersecurity for classifying malicious entities, yet they pose a significant challenge for deployment due to their high computational requirements, making them suitable for cloud or data center operations. This problem is exacerbated by the limited power of devices such as embedded systems, networked devices, and security monitoring equipment, which cannot support complex cloud-based solutions. This research presents NBcoded, an innovative approach that transforms neural networks into Boolean functions, allowing for a novel circuit design that reduces resource consumption and increases classification speed on resource-constrained devices. NBcoded leverages a complementary technique called Code2NN to recreate the original neural network from the modified Boolean functions, utilizing Code2NN to verify that the NBcoded circuits correspond to the original neural network classifiers. We conducted an experimental evaluation of NBcoded and found that it successfully recovers the original classification accuracy of the neural networks it converts, while also demonstrating a substantial speedup in classification times and significant reductions in resource requirements compared to traditional hardware implementations. For example, our results show NBcoded yields a 76% decrease in area consumption, 90% decrease in runtime, and 10 times fewer parameters on FPGA devices compared to alternative hardware optimizations. In terms of performance, NBcoded achieves a 30 times faster execution speed on Embedded CPUs and 15 times faster on MCU devices compared to other hardware optimizations. The growth gap issue for metabelian groups has been examined, and we find that non-torsion metabelian groups with finite presentations have an expansive growth pattern. Furthermore, we identify a class of metabelian groups with a more rapid growth rate compared to hyperbolic groups. Additionally, we demonstrate that torsion-free metabelian groups of finite type exhibit a more rapid growth rate than solvable groups of finite type. Lastly, we find that torsion-free metabelian groups of finite type are equivalent to torsion-free nilpotent groups of finite type in terms of growth behavior. The proof involves constructing a class of metabelian groups with a specific growth rate and exploiting the connection between growth and path complexity for these groups. These results are particularly noteworthy because they apply broadly to metabelian groups, and the path complexity approach offers an alternative method for analyzing growth behavior compared to more traditional methods. This complexity approach also yields an interesting corollary in the form of a criterion for metabelian groups with a specific growth rate, and this criterion has implications for when a metabelian group's growth rate matches that of its commutator quotient. Finally, we examine the relationship between growth rates and commutator quotients for specific classes of metabelian groups, and we explore potential implications of this relationship for nonabelian free groups. The discussion concludes with an examination of metabelian groups that are closely related to relatively hyperbolic groups, and we find that these metabelian groups exhibit a more rapid growth rate than relatively hyperbolic groups of finite presentation. The proof involves exploiting the properties of relatively hyperbolic groups and their distortion sets, and we find that the growth rate is closely tied to the characteristics of these distortion sets. The analysis also reveals a more general phenomenon in which the growth rate of a group is influenced by the characteristics of its distortion sets. The study concludes by investigating potential applications of the distortion set influence on growth rate to other classes of groups characterized by specific properties. The findings suggest the potential for an important general principle linking a group's characteristics to its growth rate. The research concludes by exploring potential avenues for further study into relatively hyperbolic groups and their geometric properties, and we highlight in particular the potential for further investigation into the solubility of relatively hyperbolic groups and their connection to generalized relatively hyperbolic groups. The investigation also examines specific properties of relatively hyperbolic groups such as their length spectrum and their connection to spectral metrics. To accurately interpret this data, we must differentiate the movement of biological entities from inanimate objects, requiring sophisticated analysis. Here, we introduce a novel statistical model that effectively extracts the movement of multiple biological entities from complex data. Our approach utilizes spectral analysis to identify distinct frequency bands corresponding to individual organisms, and then applies a statistical filter to accurately track their movement. We test the efficacy of this model using both simulated and real experimental data, and find that it outperforms existing methods by extracting a wider range of information. Furthermore, we incorporate this model into a biological study to analyze the behavior of HeLa cells interacting with quantum dots, revealing new insights into cell movement. To facilitate the use of this model, we provide a comprehensive open-source library that enables users to modify and apply our statistical filter to their own data. This study investigates the hybrid approach of solving the DC power flow problem using quantum computing, in addition to traditional methods based on convex optimization. The hybrid method leverages quantum techniques for the more complex partitioning step. The quantum approach outperforms traditional methods in terms of computational efficiency, specifically by a factor of 5-10 minutes on a local machine and 1-2 hours on a public cloud platform, for realistic power network scenarios with 12450, 29970, and 31212 buses. Furthermore, the hybrid method facilitates the rapid solution of partitioning problems with numerous circuits and multiple parameters. The results indicate the potential of hybrid quantum methods as a viable solution for the DC power flow problem. We have developed an advanced taper design that enhances efficiency in on-chip single-photon sources. This nanophotonic taper effectively aligns the single-photon emission spectrum with a 810 nm pump wavelength, achieving an impressive conversion efficiency of 56.9% among the highest reported rates. Additionally, we demonstrate a new level of control over the photon source by incorporating a nearby microsphere resonator. This microsphere can generate highly coherent light at specific frequencies through precise adjustment of its resonant frequencies. Our research showcases the potential for microsphere-resonator systems to produce multi-mode, coherent states in the near-infrared regime with remarkable accuracy. This advancement may soon enable the creation of complex, high-dimensional quantum states utilizing on-chip single-photon sources. Furthermore, our design featuring a taper and microsphere can also find application in highly sensitive optical and quantum measurements. Finally, our results may inspire new technologies involving nanophotonic devices that interface with microsphere resonators, fostering innovation in quantum communication and sensing applications. Our investigation focuses on valley Hall transport within two-dimensional materials coupled with nonuniform lattice distortions not aligned with the transport direction. Notably, this scenario diverges significantly from the conventional picture of valley Hall effect that relies on uniform strain or magnetic fields to induce valley dissipation due to inter-valley scattering. Instead, we found that nonuniform strain can cause valley transitions without exploiting valley orbital decoupling, yet valley polarization is maintained through backscattering from opposing valleys within the same nonparabolic band. Valleys in the same nonparabolic band act as 'valley mirrors', resulting in a scattering phase shift of 180 degrees. This unique property allows us to formalize a rule for valley Hall transport in combination with local valley occupation, which we apply to graphene and silicene examples. Furthermore, this concept enables the control of valley Hall currents through nonuniform strain at room temperature. Finally, the valley Hall effect can be separated from other electrostatic manipulations due to its independence from electric potential. This work lays the groundwork for the realization of valley-valve action through strain-induced manipulation of 2D valley DoS. Moreover, our findings suggest an alternative method for valley detection that is not dependent on the measurement of current or electric potential, thereby enhancing the understanding of valley degrees of freedom in 2D materials. Additionally, our results may encourage further research on valley-confined currents and edge transport within valley-protected channels within 2D materials. Ultimately, we believe this study will contribute to the development of valley-protected electronics, where strain-induced valley degrees of freedom are exploited for device applications at room temperature. In addition, our investigation also explores the potential for valley-protected applications in systems with nonuniform strain without valley orbital decoupling, thereby expanding our comprehension of valley physics in such scenarios. Ultimately, this research may pave the way for the transfer of valley concepts to the study of other non-relativistic 2D materials with valley degrees of freedom, such as phosphorene. Furthermore, we found that neural network agents not only perform better than previous methods, but also determine better parameters for the probability of incorrect measurements that are relevant to the decoding process. We applied our method to the correction of systematic and random errors, and the outcomes show significant improvements in the minimum expected decoding probability, which confirms the effectiveness of our approach. Although our experiment involved a basic single-mode interferometer, the underlying principles can be applied to more complex systems. An analysis involving quarks and gluons has been conducted to understand how various hadrons are created throughout the momentum range and we compared this to data from both Pb+Pb and Au+Au collisions. The study indicates that there is a notable relationship between the momentum of the quarks and the yield of hadrons in Au+Au collisions. Additionally, the results from Pb+Pb collisions show a lower yield of hadrons compared to quark-meson interactions at similar momentum levels. We discovered that this occurrence is correlated with a decline in the elastic cross-sections of quark-meson interactions, thereby providing a possible explanation for the non-intuitive hadron yields observed in heavy ion collisions. The calculated quark spectra in Au+Au collisions are in agreement with data from the PHENIX, ALICE, and STAR collaborations. The study also highlights an important discrepancy between the quark-gluon model and data on the observed collection of strange, non-strange mesons and hadrons in Pb+Pb collisions. We concluded that, based on the non-intuitive quark momentum dependant behavior of hadron production, there is a need for golem-mediated interactions, such as resonances, to explain the observed patterns of hadron production. The results of this study further suggest that such a mechanism is essential for understanding the observed patterns of hadron production in a much broader momentum range extending up to $10~\mathrm{GeV}$ and, therefore, plays a crucial role in the overall process of hadron creation in heavy ion collisions. The results of this systematic approach, combining the roles of quarks and gluons, should provide a solid foundation for understanding quantitative aspects of heavy ion collisions and will be instrumental in guiding and re-interpreting the analysis of these collisions in terms of various collective phenomena, such as jet tomography, conical expansion, and angular correlations, by allowing for a recoil-free extraction of quark spectra. We apply this method to the Fermi-Hubbard model on a square lattice and examine its dynamics in various states. Our findings show that, unlike analog simulations, digital-analog simulations often result in smooth, coherent system behaviors even with few body states. We also observe less variation in Coherent Forward Peierls quantum circuit circuit performance for different electron arrangements when compared to analog methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that it can be challenging for digital-analog circuits to maintain coherence over extended periods, even with the use of noise-reducing protocols. However, in certain situations, digital-analog circuits exhibit equivalent performance to analog circuits in the long term, achieving coherent dynamics with half the number of quantum circuit units. Additionally, we examine the potential applications and limitations of digital-analog quantum circuits in simulating quantum systems. We conclude that digital-analog quantum circuits are suitable for modeling systems requiring few body states but may be less effective for genuine quantum many-body effects, such as superconductivity and magnetism. Nevertheless, digital-analog quantum circuits offer an appealing, more efficient alternative to analog methods for simulating many-body systems, potentially leading to significant computational benefits. Lastly, we outline potential avenues to enhance and apply digital-analog quantum circuits in the future. In particular, we explore the possibility that digital-analog quantum circuits could serve as a transitional phase in the development of quantum algorithms or that they could be used in hybrid quantum algorithms or quantum-inspired machines. Thus, digital-analog quantum computing could have a broader impact than previously anticipated. A weight-assisted genetic algorithm is proposed to enhance its stability and effectiveness. The algorithm assigns varying weights to individual genes within a population, weighing their importance in the selection process. The optimal lighting output in a comprehensive sense is achieved through this adaptive approach. Compared to a standard genetic algorithm, the weight-assisted variant yields better results and reaches a stable output sooner. Moreover, the weight-assisted algorithm can accurately recover detailed images of objects immersed in scattering media, even at low illumination levels. Our study includes an evaluation of the algorithm's performance using scattering intervals of $\Delta\lambda=10$nm and $\Delta\lambda=20$nm in the 500-700nm range. We also investigated the effect of object distance and scattering thickness on the algorithm's performance and found that images are restored more effectively at larger object distances and smaller scattering thicknesses. The direct imaging of exoplanets often falls short due to its current limitation of detecting stars with a high signal-to-noise ratio. This has led to the development of a new post-processing algorithm called the Advanced Pyramid Corruption Recovery algorithm, which uses a data-driven approach similar to that of deep learning techniques. This method was initially tested on a dataset of simulated images of a planet and its star at different airless zones, and was found to consistently detect stars with a high degree of accuracy regardless of the signal-to-noise ratio or the planet-star brightness ratio. This successful result has led to the proposal of a new system for exoplanet detection and characterization that incorporates the Advanced Pyramid Corruption Recovery algorithm. This new system, called the PyCHASM, is set to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of ground-based planet finding surveys and will enable the detection and characterization of a large number of exoplanets in the future. The PyCHASM detector will undergo further testing in the coming months with real data from the SPHERE telescope at the Chalmers Observatory. This will involve the comparison of its performance with existing detection algorithms as well as its implementation on a large dataset of actual telescope images. The PyCHASM detector is set to improve the detection and characterization of exoplanets in the near future. This will likely lead to a significant advancement in the field of exoplanet research and will notably increase the number of planets discovered by the SPHERE telescope. In particular, the model successfully callables European options on a future asset or a credit default swap, computed by the maximum of the likelihood ratio process, struck at volatility $\sigma$ and priced by the Stratonovich stochastic differential utility framework. A model of a DUNE near detector based on a Liquid Argon Time Projector (LAT) technology is examined, with the near detector designed as a multi-circle detector surrounded by five 10 cm thick plastic modules. Each plastic module contains a hole at its center, allowing a concentrated, 5 cm radius beam of neutrinos to pass through from a proton beam source and be detected by three 10 cm x 10 cm LAr modules at the hole's center and edges. Given the near detector's orientation and position relative to the proton beam, three distinct neutrino energy ranges may be identified - a high-energy range focused on detecting neutrinos at high energies, a second range focused on detecting neutrinos at lower energies within a larger geographic area, and a third range focused on detecting neutrinos at very low energies within an even larger geographic area. In the high-energy range, the near detector may potentially detect around 10,000 neutrino events per year, and by identifying these events, the near detector may verify the DUNE experiment's measurement of a long-range neutrino interaction at a 1% uncertainty level. In the medium energy range, the near detector may detect over 20,000 neutrino events per year and may verify the DUNE experiment's measurement of a long-range neutrino interaction at a 5% uncertainty level. This research introduces a family of cluster-robust estimators known as Limited Influence Estimators, which reframes cluster-robust estimation as a problem of minimizing the impact of outliers within each cluster. By doing so, it identifies two key limitations of traditional cluster-robust estimators: they either overreact to outliers or fail to address them effectively. Upon analyzing alternative solutions, it appears that they too suffer from either overreactions or inconsistent treatment of outliers. Building on this insight, Limited Influence Estimators are shown to be based on an 'influence limited' variant of the within-cluster weighted mean, which is robust to a certain level of outliers. Moreover, this new class of estimators is found to be analytically equivalent to existing robust estimators when they are consistent with each other. Monte Carlo simulations have demonstrated that Limited Influence Estimators outperform traditional cluster-robust estimators and are often on par with alternative solutions. Notably, this new class of estimators yields the most stable results in scenarios with moderate levels of outliers. What's more, it is capable of handling an unlimited number of outliers within each cluster without a significant increase in variability. In terms of practical implementation, Limited Influence Estimators can be computed in a matter of seconds due to their analytical equivalence to existing robust estimators. In order to facilitate the use of this new class of estimators, a comprehensive open-source package is available for download at the URL: https://osf.io/mntg5/. Additionally, a demonstration of the package's functionality can be found at https://google-driv...-package-demonstration.pdf. As a result of this effort, this new class of estimators is now fully accessible to applied researchers who can incorporate it into their statistical practice. In order to facilitate the adoption of this new class of estimators by the broader statistical community, a comprehensive paper is available at the URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.11512. In this paper, the theoretical underpinnings of Limited Influence Estimators are presented along with a detailed analysis of their bias, variance, and mean squared error. Furthermore, this paper showcases the utility of this new class of estimators in a series of realistic fiscal policy scenarios. In order to facilitate the use of this new class of estimators by policy analysts, a comprehensive user guide is available at the URL: https://osf.io/m3c9e/. In this guide, the steps for implementing Limited Influence Estimators are presented in an approachable manner.

We developed the multiple-time-step integration algorithm (MTSA) to accelerate computational fluid dynamics simulations of complex systems like particle-laden flows. MTSA's stability and efficiency were theoretically proven and validated through comparison with established models, such as the standard pseudo-steady state approach. We successfully implemented MTSA in a numerical scheme for second-order Navier-Stokes equations and observed a linear reduction in computational time with the square root of the time steps. MTSA's approximate solution of the Navier-Stokes equations consists of two components: a coarse solution for the fluid flow and a finer solution for the particle motion. During each time step, the fluid flow is updated using the Stokes solution, with the particle's position and velocity determined by its initial location and velocity in the previous time step. Conversely, the particle's motion is refined by gradually updating its velocity and position as the fluid flow converges towards a steady state. As a result, the particle achieves a nearly steady-state velocity and converges to a stable trajectory. MTSA's efficiency was evaluated in simulations of a stationary cylinder in a streamlining flow and compared with conventional methods, such as the standard pseudo-steady state approach. The results show that MTSA's approximate solution deviates from the exact solution by less than 6% and is 5-7% less accurate than the pseudo-steady state approach. Nonetheless, MTSA outperformed the pseudo-steady state approach in computational efficiency, with coarser meshes and more rapid convergence towards a stable state. For example, MTSA achieved a 4.5 times faster convergence in a simulation of a particle moving past a cylinder at a 10-degree angle. In conclusion, MTSA offers a promising strategy for accelerating computational fluid dynamics simulations of complex systems like particle-laden flows while yielding highly accurate solutions. MTSA's approximate solution and validation results provide a foundation for its potential application in a wider range of flow simulations, such as those involving multiple particles and complex geometries. Additionally, the algorithm may be extended to solve other complex problems by minimizing the relative differences between coarse and fine solutions. Upon further refinement, MTSA could offer a viable alternative to established numerical schemes for particle-laden flow simulations. MTSA presents an attractive approach for reducing computational time without sacrificing accuracy in complex flow simulations, thus providing a valuable tool for researchers and engineers. We examine the thermodynamic properties of charge black holes in anti-de Sitter space, focusing on the thermal radiation emitted as the black hole undergoes evaporation. Our investigation differs from conventional approaches in that it treats the number of particles as a variable rather than a constant. Instead of specifying a fixed number of particles, we leave their definition until the end as a necessary condition for thermodynamic stability. By adopting this approach, we can capture the complex dynamics of particle creation and annihilation throughout the evaporation process. Furthermore, we expand upon previous work by incorporating both particle creation and absorption. Our findings reveal that, contrary to expectations, the thermodynamic properties of charge black holes do not adhere to standard thermodynamic principles. Nevertheless, we demonstrate that, upon carefully examining the far-from-equilibrium thermodynamic properties, we can identify the inherent potential for nonequilibrium processes to give rise to second law violations and relaxation phenomena. Our study also showcases an alternative method for constructing hydrodynamics from holographic gauge theories, one that originates from thermodynamic stability rather than symmetry. Interestingly, we observe that this approach is consistent with the properties of quark-gluon plasma. Lastly, our work is characterized by a constant width in comparison to the entropic uncertainty principle, leading to the conclusion that the width of entropiness is inherently nonphysical and can be eliminated only by specifying the number of particles. Our study suggests that the concept of particle number definition possesses inherent ambiguity, albeit one that can be minimized in theories incorporating matter fields. Otherwise, the ambiguity remains unresolved. The interaction between a liquid jet flowing through a channel and surrounding air leads to the incorporation of entrained air pockets. This has significant consequences for the jet's dynamics, particularly in situations involving small island geometries where island size affects jet disruption and leads to complex flow patterns. Investigations of the two-phase liquid-gas jet were conducted using a high-speed imaging system and numerical simulations within a framework of numerical methods including volume tracking and finite difference methods. The study examines the influence of air pockets and their impact on oscillating frequencies, often misinterpreted as resulting solely from liquid dynamics. However, the analysis reveals a more complex interplay between liquid and air dynamics, leading to disruptions and changes in flow patterns, which may have implications for understanding condensation processes in microsatellite experiments. The discovery of higher frequency harmonics and local maxima in the power spectral density compared to single-phase cases highlights the critical role of air pockets in shaping island-based oscillation patterns, effectively altering the shape and appearance of the island as seen from a camera's perspective. Consequently, the characteristic frequency of the main harmonic decreased with decreasing island size, following a linear trend, whereas other frequency components increased nonlinearly. The phenomenon of air pockets further confirms their crucial role in island dynamics and transition phenomena, paving the way to studying other nonlinear effects such as buoyancy and surface tension. The investigation demonstrates the significant influence of air pockets on two-phase liquid-gas jet behavior and encourages further exploration of condensation processes, potentially offering novel applications in microsatellite research, including accurate density ratio estimation essential for understanding various physical phenomena. The study also emphasizes the importance of accurately measuring density ratios in order to draw relevant Earth-based inferences to microgravity conditions. Based on analytical results from the power spectral density analysis, a density ratio below a certain threshold in island-sized cases is likely to result in a density ratio greater than the threshold when considering the jet and surrounding air as a single combined fluid. Consequently, this has significant implications for how density ratios in microgravity conditions might behave. The discovery of local maxima in power spectral density, denoted as'satellite peaks,' may be useful in developing an algorithm for automatically identifying island boundaries, potentially including cases where the boundaries coincide with the edges of the jet. Consequently, this may offer a novel approach to determining the size and shape of islands as seen from a camera's perspective based on these satellite peaks and characteristic frequencies. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of numerical simulations and experimental investigations of two-phase liquid-gas jet through a combination of finite difference and volume tracking methods.

Non-volatile memory provides fast access to persistent data, offering a middle ground between volatile and long-term storage. Despite this benefit, ensuring the integrity of data stored in NVM is a concern, particularly in applications where multiple threads access shared data structures. To address this challenge, our approach involves employing algorithm-level abstractions to maintain data consistency and simplify the task of implementing thread-safe operations on shared data objects, thereby reducing the complexity of programming for NVM. Building on existing concurrency models, our solution allows developers to focus on solving problems at the algorithmic level, unaffected by concerns of data persistence and consistency. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach through several examples of sorting and other algorithms, which demonstrate that combining persistent data structures with concurrent execution leads to improved performance compared to using traditional volatile memory. Our results show that persistent data structures generally outperform volatile memory structures, often by a factor of at least five. Furthermore, the advantages of NVM-based solutions exceed those of volatile memory alternatives in several real-world scenarios, as quantified through measurement data. Ultimately, the consistency provided by our LPO data structures serves as a reliable foundation for building concurrent algorithms on top of NVM, allowing developers to leverage parallelism to achieve accelerated performance. Our open-source implementation of these abstract types is accessible via the GitHub repository at https://github.com/MDenno/latent_types/tree/nvm-ccpp, including detailed instructions for compilation and testing within the GitHub repository at https://github.com/MDenno/latent_types/tree/nvm-ccpp#building. Specifically, the code for our approach to maintaining data consistency with LPO data structures can be found at https://github.com/MDenno/latent_types/tree/nvm-ccpp/include/utils/nvmccpp_utils.h. Additional measurement data and a technical report on our findings are available at https://www.dropbox.com/ or upon request to the corresponding author at [maxdenno@gmail.com](mailTo:maxdenno@gmail.com). Our primary aim in this study is to promote the use of persistent data structures in conjunction with concurrent execution on NVM for accelerating algorithmic tasks. Three-body systems in motion may result in the ejection of one particle, a process whose occurrence was long believed to follow a 64% probability of happening about three times out of four cases. However, recent studies have suggested that this widely accepted notion may be inaccurate. Our own investigation focuses on two types of three-body systems: those beginning with a linear arrangement of particles in space, an arrangement often associated with a 57% likelihood of escapes, and those starting with particles randomly dispersed, an arrangement that shows significant variability. Our findings indicate that systems starting with randomly placed particles do not, in fact, consistently adhere to the long-held 64% prediction. Additionally, we find significant agreement between the statistical properties of these systems and theoretical predictions based on different models of weak encounters. Ultimately, our results suggest that escapes from these three-body systems are a result of either pre-collisional, temporary arrangements or post-collisional, temporarily aligned configurations. Our work also examines how particle mass ratios influence both the probability of escapes and the statistical characteristics of these systems, finding that mass ratios significantly impact the likelihood of escapes. Furthermore, we find that when particles have similar masses, systems starting with randomly dispersed masses and those beginning with a linear arrangement exhibit comparable escape probabilities. Our investigation also sheds light on the internal arrangements of these three-body systems and sets the stage for future studies on the dynamics of these systems. Ultimately, we hope that our findings will contribute to a greater understanding of the generalized Darwin model and the origin of planetary systems. \\

Keywords: Three-body systems, encounters, escapes, probability, generalized Darwin model, planetary systems, star systems, binary systems, gravitational interactions, galaxy clusters  \\

The ratio of (prompt $\psi$(2S) + prompt D$^0$) to prompt J/$\psi$ shows a significant dependence on transverse momentum and rapidity, ranging from a 0.15 reduction in the 3-8 GeV/c transverse momentum range at positive rapidity to a 0.35 reduction in the 2-6 GeV/c range at rapidity between -1.2 and -1.5. The study also found that the suppression rates of heavy mesons, such as D$^0$, are similar to those of $\psi$(2S) and J/$\psi$. The study's results are compared with theoretical models, which suggest that these mesons sink below the J/$\psi$ yield at high momenta. We examine the properties of equivalence relations within the context of continuous logic. By leveraging a specific complete metric space, we show that equivalence relations can be regarded as complete metric spaces themselves. Furthermore, we define a natural topology on the space of all equivalence relations and demonstrate that this space is complete. Our work is centered around proving that an ultrapower construction is equivalent to a space of equivalence relations. To achieve this goal, we draw inspiration from Henson and Forbess' work on continuous desingularization. Additionally, we incorporate novel applications of the properties of continuous metrics that treat countable structures as metric spaces. Our findings are significant as they provide a metric interpretation for model theory concepts such as types, stability, and infiniteness within the context of continuous logic. A significant outcome of our study is the discovery that every type in an equivalence relation is realized in an ultrapower construction, which has far-reaching implications for the study of types in such spaces. As a concrete example of our theorem in action, we analyze the characteristics of types within the realm of continuous fields of metric spaces. Our results also enable us to investigate the properties of infiniteness within the context of continuous fields of metric spaces. We utilize a simple metric topology on the space of continuous fields to demonstrate that isometric embeddings between certain fields can be extended consistently across all equivalence relations within those fields. Our study of continuous fields of metric spaces also enables us to examine the properties of types in relation to realized types within equivalence relations of those fields. To facilitate our analysis, we adopt a simplified metric topology on the space of continuous fields consisting of metric spaces and isometric embeddings between their ultrapowers. Our findings reveal that the notion of completeness in continuous fields is a combination of the completeness of individual metric spaces and the consistency of realized types within equivalence relations of those fields. Our examination of continuous fields of metric spaces also allows us to investigate the properties of stability in relation to realized types within equivalence relations of those fields. We demonstrate stability in certain fields by showing that the consistency of realized types within equivalence relations of those fields is sufficient to ensure stability in those fields. Our study of continuous fields of metric spaces is significant as it provides a unified understanding of the properties of types, stability, and completeness in relation to model theoretic concepts and their corresponding metric properties. This research paper outlines a deployment strategy leveraging the capabilities of software deployment units, SDEUs, to effectively manage fluctuations in software development. The SDEU deployment approach utilizes the singular value decomposition, SVD, to identify and respond to evolving trends within the software. By treating source code changes as anomalies in the SVD process, this method achieves real-time monitoring and adaptation. The performance of the SVD method is compared to that of another adaptive source code analyzer, ACORN, using eight open-source applications and ten complex source code files. The results indicate the SVD method's capacity to detect trends and anomalies efficiently. The integration of the SVD method with deployment units enables seamless handling of software changes during deployment. The paper concludes with proposed future research directions. Deep learning algorithms utilizing Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have achieved impressive results in natural language processing and other sequence-related tasks. However, traditional RNNs often struggle with retaining context in long sequences, leading some researchers to employ attention mechanisms and current transformers with multi-head attention for improved retention. Despite these advancements, some tasks still find head-to-head comparison guides scarce. In this research, we introduce a comprehensive, easy-to-use library, called seqrnn-benchmark, to benchmark various RNN-based sequential models, including attention-enhanced methods, on a range of common datasets. Our results not only verify the superiority of attention-enhanced models but also uncover that the multi-head attention technique offers no significant advantage over its single-headed counterpart under the same architecture and dataset conditions. Nonetheless, the beneficial impact of attention is largely abolished by increasing sequence lengths. Consequently, we suggest combining attention with other optimization techniques like gradient clipping and regularization to counteract gradient bursting for enhanced performance in the face of long sequences. Our research findings are substantiated by a related Python library, seqrnn-benchmark, that allows researchers to reproduce our results and conduct further comparisons in the field of deep sequential models. This benchmark library can be accessed through the following GitHub link: https://github.com/dimdev/seqrnn-benchmark. Our related slide presentation can be found at https://speakerdeck.com(dimdev)deep-learning-for-sequential-data. Additionally, our research paper providing an in-depth analysis is accessible at https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06216. Lastly, our related blog post summarizing our study can be found at https://dimdev.info/2017/03/06/sequential-data-benchmark. Our Twitter profile is accessible at https://twitter.com(dimdev).

Discovering a connection between the X-ray polarization angle and the magnetic field orientation at lower energy observations is key to confirming this theory. To better understand Polarized X-ray emission, a detailed description of the radiative process is required. A computational model created specifically for this study accounts for the synchrotron production, transfer, and emission of polarized X-rays. This model has been simulated on a comprehensive grid covering 1-20 GeV with various inclination angles between the magnetic field and the line of sight. A comparison between the simulation outcomes and observed X-ray spectrum shows excellent agreement, indicating that the model used is accurate. Furthermore, analyzing the distribution and intensity of the polarized X-ray radiation reveals specific regions of high emission within the remnant. It has also been observed that the 22-diffusion radius of polarized X-rays closely matches the brightness distribution of the eastern and western lobes of Cassiopeia A. The problem of finding a set of distinct subset sums requires determining all non-overlapping subsets of a specific size from a given set of numbers. When the subset size equals or exceeds half of the total numbers in the set, a necessary and sufficient condition for solvability is known based on the cardinality of the set. However, no such criterion exists for smaller subset sizes. We establish a sufficient condition for solvability in this case, stating that the set can be split into two non-overlapping subsets with sums adding up to the same value. Additionally, we introduce a method for finding a set of distinct subset sums of a specified size from a given set of numbers, which can be applied efficiently using a graph traversal technique and polynomial-time algorithm. Conversely, we show that verifying the solvability of a set for all possible subset sizes is a computationally complex problem. However, we identify a specific size of subset sums that can be efficiently confirmed as solvable - namely, subsets of the same size as the total number of elements in the set. We also outline a probabilistic approach for approximating the solvability of intermediate subset sizes. Lastly, we investigate the relationship between the minimum and maximum values within a set and its subset sums, and prove that determining the minimum value of a set whose subset sums exceed a given value is a computationally complex problem. However, we reveal an efficient polynomial-time algorithm for finding the maximum value of a set whose subset sums do not exceed a given value. Moreover, we establish that determining whether a set has distinct subset sums of a specific size is a computationally complex problem when the size of that subset is or becomes relatively small compared to the total numbers in the set - specifically, smaller than one-tenth of the total numbers in the set. Conversely, we show that efficiently solving this problem is achievable when the size of that subset is at least one-twentieth of the total numbers in the set. This study examines how a deconfinement phase transition within quark stars behaves in the presence of a rotating quark star's gravitational field.  By employing a relativistic mean-field model, researchers have calculated the mass and radius of quark stars based on different parameters in the free energy density of cold, dense matter.  Additionally, equations for the moment of inertia and gravitational redshift were derived.  Our findings indicate that a deconfinement phase transition significantly influences the quark star's structural properties.  Specifically, when the adiabatic index of the quark phase, σ, is less than approximately 3, a deconfinement phase transition leads to quark star configurations with smaller radii.  This peculiar behavior stems from the quark phase's ability to shrink due to the deconfinement phase transition, even in the presence of negative pressure within the crust.  Consequently, a deconfinement phase transition may yield quark star configurations with smaller radii and lower masses, which could be interpreted as an explanation for the quark star's observed low-mass scenario.  This research aims to clarify the role of a deconfinement phase transition in the quark star's structural characteristics.  Our findings may be useful in guiding future observations of quark star binaries in the detection of gravitational waves.  Furthermore, a deconfinement phase transition could be explored in the context of neutron stars, which share many structural features with quark stars.  Our results also highlight the necessity of incorporating a deconfinement phase transition in quark star models, especially for accurate binary observations of quark star candidates in the future.  Lastly, the presence of a deconfinement phase transition may offer an alternative scenario for the formation of quark stars, which could provide valuable insights for astrophysicists.  Our analysis primarily focuses on the characteristics of rotating quark stars, which may be extended to other compact stars in future studies.  This research aims to enhance our comprehension of dense, twisted matter in the dense, spinning environment of quark stars.  Our findings could be applied to the study of dense, twisted matter in the dense, spinning environment of both quark and neutron stars.  Our results may also be useful in guiding future observations of the dense, twisting regions of compact star binaries in the context of gravitational waves.  Ultimately, our goal is to increase our understanding of complex, dense, twisting matter in the dense, spinning environment of both quark and neutron stars.

This method is first tested in a series of pure dielectric materials with varying phonon frequencies. The results show that, unlike traditional methods, nonadiabatic Born effective charges are not entirely independent of electron-phonon interactions. In fact, a significant interaction exists between 100% adiabatic and nonadiabatic charges in silicon, highlighting the importance of clean and perfect conditions for simulating nonadiabatic responses. However, when defects are introduced, the nonadiabatic and adiabatic approaches converge. This finding is consistent with previous studies on superconductors. This research examines the interplay between magnetoelectric interaction and topological effects in a model 2D system exhibiting Witten, or magnetoelectric, coupling. Our computational findings show that combining Witten coupling with a Zeeman term results in the emergence of a topological insulator at a specific critical point of the system, which transitions from a disorderd to an ordered state. Our calculations also demonstrate that the gap induced by the Witten coupling increases linearly with an applied magnetic field, thus exhibiting a magnetoelectric property. In addition, we apply a non-Abelian bosonization method to investigate the transport properties of this model and show that a thick surface region exhibits $T$-invariant 1D Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid behavior with specific hydrodynamic contributions. Our study fully incorporates the long-range nature of the Witten coupling. Furthermore, we have modified the model to remove its disorder, which involves replacing the Witten coupling with a long-range potential coupling in the ordered state. A low-dimensional model is derived for systems with significant delay effects, but low spatial dimensionality, by applying techniques such as dimensionality reduction and state diffusion representation. This low-dimensional model is built upon the notion of an invariant manifold in a larger phase space that encompasses both the system's primary state variables and delayed variables. The resulting state space, although reduced, still appears complex and chaotic, according to our findings, even in the absence of noise. The existence of an invariant manifold with a center-stable manifold structure is confirmed by our numerical investigations. The findings of this study can be extended to a broader class of nonlinear systems of partial differential equations with delay, and the results are also compared with similar systems that lack spatial dimensionality, such as Taylor system and the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation. This paper draws together previous research on how certain optimization techniques, like gradient descent, can successfully converge to local minima on specific, structured sets of data. It's demonstrated how to automatically identify and analyze these data sets, characterized by differentiability manifolds, across a wide range of functions and tasks, including regression, classification, and transduction. Our method employs a novel algorithm that explores each manifold through an evolving set of points, producing a detailed map of its geometry. By effectively replicating the conditions required for convergence in smaller, artificially constructed data sets, this algorithm allows for the successful application of gradient descent on complex tasks that were previously inaccessible. Our technique further extends to provide a reliable evaluation of the convergence rate and performance of gradient descent. Our experiments showcase the substantial improvements in convergence time that our optimization strategy offers over traditional methods. Imitation learning seeks to align an agent's behavior with that of an expert by generating expert actions based on observations from both expert and agent trajectories. However, discrepancies between these two trajectories can hinder the imitation process and lead to mislearning. To address this limitation, we introduce Variational Interactive Imitation Learning (VIIL), a new method that closes the gap between expert and agent behaviors using a variational approach. By modeling the conditional distribution of expert actions given expert observations, VIIL enables the separation of an agent's performance issues from the underlying behavioral rules encoded in the expert trajectories. Through a variational free-space exploration technique, VIIL also optimizes the diversity of agent actions within the boundary of the estimated conditional distribution of expert actions. We evaluate VIIL on multiple complex tasks, including a simulated robotic push-task and a real-world cooking task, and demonstrate its ability to separate an agent's skills from its current behavior and accurately imitate the underlying skills. Notably, VIIL achieves state-of-the-art performance on these tasks, often outperforming existing methods by a significant margin. Our work provides a new argument for the existence and expressiveness of an agent's performance space, and shows that VIIL can accurately map an agent's performance space, offering a new direction for study and potential applications in life-long learning and skill transfer. Research suggests that angular momentum in clouds of gas plays a crucial role in the formation of planets and stars. Existing theories on disk fragmentation, however, assume uniform angular momentum distribution, leading to inconsistencies when comparing theoretical models to the distribution of angular momentum in actual disks. To resolve this discrepancy, we conducted a study on non-uniform angular momentum distribution in protoplanetary disks, specifically those surrounding isolated protostars in a low-mass star formation environment. Our findings reveal that, given the observed distribution of angular momentum in such disks, the region near the disk's center has a gas density that is an order of magnitude lower than currently estimated, suggesting that the rate of gas accretion onto the central star is also significantly lower. In addition, our models predict the formation of massive planets (~1 solar mass) at greater distances from the star than current estimates, primarily due to the influence of the disk's overall structure. Finally, our analysis indicates that the low mass of close-in planets in such disks cannot be attributed to gravitational interactions with a second, distant protostar as previously proposed, due to the insufficient mass and radial velocity dispersion characteristics of the disk at distances from the disk's center. Instead, the mass of close-in planets in these disks must have originated from mergers of growing planetary embryos within the disk. Our theoretical models, specifically those involving the rapid growth of massive, non-uniform planetary seeds, provide the most plausible explanation for the observed mass distribution of close-in, small-radius planets. Our study also highlights the need for future observations on the distribution of angular momentum in protoplanetary disks and the resulting formation of planets. In particular, further investigation is required into the protoplanetary disk around the 4.7 solar mass star, HD 69830, which contains multiple, heavily weighted close-in planetary systems. Our theoretical models, specifically those for angular momentum distribution in protoplanetary disks, are consistent with the observed mass distribution of planets in this system, specificially the two gas giants orbiting at approximately 3.2 and 0.79 AU, as the ratio of their masses is nearly equal. Our study, however, cannot rule out the possibility of an early, rapid gas accretion phase for the central star, as this would result in a reduced mass ratio between the two innermost planets. In addition, our models, although consistent with the observed mass distribution of planets in this system, cannot rule out the possibility of an early, rapid migration of the innermost planet either. Association rules have been widely utilized in various domains to uncover contextual information implicit within transactional data. Research has primarily focused on reducing the redundancy inherent in these rules by utilizing concepts from a related knowledge base. We build upon existing studies by proposing an approach that characterizes redundancy among association rules using a related knowledge base, with improvements comprising both the breadth of applicable knowledge bases and the precision of resulting reductions. Firstly, we generalize existing notions of redundancy by defining association patterns, which encompass regular, association rules. We demonstrate that patterns are encompassed by a maximal association substructure, which is logically derivable from a given dataset. We then define two types of redundancy - itemset and pattern redundancy - and derive separate algorithms for each with time complexities of O(m*n) and O(n*log(m/n) + m), respectively, with respect to the number of items (m), instances (n), and memory usage. We showcase results from eight diverse datasets, including both small scale experiments and analysis of a dataset originating from a pharmaceutical company. We then address scalability challenges by proposing data preprocessing techniques to transform large datasets into smaller ones with reduced dimensions, thereby enabling efficient computation of redundancy on a smaller scale. We showcase the effectiveness of our approach by comparing it to existing methods and demonstrating its applicability to various association mining tasks, including discovery of hidden patterns, reduction of noisy rules, and compact representation of rules. Our work culminates in the development of an open-source tool, called HiddenPattern, which utilizes the proposed techniques to determine redundancy and provides users with the ability to interactively parameterize computations and visualize results. The tool has successfully been applied on several datasets, including analysis of compact representations, rule implications, and discovery of contextual patterns. Lastly, we outline potential future avenues for research and development. To the best of our knowledge, our proposed approach represents the first general methodology for calculating redundancy using a related knowledge base with improved precision and scalability. Offenders with mental health issues have a potential treatment alternative to
incarceration, which has proven effective in reducing crime rates. However, there
is a lack of data on which types of mental health disorders respond best to treatment.
Using a dataset of 88,139 offenders from the Florida Department of Corrections with
specific mental health conditions, we conducted an analysis to identify which disorders
are most responsive to treatment and which amenable crimes they are used to commit.
Our results reveal that individuals with anxiety, depression, and personality disorders
are 21-35% less likely to relapse compared to those with schizophrenia. Furthermore,
our findings show that each disorder is associated with distinct recidivist crimes and
we expose inconsistencies in how these conditions are reported by the corrections system.
By providing a framework for mapping mental health disorders to crime types, our study
can inform data-driven decisions to guide more effective treatment allocation for Florida
offenders and similar systems, ultimately enabling a more targeted and successful parole
program. Our analysis highlights potential improvements, such as providing more resources
to crimes associated with schizophrenia, such as violent offenses, and prioritizing
mental health treatment for offenders who commit disorders like theft and property crimes.

This uncertainty metric is based on a probabilistic model that measures map congruence and uncertainty. This uncertainty is further broken down into structure and instantiation uncertainties. By optimizing measurement collection, we reduce the number of unnecessary readings and misclassifications, and consequently, we can create maps with fewer categories and exceptions, yielding better results in map estimation and inference. This approach is compared to non-adaptive methods that collect measurements uniformly or randomly, and we experimentally verify that our metric allows us to speed up the measurement process by up to 50%. Additionally, we obtain better results in map estimation and location recognition, as evidenced by higher accuracy rates and cleaner maps. This efficiency enables us to take advantage of our adaptive method even when the measurement process is slow, and in scenarios with limited resources, where both the training and testing processes involve online and wireless communication. In order to facilitate the use of our uncertainty metric for any dataset, we provide a basic implementation and the measured data used in this study. One major limitation of machine learning algorithms is their reliance on extensive, carefully curated datasets. Anomaly detection poses an especially challenging problem within this context, as it requires identifying unusual data points without the guidance of labeled examples. To address this issue, this thesis explores the potential of unsupervised learning techniques to facilitate anomaly detection. To accomplish this goal, we adopt a comprehensive approach that encompasses three primary objectives. Firstly, we conduct an in-depth examination of cutting-edge anomaly detection algorithms. In particular, this study focuses on density-based, copy-based, state-based, and meta-learning methods for anomaly detection. By incorporating graph neural networks and other advanced techniques, we aim to enhance the understanding of unsupervised anomaly detection algorithms. In addition to empirical analysis, we utilize a quantitative framework to evaluate and compare the effectiveness of these algorithms on diverse datasets. This framework integrates multiple proximity estimation methods that are often utilized in unsupervised anomaly detection, including the use of dimensionality reduction techniques, similarity metrics, and graph neural networks. By incorporating meta-learning, we pretrain feature extractors on base tasks and leverage subgroup information to identify anomalous data points. To further optimize the anomaly detection process, we utilize feature aggregation methods that integrate multiple proximity estimates to identify exceptional data points. The empirical comparisons of density-based, copy-based, state-based, meta-learning, graph neural network-based, dimensionality reduction-based, and feature aggregation-based anomaly detection algorithms reveal notable variations in their performance on diverse datasets. By incorporating meta-learning and graph neural networks, we significantly enhance the anomaly detection accuracy of subgroup-based algorithms and achieve state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets. In addition to empirical analysis, we contribute two anomaly detection methods - meta-learning-based and feature aggregation-based - to the existing literature of unsupervised anomaly detection. This study investigates the performance of verification systems that can be easily integrated into existing software development cycles. We compared three such systems: Unittest (a widely used testing framework for Python), Unreach-Const (a tool that uses reachability analysis to find code errors), and KLEE (a state-of-the-art program analyzer) for constructing counterexamples. Our evaluation of these systems was conducted in two stages. Firstly, we assessed their performance when verifying correct code without any semantic flaws, and secondly, we did the same but this time when the code had semantic errors that could be pinpointed. The results from our analysis indicate that for the case where the code is free from flaws, KLEE outperformed the other two systems across all metrics. Conversely, when the code had semantic errors and semantic validation was required, Unreach-Const proved to be more effective than KLEE and notably, the difference in performance between it and KLEE was most pronounced. Notably, this improved performance of Unreach-Const came at the expense of increased processing time, thus it cannot be said to be universally superior to KLEE. In a broader scheme, this study's findings highlight the varied effectiveness of different verification systems, and how their performance can be highly sensitive to the condition of the code being verified (whether it has semantic errors or not). In recent years, there has been a growing need for protecting sensitive information in datasets, leading to the development and application of various privacy preservation techniques. Most existing methods concentrate on safeguarding individual data records, failing to acknowledge the interconnections and dependencies between them. A few studies have explored cross-record relationships, though primarily within the context of structured data, and through methods that are difficult to scale and adaptable. We propose an innovative approach that leverages graph theory to recognize interrecord dependencies in both large and small datasets containing diverse, unstructured record types. Our method graphically represents record relationships and then employs community structure analysis, accompanied by a novel algorithm, to identify sensitive information linked to multiple records. This approach enables the incorporation of external knowledge to enhance its effectiveness. We validate our method through experiments involving multiple datasets and showcase its practical applications in real-world scenarios. We conducted a study using ALMA to observe the gas emissions in CO, C$_2$H, and SO within a sub-au size area of the HH30 protoplanetary disk at a height of approximately 0.1-0.2 AU above its midplane. Our high-resolution observations revealed distinct gas emissions around the disk's center that varied based on radius and depth. The CO emission was found to be concentrated at larger heights than expected, while C$_2$H and SO emissions were confined to an extremely narrow layer near the midplane with no apparent center-related peak. We attributed these findings to the effects of temperature and C/O ratio fluctuations within the disk's turbulent and spinning dust particles, supporting model predictions that the gas particles at the disk's midplane remain chemically frozen despite thermodynamic interactions. Observations of C$_2$H emissions may provide valuable constraints on disk diffusion models due to its rapid destruction when exposed to radiation, while SO emissions, being more resilient, can serve as an indicator of disk viscosity variations. Our analysis further reveals a significant decrease in SO column density around HH30's inner cavity compared to CO, a feature that could be the result of a gas belt existing outside the telescope's angular resolution or a gas particle migration under turbulent forces that affects the SO column density calculation. We also propose SO emissions to be an effective probe of the radial variation of C/O ratio in protoplanetary disks. Our ALMA data reveal SO column density decreasing from 10 to 20 AU and, assuming a gas belt exists at around 30 AU, we also detect a low-level SO emissions in the outer cavity of HH30, suggesting the presence of gas particles there as well. Our study demonstrates the potential of high-resolution gas emissions observations to reveal the complex structure of protoplanetary disk's gas density and chemical composition. We propose a chemical model where the C/O ratio plays a crucial role in determining the column density distribution of key species such as C$_2$H and SO in the disk's atmosphere. We further present a model of SO column density variation based on C/O ratio and radius in the disk, offering a future direction for research in understanding chemical processes in protoplanetary disks. Our study also emphasizes the importance of considering the effects of turbulence on chemical composition in the disk's atmosphere and radiative diffusion in chemical model simulations. We present a simplified model of SO column density as a function of C/O and radius in the disk, offering a future direction for research in understanding chemical processes in protoplanetary disks.

We have developed the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), a powerful software tool for in-depth and flexible analysis of time-stamped data. Unlike common techniques that rely on data transmission speed to calculate event rates, our method directly extracts time-stamped data and accurately calculates rates, even from complex data sets. This approach enables an almost unlimited number of time slots, eliminating restrictions seen in other methods. Furthermore, our tool can detect events within a predefined time frame and identify correlated events between different subsystems. To verify ETA's effectiveness, we compared its results with those from standard methods using data from the ATCA correlator system. Our findings confirm that ETA calculates rates precisely and identifies correlated events perfectly, whereas standard methods can only approximate these results. We also demonstrate ETA's capability to analyze data from various time-stamping schemes and its ability to handle large data sets. This work highlights ETA as a valuable resource for time-stamped data analysis and confirms its suitability for use in radio astronomy applications. Additionally, our method can be applied to any field where time-stamped data is employed. Specifically, for a one-parameter semigroup $\beta$, the commutant $C[\beta]$ is the closure of the image of $\beta$ in $B$. The discovery of gravitational waves from the merger of two 30-solar-mass black holes in 2019 provided new life to the concept of dark matter being comprised of primordial black holes, particularly those of intermediate mass. Predictions indicate that primordial black holes in the range of 10^-17 to 10^-19 solar masses could account for all dark matter. We examine the feasibility of detecting these intermediate-mass primordial black holes using a 100-meter class gravitational detector in a quantum-state-dependent search method. This research presents the $\omega$-analogues of Dowling polynomials, a group of exponential combinatorial functions that share connections with other notable structures such as partial permutations, ball partitions, and Dyck paths. Like Dowling polynomials, our $\omega$-analogues can be interpreted through the lens of partial permutations, with additional freedom to append any number of zeros. By extending this partial permutation perspective, we define $\omega$-analogues of Dowling polynomials with zero appendages and explore their relationship with ball partitions and Dyck paths. Using the basis of a key result by Carlitz and Levinson, we derive recursive formulas for these $\omega$-analogues and establish a correspondence between the values of $\omega$-analogues and $q$-analogues. Furthermore, we define $\tau$-analogues of Dowling polynomials, incorporating the weight function $\tau(n) = n^2$, which shares connections with the number of ball partitions of $n$ and the central binomial coefficients. Additionally, we study $\tau$-analogues of Dowling polynomials with zero appendages and examine their relationships with the $q$-analogues of Dowling polynomials and the $\omega$-analogues of Dowling polynomials. Our investigation into $\tau$-analogues of Dowling polynomials reveals intriguing links to the counting principles behind Dyck paths. To facilitate the analysis of these $\tau$-analogues, we introduce a novel combinatorial structure, the $\tau$-paths, which provide an alternative to the nested Dyck paths and unfold in an irregular pattern. Our results provide a deeper understanding of the study by Batshoun, Dil, and Huh, which initially presented $\tau$-analogues of Dowling polynomials without providing a direct combinatorial explanation for their recursive formulas. Our work aims to bridge the combinatorial aspect with the algebraic characterization in the mentioned study. Additionally, our findings offer a deeper insight into the links between the $\tau$-analogues of Dowling polynomials and the central binomial coefficients, presenting an alternative to the elegant solution proposed by Dil and Huh. Our research presents the $\omega$-analogues and $\tau$-analogues of Dowling polynomials as a unified concept, with unique generating functions representing the common structure behind this group of combinatorial functions. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing models, including those utilizing concurrent temporal knowledge graphs and separate entity and relation tables. Our code is available at https://github.com/JayceyLiu/TempComplex. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method on two existing datasets for relation prediction and concept classification, respectively. Our findings show that TempComplex surpasses the state-of-the-art models, achieving significant improvements on both tasks. Specifically, for relation prediction, our method exhibits enhanced performance, averaging 0.187 NME (Normalized Mean Error) with a 1-9 scale, significantly higher than the best existing model (0.233 NME). For concept classification, TempComplex attains a 0.794 AUC (Area Under the Curve) on the TEC dataset and 0.853 AUC on the CKBC dataset, surpassing the existing models (0.794 AUC and 0.819 AUC, respectively) and marking the first success in this field. Our analysis into the properties of temporal concepts also sheds light on the underlying mechanisms of our method. In addition, our study explores the applicability of our method in a multigraph setting. Our findings suggest that applying our method to concurrent temporal concepts within a single graph yields more satisfactory results than utilizing separate graphs with single temporal concepts. This knowledge could be exploited to enhance existing multigraph knowledge graph embedding methods. Lastly, our investigation into the relations extracted from CKBC highlights the diverse range of temporal concepts and their applications in the field of computer science. Our findings could serve as a foundation for future research into temporal entities within concurrent knowledge graphs. In conclusion, our work, TempComplex, marks a significant advancement in the field of temporal knowledge graph embeddings, embodying novel theoretical contributions, experimental outcomes, and valuable insights for researchers and practitioners alike.
