We analyzed the atmospheric properties of temperate planets by examining mass, size, and atmospheric retention properties. Our research indicates that planets with small atmospheres have a different composition from those with massive atmospheres, as measured by Kepler transit data. The key distinction lies in the relative abundances of carbon and nitrogen gases. To understand the observed patterns, we turned to models of volcanic activity and atmospheric escape, considering factors such as the energy input from stars and the characteristics of a planet's interior. Our results demonstrate that a simple model based on the planet's mass and atmospheric retention can account for the varying compositions of small and massive atmospheres. This model also enables us to estimate the degree of volcanic activity and atmospheric escape in each planet, ultimately providing insight into the potential habitability and biosignatures in their atmospheres. Our analysis specifically highlights several key features: 1) a temperate planet with a small atmosphere may experience heat-induced gas stripping, leading it to have a carbon-poor and nitrogen-rich composition; 2) a planet with a massive atmosphere may experience similar compositional alterations due to atmospheric expansion, thus resulting in a carbon-rich and nitrogen-poor composition; 3) to avoid these compositional alterations, a temperate planet with a small atmosphere must have energy input from the star or a large internal energy source, while a planet with a massive atmosphere may have atmospheric expansion or be affected by other atmospheric processes, resulting in a different composition from those with small atmospheres. Our study provides a framework for classifying and understanding atmospheric properties in temperate planets, enabling future comparisons with actual data from future missions like JAMES Webb Space Telescope and the Giant Magellan Telescope. A novel neural network learning system is introduced, which utilizes a discrete McCulloch-Pitts network architecture similar to the classic Hopfield model but expands upon it by incorporating a systematic training mechanism based on discrete synaptic weights. This algorithm trains the network to represent any arbitrary function of multiple variables by adjusting the synaptic weights according to a predefined scheme. Consecutive updates lead to a sequence of stable states, eventually resulting in the convergence to a unique stable configuration representing the function's value for the given input variables. Numerical experiments demonstrate the network's ability to learn various tasks, such as classification and data fitting, in a discrete domain. Additionally, the developed framework shares similarities with the neural behavior of gene regulatory networks, making the model suitable for the artificial life simulation in the discrete domain. Furthermore, the work takes advantage of the discrete McCulloch-Pitts network's robustness against noise and its simple implementation, which can be utilized in scenarios involving limited-resource devices. The achievement of competitive scene text recognition performance heavily relies on the quality of training data, specifically a comprehensive Out-Of-Vocabulary dataset. Our research builds upon this insight, introducing a converged training method for models tackling out-of-vocabulary, semi-supervised, and unsupervised text recognition tasks. During training, a converged model processes both in-vocabulary and out-of-vocabulary images simultaneously. Furthermore, our approach allows a single model to effectively handle semi-supervised learning and unsupervised training, overcoming limitations of previous methods. Through rigorous evaluation of our method across diverse datasets, we achieve exceptional results and surpass state-of-the-art benchmarks. Notably, our model displays robust performance on the out-of-vocabulary ChineseText and EnglishText datasets, accurately decoding 44.76% and 31.29% of previously unseen words, respectively. Moreover, our approach excels in semi-supervised learning, boosting Acc-5 from 78.95% to 81.90% on the Street View Text dataset. Furthermore, our model successfully applies transfer learning to unsupervised settings, enhancing Word-5 accuracy by 8.09% and 7.94% on the SynthText dataset for English and Chinese, respectively. We introduce an adaptive online monitoring system that efficiently detects shifts in conditions and isolates underlying causes, even under limited resource constraints. The system comprises two interconnected algorithms: a density-based change point detection method and a failure mode isolation technique, which approximate the posterior predictive distribution of non-parametric Gaussian mixtures using kernel density estimation and unconstrained two-problem optimization. We evaluate the system through comprehensive testing, including scenarios of varying real-time observation latency and under 5 different scenarios of system performance. The results demonstrate that this online monitoring system effectively detects changes and isolates issues in real-time, even at latency levels up to 10% higher than the sample size, and outperforms existing methods of change point detection and failure isolation in terms of accuracy and latency, and provides on-demand latent variable estimation. We examined three young thin disk star clusters: Gaia-Sausage Enceladus (GE), Wukong/LMS-1, and their progenitors' formation durations which are consistent with their age differences. Our analysis focused on the self-consistent distribution of star cluster formation durations which showed a peak around 1 Gyrs, with a significant decline after 1.5 Gyrs. Both GE and Wukong/LMS-1 fell within this general trend, with their formation durations estimated at approximately 1.1 Gyrs. On the other hand, the progenitors of these clusters were found to be younger, with GE's duration estimated between 0.2-0.5 Gyrs and Wukong/LMS-1's duration estimated at 0.27 Gyrs. This discrepancy is likely due to the fact that GE and Wukong/LMS-1 are both older rather than primarily young clusters. Moreover, their metal content [Fe/H] averages -0.79 dex which is close to the solar value, suggesting a wider spread of this value. In contrast, the young cluster's metal content was found to be higher, at [Fe/H] = -0.68 dex. With Gaia-Sausage Enceladus's age and Wukong/LMS-1's age both exceeding 1 Gyrs, it's possible that these clusters formed after the cluster-population dynamic changed following the Gaia-Enceladus-Wukong merger. This event may have initiated a decline in thinner disk star cluster formation durations. Alternatively, the fall-off might be a natural outcome of the typical cluster-lifespan extension over time. In any case, the key role of Gaia-Sausage Enceladus in this study is that its formation duration helps to rule out a younger, massive merger involving the LMS-1 cluster (also referred to as the 'Massive Splash' scenario) which would have left behind a larger number of younger thin disk star clusters with similar properties to Gaia-Sausage Enceladus. This conclusion is consistent with the findings from an earlier study which used kinematic data to rule out this scenario. On the other hand, the both situations agree that Gaia-Sausage Enceladus's formation lasted a shorter time compared to its progenitors within Gaia-Enceladus-Wukong. This discrepancy may be a result of the Gaia-Enceladus-Wukong merger that formed this cluster.

To train machine learning models efficiently, a large number of accurate labels is typically required. In reality, many tasks lack sufficient labeled data or have inconsistent, low-quality labels assigned by humans or crowd-sourcing methods. To overcome these challenges, we've developed a novel approach using selective labeling to enhance model training gradually. Unlike traditional methods, selective labeling enables the model to learn from high-quality human labels in an online setting, either by expanding existing classes or creating new ones. Our technique employs unsupervised clustering to detect emerging sub-groups within the data distribution and accurately predict the existing classes. The model then focuses on the most distinct sub-groups separately and is updated using labeled data only where necessary. The process is repeated in a iterative cycle, resulting in improved performance and more stable training outcomes compared to conventional supervised learning methods. The benefits of selective labeling are demonstrated through our analysis of the Wikipedia to KAGLE competition dataset, showing a notable advantage in terms of computational cost and convergence speed. The accompanying code is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/AliceSynSense/S selectiveLabeling. Firstly, it is essential to understand that the code needs to be run in sequence as outlined in the user instructions, and our model is best suited for situations where existing datasets are available for processing. Secondly, the code has not been optimized for maximum performance and further refinements could be made. The current version is primarily intended for educational purposes in the AI and Data Science community. The code is divided into two primary modules: dataset_preprocessing.py and separate_training.py. The former is responsible for data clustering, preparing the data distribution, and selecting the most challenging sub-groups. The latter focuses on iterative training, either class-by-class or sub-group basis using labeled data only where necessary. The main function, fit_transform(self, X), is used for initializing the model, while update_model(self, X) is employed for updating the model distribution after each iteration. The model achieves optimal results with hyperparameter tuning via grid_search.py. The accompanying figure, model_architecture.png, illustrates the architecture of the selected classifier. The analysis presented demonstrates the effectiveness of the selective labeling approach, resulting in better performance and convergence compared to conventional methods. The benefits of selective labeling are evident in the Wikipedia to KAGLE competition dataset, showing a notable advantage in terms of computational cost and convergence speed. The approach has numerous applications in situations where existing datasets are available for processing. Furthermore, the code is expected to contribute to the development of more efficient, online training algorithms for semi-supervised learning tasks

We investigated the electronic structure of the EuS/InAs(100) interface using soft X-ray photoemission spectroscopy (SX-PSIS). Our findings reveal that the interface exhibits a significant electronic disturbance from the InAs valence band maximum, attributed to derivative-type vacuum charge fluctuations. Notably, the SX-PSIS spectrum obtained at a cross-over point in momentum space displays a pronounced peak at approximately 2.5 eV, analogous to the spectrum observed in InAs bulk spectra. Through density functional calculations, we probed the density of states at the interface and found that the photoemission intensity arises from InAs-like states within the insulating EuS layer, confirming our experimental observations. These findings strengthen the importance of spontaneous charge fluctuations in ferromagnetic/semiconducting interfaces, as exemplified by the EuS/InAs system. Additionally, our study demonstrates the capability of SX-PSIS to probe the density of states at the interface with sub-0.1 eV energy resolution, which can facilitate the investigation of other surface states and interfaces. Based on these findings, we recommend the use of SX-PSIS as a powerful tool for examining the electronic structure of interfaces and, by extension, contribute to the advancement of understanding spin and charge coupled physics in such systems. Moreover, our analysis highlights the potential for further exploring the electronic structure of interfaces through band structure calculations, as seen in the case of InAs(100) and EuS. By doing so, it may be possible to create novel ferromagnetic/semiconducting interfaces with unique properties by designing combinations of elements like EuS and InAs. By examining the interface between InAs and various ferromagnetic materials/monolayers, it may be possible to create a comprehensive understanding of the electronic structure and properties of such interfaces. Current methods of cutting unwanted neural network branches by reducing the size of shared weights can be inefficient because they disable some original functions of the branches despite reducing their capacity. To resolve this issue, we have developed ClickTrain, a novel and efficient technique for accurate neural network pruning that utilizes existing training data to determine the importance of branches. Firstly, ClickTrain detects and evaluates the impact of each branch in the network using a dynamic analysis technique. To effectively train its parameters, ClickTrain utilizes a gradient-based optimization method. Consequently, ClickTrain achieves higher inference performance compared to traditional pruning techniques. Additionally, ClickTrain delivers better results than existing layer-wise optimization methods in both training efficiency and inference speed while requiring significantly fewer computations during training. Our experiments on standard datasets have shown that ClickTrain can increase the efficiency of the network without sacrificing its accuracy: it produces a 90% reduction in the number of parameters with only a 1% decrease in top-1 accuracy for the ResNet-50 network; achieves state-of-the-art results on the ImageNet dataset with a 73% reduction in parameters and only a 2% decrease in top-1 accuracy for the MobileNet-V2 network; produces models with a reduced computational complexity of 10x to 30x with minimal accuracy losses for image classification tasks while also accelerating inference on real-world images up to 38% faster with little retraining. The discovery of gravitational waves from merging compact objects, specifically neutron star pairs, has opened a new era in astrophysics allowing the testing of general relativity in extreme conditions and providing valuable information about the behavior of highly dense objects and the properties of the hot, dense plasma that arises during such events. Electromagnetic radiation observed simultaneously with gravitational waves provides a precious window of time into the merger process, revealing the inner workings of neutron star coalescence and providing novel constraints on equations of state and physical processes occurring at high temperatures. This review provides an in-depth examination of current knowledge and future prospects of observing neutron star coalescence events both directly and indirectly through various channels in the electromagnetic spectrum, highlighting key events such as GW170817 and anticipating new discoveries that will arise from upcoming observations. Specifically, the topics covered include nonthermal particles produced during nonmagnetic and magnetic mergers, characteristics of nonmagnetic and magnetic neutron stars, and how their coalescence events can illuminate these unknowns. The potential for observing neutron star coalescence events directly through the detection of all-sky gamma-rays, particularly via the Cherenkov Telescope Array, is also discussed along with the testimony of neutron star death in supernova events. Furthermore, the significance of observing neutron star coalescence events indirectly via the detection of optical/UV emission, particularly present but faint in GW events, is also covered along with many more aspects and possibilities of new developments in this field that could emerge in the near future. Lastly, the review concludes with the future expectations and new developments that will arise from upcoming observations, particularly with the involvement of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, the James Webb Space Telescope, and the Athena space telescope. A critical aspect driving research into this field is identifying reliable indicators of biosignatures in exoplanet atmospheres. Directly observing gas phase condensates, a byproduct of atmospheric chemistry reactions, could serve as definitive evidence of past or present life on distant planets. A novel detection technique has been developed to identify free-floating gas giant planets with sub-neptune sized companions, specifically tailored for use on the James Webb Space Telescope. A statistical analysis of these interdependent planets within a population is essential for informing a comprehensive model of planetary formation, thus this research aims to address two primary objectives: first, accurately determine the frequency of isolated gas giants within a specific mass range and, second, identify any notable trends in systems containing both gas giants and sub-neptune planets. In complex decision-making scenarios with large decision spaces, identifying the optimal operational policy can be challenging. To mitigate this issue, existing methods are either restricted to smaller policy spaces or rely on approximate value-function evaluations. To tackle these limitations, this paper presents a sampling-based primal-dual algorithm termed SDCA-GP. The approach is tested in a multi-robot planning scenario with a complex decision space and a sparse reward structure. The results show that SDCA-GP achieves superior performance compared to existing methods. To validate its effectiveness in larger policy spaces, the authors simulate a decision space with 10,000 to 1,000,000 possible outcomes, which demonstrates a notable improvement in both sample efficiency and performance compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, the algorithm's convergence rate is analyzed and the sources of performance enhancement are examined through multi-dimensional policy examination. The study verifies that SDCA-GP successfully identifies the optimal operational policy in decision spaces with up to 50,000 outcomes and achieves an average 95% of the optimal reward in spaces with 1,000,000 outcomes. The classifier relies on a hand-crafted feature set that includes 27 distinct characteristics of the top-left 8x8 pixel block of an image, as well as information about the overall pixel density. Each character in the set (0-9, plus signs, minus signs, and null) has a unique set of responses that indicate its identity. Though not surpassing the performance of existing symbol recognition methods, our simple classifier achieves an accuracy of 94% on a test dataset of 1000 images. The main purpose of this research is to demonstrate a mathematical approach to designing a k-neighbor classifier and explore its connection to the broader problem of symbol recognition. Additionally, this project showcases the effectiveness of a computational technique known as evolutionary computation in designing a classifier that experts might consider too simple. The underlying code for this project is available at https://github.com/djhuang/math-symbol-neighbors. The related video can be accessed at https://youtu.be/OFKUVn7hIjE. Although not highlighted in the video, our classifier successfully identified symbols in the set of {0, 1, 6, 8, 9, +, -} that were rotated up to 30 degrees. To our knowledge, this research is the first to apply a k-neighbor classifier in the context of symbol recognition and related tasks, and it contributes to the broader field of computer vision. Epidemic spreading in complex networks is influenced by various factors, including network structure, disease characteristics, and control strategies. In this study, we examine the efficacy of predicting epidemic outbreaks in uncontrolled and controlled spread scenarios. Our analysis reveals that networks with dense cluster structures exhibit higher predictability compared to those with fragmented and disconnected components. Predictability is also linked to the degree of network bridgeness, with highly connected bridging nodes pinpointed as key predictors. Our statistical model quantifies the relationship between network density and predictability, yielding accurate predictions for various disease parameters and network architectures. Specifically, our models accurately forecast the threshold of epidemic outbreak and final epidemic size in scientific and social networks with remarkable precision, often surpassing the theoretical predictions. These findings have significant implications for enhancing prediction capabilities in network biology and informatics. Furthermore, we adapt our statistical model to estimate the effectiveness of targeted intervention strategies, incorporating the proportion of network bridgeness as a key predictor. Our approach yields accurate predictions of final epidemic size and showcases its applicability in modeling the spread of COVID-19 in European countries and SARS in Chinese hospitals. Our analytical technique employs an innovative combination of maximum likelihood estimation and Bayesian inference, facilitating the incorporation of multiple network realizations and error margins in our predictions. In particular, our models exhibit outstanding accuracy in predicting final epidemic size for the COVID-19 pandemic in Germany, with a median absolute error of 5.4%. Our analytical strategy and associated code are accessible at https://github.com/cosmopoint/PredictingEpidemics. A promising approach, Safety GAIL, enhances reinforcement learning policies to adhere to multiple safety standards by modifying the adversarial loss in a Gaussian Mixture Model. Despite its effectiveness, Safety GAIL has a significant drawback in reinforcement learning - it often propels the agent to the intersection of multiple safety constraints, rather than finding a seamless path that satisfies all of them. In our research paper, we address this shortcoming by introducing an optimization technique that iteratively adjusts the Gaussian Mixture Model to create a safety convex polygon. This technique is based on a new convex optimization method. As a result, our agent is able to navigate more efficiently along a safe path. Furthermore, our Safety GAIL variant exhibits faster convergence and fewer safety violations during training. In addition, our safety convex polygon enhances Safety GAIL by increasing its applicability in a broader range of reinforcement learning tasks. In order to achieve this, we developed a simulative task where an agent learns to navigate through a more complex region while evading hazards. The success of our approach is confirmed by our experimental findings. The source code for our project is available at https://github.com/xyxssap/Safety_GAIL_CVC. A systematic method is developed to list all twin primes up to a specified number by selecting specific pairs of Mersenne primes, demonstrating its efficacy in identifying twin prime pairs beyond the tested limits of $p=10^{10}$ and $p=10^{13}$. This paper presents a comprehensive approach to controlling mobile platforms equipped with sonar sensors using a layered control system (LCS). The bottom-layer controller operates in real-time to process raw data from sensors and maintain the platform's stability. A medium-layer controller utilizes a 2D map and a filter-based strategy to identify obstacles and optimize movement. A top-layer controller leverages a modular control system to facilitate task execution and adaptability. Through navigation tasks and field testing, our method has demonstrated significant performance improvements over conventional control systems. Additionally, our approach allows any mobile base with sonar sensors to utilize its capabilities, thereby enhancing existing platforms like the ROS-Navigation package. The associated code is available on GitHub at the provided link.

This paper proposes a method of extending the concept of Tukey-order between models, which enables us to compare various cardinal characteristics in set theory. By applying this notion, we can demonstrate numerous instances of implication between different cardinal characteristics, often with more streamlined arguments compared to existing proof methods. In addition, exploring the Tukey-order with models reveals interesting phenomena regarding the limited variability in certain cardinal characteristics. Specifically, we find that the true countable cofinalization hierarchy does not exhibit nontrivial oscillations, whereas the same hierarchy exhibits oscillations for models, leading to potential applications in set theory with large cardinal axioms. Furthermore, we identify an upper bound for the true countable cofinalization number relative to the chain condition, which is consistent with a specific maximal value. Finally, we examine the relationship between recursion theory and set theory with large cardinal axioms, focusing on the notions of minimal pairs, quick pairs, and maximal pairs for recursive functions, as well as the corresponding minimal, quick, and maximal orders. Our findings include the existence of minimal pairs for any recursive function with a short axiomatic prime complexity trace, the existence of quick pairs for any recursive function with a prime complexity trace greater than or equal to a specific high threshold, and the non-existence of maximal pairs for any recursive function with a prime complexity trace exceeding a specific very high threshold. We also prove that the existence of maximal pairs for a specific class of recursive functions is an unconditionally strong large cardinal property, independent of whether it implies or is implied by other consistent axioms of infinity. We conclude by showing that the concepts of minimal, quick, and maximal orders for natural numbers are equivalent to their corresponding set-theoretic analogues based on Tukey-order with models. This research enhances the performance of dynamic treatment policies by integrating the pessimism principle into Thompson sampling. We develop a new algorithm, pseudo-posterior sampling, which is akin to Thompson sampling but with an adjusted optimization approach. This modified approach is more resilient to model errors and can be efficiently simulated in line with its probabilistic counterpart. We establish a regret bound for pseudo-posterior sampling, which is comparable to Thompson sampling under optimal conditions. Moreover, by leveraging a novel subgradient bound, we prove that including a pessimism adjustment results in a regret per time step of O(\sqrt{T} / H). We also simulate pseudo-posterior sampling in in-adaptive in-treatment testing scenarios, which involves adjusting treatment policies based on real-time patient responses. The results indicate that this algorithm yields superior outcomes compared to fixed treatment strategies. Notably, in scenarios with limited data availability, pseudo-posterior sampling demonstrates relative robustness to model inaccuracies. We validate its performance using data from two healthcare trials. Further details regarding in-adaptive in-treatment testing are described in our companion paper. We develop a theoretical framework to compare different scenarios of quantum systems, enabling measurement devices and states that fail to be nonlocal or contextual within a particular framework to potentially exhibit these properties in another scenario. Our analysis is grounded in a general concept of product frameworks, which enables a detailed examination of quantum nonlocality and contextuality through constraints on conditional probabilities derived from state and measurement unity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any product framework has an equivalent set of probabilistic inequalities, enabling us to quantify nonlocality and contextuality in terms of a system's distance to violating inequalities. We use this framework to study the nonlocality of multi-qubit GHZ states and find that a general class of states, including GHZ states, cannot be nonlocal in certain scenarios if they are nonlocal in others. Our work provides a systematic approach for comparing different quantum scenarios and reveals connections between contextuality in projective measurements and nonlocality of systems, ultimately enabling a more in-depth understanding of these phenomena. Our method for calculating distances between probabilistic distributions via the quantum relative entropy also provides a concrete metric for comparing nonlocality and contextuality in quantum systems. Our computational tools for verifying nonlocality and contextuality, based on the parametric universal framework, offer a convenient resource for researchers. The results show a surge in pairing for both the two-band and three-band models when each band is filled to 0.7145 and 0.5 electrons, respectively. This paper introduces a novel, unified deep network architecture called SED$_{rgb+rgb}$ for salient object detection, which simultaneously processes both RGB and RGB-D images. The traditional approach involves training separate models for RGB and RGB-D data, but our proposal integrates these inputs within a single framework. This allows the model to effectively capture object features from color and depth cues. We draw inspiration from the success of feature fusion techniques and the potential of guided filters in object recognition. Our proposed model outperforms current top-performing methods in salient object detection tasks, according to comprehensive evaluation metrics such as F-measure scores, area under the curve of precision-recall, mean squared error, structural similarity index, and normalized color coefficients. Furthermore, our model operates at a relatively low EPE (endpoint error) speed of 50.14 ms on a NVIDIA 1080Ti GPU, thereby balancing both accuracy and efficiency. We participated in the 2021 JCDT abusive content challenge to assess our methods for detecting abusive content in Arabic, with support from automated translation of non-Arabic entries, as the language is often used on Twitter alongside English. The resources provided were two datasets, arrest_and_together, from ArabicTweet, with different classes for abusive content, and an English dataset from Twitter's WAT project. Our approach for detecting abusive content involved two stages: first, we used a multilingual transformer model to classify Arabic tweets and non-Arabic tweets separately, and then we used a multiclassifier by combining the outputs along with their corresponding language. For the English dataset, we used a multilingual transformer model to directly classify the tweets. We evaluated our strategy on the provided datasets by calculating various metrics such as F1 score, accuracy, and average precision for each class. Our results showed a significant macro F1 score of 0.67 on the Arabic dataset and 0.67 on the English dataset. After being provided with the test data and related information during the competition, our macro F1 score improved substantially, reaching 0.79 for the Arabic dataset and 0.81 for the English dataset. In an effort to validate our approach, we conducted further analysis, applying two distinct models to the data, the first a multilingual XLT-Bert and the second a multilingual XLT-Bert with language-specific components disabled, using English language data. Additionally, we developed a system to automatically translate Arabic tweets to English in order to participate in the English language classification task, and our macro F1 score for the English language dataset was 0.75. Ultimately, our approach to detecting abusive content showed promising results, and our research indicates the effectiveness of transformer models in this sensitive area. Our code is available at the GitHub repository https://github.com/amanueledee/jcdt-19-arabic.

This knowledge could also be used to develop quantum-compatible interfaces between quantum devices and classical electronics. In this research, we investigate how various topological and geometric characteristics of a bounded convex domain in the complex plane influence the behavior of a specific type of operator that arises in the context of resonant functions. Our findings reveal that the presence of non-trivial analytic discs in the boundary, bounded holomorphic chains, and removable sets significantly impact the properties and examples of composition operators. Additionally, we establish criteria for the compactness, injectivity, surjectivity, and isometry of these operators, and our results are illustrated with numerous examples and case studies. One notable outcome of this investigation is that the presence of just one non-trivial analytic disc in the boundary suffices to ensure the compactness of the composition operator. To facilitate our analysis, we introduce a new concept of 'good' boundaries for convex domains, which provides a useful framework for understanding the resonant functions and their associated composition operators. Furthermore, this study paves the way for future exploration of other geometric characteristics, such as bounded holomorphic chains and removable sets, which also play significant roles in the resonant function's behavior and composition operators. To summarize, this research demonstrates that the complex structure of a bounded convex domain can have far-reaching and intriguing consequences for the behavior of its composition operators. By delimiting the boundaries to convex domains, which are essentially resurgent domains with trivial analytic limits, we ensure the existence and uniqueness of the composition operators, while the presence of non-trivial analytic limits leads to diverse and fascinating properties of these operators. Consequently, the classification of bounded convex domains can be directly linked to the classification of their composition operators. For instance, convex domains with a single non-trivial analytic limit are distinguished from those with multiple such limits, which in turn can be compared and contrasted with hyperbolic convex domains and those that are not convex. Moreover, the presence of bounded holomorphic chains and removable sets adds an extra layer of complexity to the behavior of the composition operators, leading to even more intriguing properties and examples. Therefore, the geometric characteristics of a bounded convex domain significantly influence its associated composition operators, which can be exemplified by a variety of concrete cases and applications. For instance, the hyperbolicity of a convex domain implies the compactness of certain composition operators, while non-convex boundaries lead to diverse and fascinating properties of these operators, which are exemplified by the following cases: the composition operator is compact if and only if it has a trivial resonant function; compactness is equivalent to injectivity when the resonant function is non-trivial

The widespread adoption of GPU computing has led to a high demand for efficient memory management, ultimately resulting in the utilization of a complex array of memory allocators, each tailored to address specific challenges. Nevertheless, these memory managers, although optimized, still fail to ensure the consistent allocation and reallocation of memory blocks as required by most modern GPU applications, thereby hindering full hardware utilization. In response to these limitations, we have developed DynaSOAr - a dynamic memory allocator perfectly suited to modern GPU computing. By leveraging a tree-data-structure-based approach to partition memory blocks, DynaSoAr effectively adapts to varying memory requirements, efficiently recruits free memory chunks, and guarantees lateral memory partitioning. Through comprehensive testing on a range of applications, DynaSoAr has demonstrated substantial performance improvements, with average speedup rates of 2.4x to 6.2x and actual real-time reductions of 100% to 98.5% in making use of spare memory capacity. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's optimized allocation and deallocation mechanisms result in significant time savings of up to 5.9x when compared to the SOAR allocator. By addressing the memory allocation needs of complex GPU applications, DynaSOAr has successfully eliminated all real-time breaches and eliminated all instances of underutilized memory, thereby paving the way for the full utilization of modern GPU memory and hardware capabilities. In conclusion, DynaSOAr stands out as the only memory allocator capable of directly taking advantage of the parallel processing capabilities afforded by current high-performance GPUs. We develop methods for estimating the robustness of decision functions in situations where there is uncertainty about the true parameters. Our approach involves approximating the potential loss that could arise due to model mispecification by maximizing a likelihood function. This method is based on two key concepts: "epsilon-robing" and "gamma-robing". "Epsilon-robing" involves finding the worst-case distribution of parameters within a specified range, while "gamma-robing" involves constraining the amount of weight assigned to parameters outside a specified range. We provide mathematical expressions for both types of robustness and demonstrate how they can be estimated in practice, along with a demonstration of their implementation in R. Additionally, simulation results show the performance of our robust estimation methods in terms of accuracy and computational speed. Furthermore, the study includes a case study on a US tax policy to illustrate the practical application of our robust estimation techniques, comparing the robustness of two tax functions in terms of the maximum 10% and 25% weight assigned to parameters outside a specified range. The results show the potential for significant differences in robustness estimates in comparison to standard specification methods. These methods are particularly useful when there is uncertainty about the true parameters and when counterfactual predictions are necessary. The code for the analysis is available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/krlexamples/robustness/tree/master/vignette. The Central Molecular Zone, a thin layer of molecular material surrounding the Galactic center, defies simple categorization as a protoplanetary disk or a diffuse molecular layer. Despite being relatively thin, it exhibits density gradients that outpace its velocity fluctuations. Our investigation focuses on the structural anisotropy within a specific molecular zone region near the Galactic center, using data from the CO $J=2-1$ emission. Moreover, it's known that the free lattice over a set of generators corresponds to the forest consisting of only the identity tree, rooted at those generators. Consequently, the free G\^odel algebra over a set of generators corresponds to the forest consisting of only the identity tree, rooted at those generators, within the set of up-closed subsets of the forest's set of rooted trees. Based on this, an asynchronous algorithm is developed for a general class of problems with non-smooth, non-convex, and non-differentiable characteristics. The methodology is tested on benchmark signal processing tasks and compared with synchronized approaches, demonstrating a speedup in computation time. Specifically, substantial gains in efficiency are observed for larger block sizes. Furthermore, it is proven that the asynchronous algorithm converges to a fixed point, which aligns with the optimal solution obtained through synchronized execution. However, achieving the optimal solution is not guaranteed with finite computations due to the persistence of oscillations. A corresponding criterion for determining oscillation persistence is presented. Ultimately, empirical results confirm the efficacy of the proposed asynchronous method in producing comparable outcomes to the benchmark methods. A groundbreaking technique in quantum imaging has achieved the feat of imaging sensitive samples without actually exposing them to light. This is made possible by a process where light reflects off the sample and then interacts with the sample again in a subsequent measurement, all while utilizing the non-local properties of entangled photons. However, the method currently has a major limitation in that it requires the sample to be a perfect reflector. Researchers are working on overcoming this issue and have come up with a new approach that enables the detection of non-perfect samples using two alternative methods. One method involves using post-selection of entangled photons while the other method involves using a metasurface to enhance reflection. The effectiveness of these samples is represented by a parameter called ID$\eta$, where a higher value indicates a more effective interaction-free image. The study shows that using metasurfaces can increase the quality of entangled photon sources and subsequently improve the ID$\eta$ parameter, thereby enhancing the interaction-free image of non-perfect samples. This technique holds great promise for applications in super-resolution imaging, the analysis of micro-samples and the detection of hazardous materials. Furthermore, the use of metasurfaces opens up new avenues for entangled photon sources that are suitable for a wide range of applications. The research has successfully improved the quality of entangled photon sources, measured in terms of their cone angle, angular stability and stability over time. Specifically, the use of metasurfaces has been shown to outperform traditional lens-based sources by achieving a 20 times improvement in the cone angle. This breakthrough has significant implications for the advancement of metasurfaces and has the potential to open up new avenues for research in the field of entangled photon sources. The innovative use of metasurfaces not only enhances the quality of these sources but also enables them to be thin and lightweight, measuring just 0.0847 THz in thickness. This distinctive characteristic sets metasurfaces apart from other entangled photon sources based on traditional refractive systems. We examine how thermodynamic systems' energy changes are represented in terms of work performed at a microscopic level. A specific example in N-dimensional space illustrates this concept, where a system's trajectory is guided by a force, and its internal state evolves guided by a metastable potential. From this example, we define dissipated work in relation to a system's internal state dynamics, and show it's consistent with both thermodynamic and statistical mechanics principles. Furthermore, this example highlights an important distinction between work done by the system, and it's relevance in thermodynamic first and second laws applications. Additionally, it's useful for developing techniques to manipulate a system's trajectory to minimize work done on it, and we discuss potential applications in fields like quantum computing and thermodynamics. A possible approach to achieving this involves using optimal control theory. We also connect the concept of norm of a trajectory in a statistical mechanics context, and show it's related to the thermodynamic entropy production and the average dissipated work. Finally, we offer some general reflections on the role of work in physics and its implications in theoretical models development. \textbf{Note:} A shortened version of this article was presented in a conference talk at the International Josiah Willard Gibbs Symposium on Physics. Additionally, a revised version incorporates and integrates previously published results from our group. In particular, the willow-leaves orbit scenario, the negative dissipated work scenario, and the thermodynamic phase transition scenario were studied before, but this version incorporates new findings, and provides a new physical system to model dissipated work in different domains. Also, the concept of norm of a trajectory was also studied in a different context, but this version incorporates new findings that connect it with entropy production and dissipated work in various domains. Lastly, the discussion on the relevance of work in physics and its implications in physics was also studied in a different context, but this version incorporates new findings that connect it with the entropy production and the norm of a trajectory in various domains.}

A key focus lies in understanding the behavior of curvature weights within this geometric framework, where the study of the cotangent bundle reveals a distinct relationship in comparing it to the universal bundle of a manifold. A notable outcome of this study is the discovery that, for a manifold whose universal bundle exhibits positive curvature, the corresponding curvature weights within the cotangent bundle are negative, while the converse is also true. An important consequence of this relationship arises in the context of Riemannian submersions, where the cotangent bundle's geometry exhibits a distinct decay in curvature weights compared to the universal bundle, thereby yielding a decay in scalar curvature that is essentially exponential. In two dimensions, a finite-sized particle in a square torus undergoes a +C quantum walk. The system's thermal state is analyzed under the influence of a trapping potential that mimics the effects of an optical patchy sky. The probability distribution of the particle's ground state position is derived for small trapping strengths and extended to higher energy states. The rate of participation growth for both the ground and thermal states is examined, yielding interesting findings. A comparison with a 2D infinite quantum walk reveals distinct differences in participation behavior. Notably, at the 'detrapping angle,' the participation ratio exhibits unusual, non-random fluctuations in finite-sized systems. Furthermore, the correlations between the particle's x and y coordinates within the thermal state are calculated, including an unusual 'dip' at the detrapping angle in finite systems. The findings provide valuable insights into the effects of particle number and domain size on these quantum walk phenomena. The study also sheds light on the potential application of quantum trapping to control the storage and release of coherent quantum states at near-absolute zero temperature. Additionally, the research offers a new method for detecting the detrapping angle through participation ratio and correlation analysis. Due to its focus on a finite-number of particles, this work offers a more realistic view of quantum mechanics at the microscopic level. Furthermore, the study opens up avenues for exploring trapped quantum walks using coherent quantum states and their potential uses in quantum computing and interference experiments. Conversely, a trapped quantum walk can serve as a model for the study of noise and decoherence in a quantum information system. Lastly, the research has implications for using trapped quantum walks as a means of distinguishing between different types of connectivity in a 2D network. To our knowledge, this study is the first to incorporate particle number effects into the theory of trapped quantum walks, thereby providing a more realistic and interesting model for quantum information applications. Additionally, the participation ratios derived in this study may be useful as a measure of network connectivity. However, it should be noted that the concept of particle number is primarily relevant to finite-sized systems and loses significance in infinite systems. Also, the research reveals distinct differences in behavior between trapped and untrapped quantum walks, as well as unique 'dip' features in the correlation functions that can serve as markers for the detrapping angle and participation ratio peaks. Recently, ViT-Hub has hosted the DINO self-supervised method, developed by randomly grouping nearby patches together and using a self-supervised strategy based on discriminative clustering, resulting in impressive results: zero-labeled performance comparable to that of supervised methods on ImageNet, and better than CLIP on ImageNetILS and Kinship Visual Identification. However, this work reveals that DINO's success can be attributed to an inherent bias in the technique: patch clustering tends to group patches that appear nearby in a sample. Consequently, self-supervision only needs to learn the characteristics of each sample's internal structure. As a result, the method achieves excellent performance, but the learned representations are essentially equivalent to those obtained through patch classification. To mitigate this bias, this study proposes two techniques: patch clustering with sample rearrangement and multiple learning iterations. The patch clustering method can be applied to any self-supervised CLIP-like model without altering its original training procedure, resulting in improved performance on standard benchmarks. The findings suggest that weakly-unbiased clustering methods are capable of generating effective cluster labels, ultimately leading to higher quality representations. The code will be hosted at https://github.com/tsuchyaku/viT-Hub-DINO. Additionally, the DINO model can be accessed through https://github.com/tsuchyaku/DINO. Finally, the paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.03170. The experiments were conducted with support from https://github.com/tsuchyaku/CycloneG.

Analyzing the model's properties, we discover that it exhibits a unique, two-layered potential structure consisting of an upper layer with a constant negative pressure and a lower layer exhibiting cyclic behavior. Furthermore, we find that the model's viscosity coefficient is directly proportional to the rate of expansion, specifically $\eta \propto \dot{\mathcal{H}}$. In the long-term past, the model's behavior can be approximated by two distinct phases, namely a Newtonian phase and a "quasi-Quintessence" phase. Notably, the model's power-law spectral density has a specific form, which diverges at low frequencies, while its autocorrelation function exhibits a more complex, oscillating behavior. Additionally, the model's variance grows exponentially over time. Furthermore, two parameters, $A$ and $\tau$, control the phase and amplitude of the model's response, respectively. In a higher-frequency regime, the model's displacement power spectrum displays a different form. The findings provide a thorough understanding of the model's properties. Conversely, we find that the model's response to arbitrary past states is highly non-trivial. In a specific scenario where the history of the universe is linear, we demonstrate that the model exhibits a non-trivial, non-Markovian behavior. This study showcases that non-parametric models of dark energy can be highly sophisticated, exhibiting various complex characteristics. Importantly, the model's properties are not linked, thus enabling us to study each property independently. Ultimately, the study's findings emphasize the significance of examining the general properties of physical systems rather than imposing specific models on the data. The study explores the uniqueness and solution of the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations in 2D and 3D with smooth periodic initial conditions. It demonstrates that the solutions are smooth and maintain their smoothness over time. Nevertheless, in higher dimensions beyond 2D, the problem is inherently non-uniqueness, whereas in 2D, constraints exist that ensure a singular non-uniqueness of solutions. To address this, the analysis employs a novel approach of actively manipulating the vorticity initial conditions through a continuous family of perturbations. Importantly, the findings indicate that small external influences can significantly impact the accuracy and uniqueness of solutions, particularly in 3D where perturbations are observed to cause an exponential growth of the distance between nearby solutions and their vorticity. The study also yields insights into the behavior of smooth solutions in 2D and 3D for arbitrary time and non-smooth solutions in 3D for arbitrary time, leading to a key conclusion that the uniqueness of the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations is restricted to 2D dimensions. The results have been generalized to derive similar outcomes for the compressible Euler equations. Moreover, the analysis has been applied to derive constraints on possible growth rates of solutions to the incompressible Euler equations in 3D and to the Boussinesq system in 3D, thereby linking them to the growth rates of non-uniqueness of the Cauchy problem. Lastly, the findings have been further extended to the context of the Vlasov-Popovski equation in 3D. We introduced Stable Artist, an user-friendly tool that facilitates artistic control over generated images. Building on existing research, we developed enhancements to the SVE framework to enable users to modify imaginative paintings and abstract artwork. The interface allows users to adjust brush strokes, color palettes, and other artistic details in a imaginative painting, and applies these changes to the underlying code via latent vector manipulation. To streamline the user experience, we implemented multiple features, including automatic camera adjustments and advice functions. The effectiveness of Stable Artist was tested through user studies involving both expert artists and novice participants. The results indicate that users can effectively control the artistic characteristics of generated images while producing coherent and visually appealing results. Furthermore, post-study interviews revealed exciting insights into how artists approach and interact with the interface. Quantifying the uncertainty of predictions is a crucial aspect in assessing the reliability of deep learning models beyond simple generalization performance metrics. By treating weights as variable distributions, Bayesian approaches can yield a measure of confidence in predictions. However, this method is hindered by traditional Bayesian inference, which is computationally expensive and often impractical for modern deep learning frameworks. In response, researchers have developed new techniques of variational inference and Monte Carlo methods on graph structures. Despite these advancements, a reliable method for approximating the predictive distribution does not currently exist for complex models such as ResNets. In an effort to bridge this gap, our study determines that a simple approximation method, leveraging localized variational Bayes with batch normalization, accurately estimates the uncertainty of predictions in a wide range of datasets. In addition to our findings, our study also reveals that batch normalization maintains its statistical properties in the presence of stochastic weights, a discovery that contrasts with prevailing beliefs. As a result, our research makes batch normalization a key component in the construction of uncertainty models, opening the door to the development of reliable and accurate deep learning models. In particular, our uncertainty model outperforms existing methods in the tasks of classification and robust image manipulation, and demonstrates a level of reliability rivaling state-of-the-art synthetic data on challenging semantic segmentation and object detection tasks. In addition to its efficacy, our study also highlights the benefits of informative priors in regularizing the behavior of deep learning models and producing high-quality results in semantic segmentation and object detection tasks. An analysis of dark matter-nucleon scattering cross sections has been conducted, taking into account direct detection experiments' sensitivity limits. The focus has been on light dark matter, weighing less than 10 GeV/c^2. The calculation of signal and background components within the SI channel has been thoroughly considered. The assessment relies on measurements of the J/$\psi$ leptonic decays from the PAMELA and AMS-02 space missions. Significantly, the calculation of dark matter-induced J/$\psi$ production has been carried out using a combination of jet data from these missions and Monte Carlo simulation matching 75% of jet data. The result shows that the constraints derived from J/$\psi$ indirect detection are more stringent than those from direct detection experiments, especially for dark matter masses less than 6 GeV/c^2. The analysis also indicates that incorporating visible J/$\psi$ decays into the indirect detection analysis has a negligible impact on the limits of dark matter-nucleon cross sections. However, the indirect detection limits are sensitive to the fraction of visible J/$\psi$ production, ranging from 14% to 75%. The calculated dark matter-nucleon cross section limits are in agreement with previously published direct detection sensitivity bounds, exhibiting a direct vs. indirect detection sensitivity comparison. The analysis demonstrates that the indirect detection limits of dark matter-nucleon cross sections are unaffected by uncertainties in rapidity distribution, coverage in rapidity, and differential energy spectrum of dark matter. The numerical code utilized in this study has been made publicly accessible. The code allows for the calculation of indirect detection limits of dark matter-nucleon cross sections, taking into account various fractions of visible J/$\psi$ production. The code can be modified to accommodate future space missions, such as the Lucy mission, by inputting its anticipated parameters including sensitivity, proton intensity, and cosmic proton flux. The expected cross section limits of dark matter-nucleon scattering within the range of 10^-10-10^-9 cm^2 for masses less than 6 GeV/c^2 are also forecasted for the upcoming Lucy mission. The anticipated future sensitivity of indirect detection limits is anticipated to be one order of magnitude better than the current analysis' sensitivity. The properties of a non-supersymmetric gauge theory, where a U(1) field is coupled to a massive fundamental field in (2+1)d, are explored through an effective field theory description that incorporates both dynamical and thermal phases. A higher-dimensional instanton trick is used to analyze the bound monopole sector of the theory, which yields an effective Lagrangian that describes the monopole-charge interaction. The Lagrangian exhibits an external magnetic field as a topological defect that truncates the monopole spectrum, transforming the original theory into an effective QEM with twisted boundary conditions. The effective Lagrangian is further studied through an Seiberg duality transformation, which reveals that the twisted QEM is self-dual with a non-trivial Wess-Zumino term. The self-dual point corresponds to an anisotropic Lifshitz invariant Seiberg duality, which provides an effective description of the critical properties of the original theory. The self-dual model exhibits a non-trivial renormalization group flow, which redefines the monopole charge and the external magnetic field. The RG flow equation is analyzed, which suggests that the external magnetic field may have a non-monotonic effect on the bound monopole state properties. By doing so, we can accurately gauge the improvement in model prediction power, unaffected by shifts in distribution. Moreover, to accommodate diverse weather models, each providing a prediction for a specific period of time (e.g., current, future, past), we modify the traditional evaluation process by scrutinizing the predictions made by each model at a particular time against the corresponding predictions in the training data for the same time period. This meticulous assessment enables us to evaluate and compare the performance of weather forecasting models effectively. To illustrate the utility of this approach, we employed numerical weather data and the SkipGram model, utilizing grid search for hyperparameter optimization. The results show that the normalized evaluation yields a notable 70% improvement in estimated relative acceleration in model prediction performance compared to the conventional method. Moreover, integrating the temporal aspect of weather forecasting predictions led to the discovery of domain-specific details, underscoring its practical value. In this research, we examine the relationship between model size and benchmarking accuracy, and develop an approach that uses smaller models to achieve more precise results. The application of active force methods has expanded spatially active matter modeling beyond traditional harmonic potentials, enabling the simulation of complex, anharmonic systems. However, it remains unclear whether the fluctuation dynamics of these active force systems align with existing predictions from fluctuation drive theory, originally developed for harmonic systems. In this research, we examine fluctuations in both harmonic and anharmonic systems governed by active force theories and find significant discrepancies between anharmonic and harmonic cases. Interestingly, we discover that fluctuations in the anharmonic system sometimes exhibit greater variability than their harmonic counterparts, sometimes lower. In an effort to rectify the discrepancy, we propose a revised fluctuation drive theory, validated through the evaluation of fluctuations in systems of active elements driven by chemical reactions and motility. Notably, the revised fluctuation dynamics accurately predict the behavior of fluctuations in systems where asymmetry is introduced through the presence of only one type of reactant. Furthermore, the revised fluctuation dynamics are shown to be applicable to more complex spatially active matter systems, consisting of a bath of reactants and anharmonic potentials, providing a comprehensive framework for the understanding of fluctuations in both harmonic and anharmonic systems. In conclusion, the reformulated fluctuation drive theory represents a crucial advancement in the development of active force theories and the broader class of spatially active matter models. The utility of this theory is exemplified through its application to the evaluation of fluctuations in a system modeled after the propulsion of E. coli bacteria. The results obtained using active force theory are found to be in reasonable agreement with the fluctuations measured experimentally. The measured fluctuations are found to be higher than the predictions derived from the harmonic model of fluctuation drive theory. The analysis presented here offers valuable insights into the importance of anharmonic contributions to the behavior of active force driven systems. We investigate a prominent multi-task reinforcement learning method known as Multi-Dynamics Model (MDM) learning, in which a single model predicts the dynamics for each task. However, relying solely on this model can sometimes hinder performance, as it becomes prone to 'dynamics confusion'. In an effort to mitigate this, we introduce an approach called Constrained Maximum Entropy (CME) that optimizes policy search while constraining the output of the dynamics model to match expected future rewards in target states. Unlike previous attempts to utilize the dynamics model in policy evaluation, CME incorporates the model in a way that's agnostic to its representation and does not necessitate its direct prediction. Instead, a coarse-grained coarse-grain output constraint is imposed on the model, which also accounts for its prediction errors. In our experiments, CME demonstrates successful integration of dynamics models in multiple challenging at-large settings, encompassing continuous and discrete action spaces. In some cases, CME outperforms alternative strategies, while in others, they achieve comparable results. In specific scenarios, CME is notably more effective than dynamics-model-based evaluation methods. In addition to these evaluations, CME is found to be robust in scenarios where the quality of dynamics models is subpar. In line with expectations, CME exhibits the best outcomes when models are of high quality. In contrast, MDM learning performs well when models are highly accurate but may underperform in scenarios with lower model quality. In order to validate the theoretical soundness of our approach, the accompanying theorem analyzes the properties of our method. In terms of practical implementation, the proposed method is computationally feasible even in complex settings, as evidenced by our results. In particular, the evaluation of our core idea, CME, does not significantly hinder performance when compared to alternative strategies. In specific scenarios, the constraint is imposed on coarser-grain outputs up to a depth of three steps ahead. In contrast, the dynamics model itself is often characterized by a depth of six in our evaluations. In addition, the data collections used in the performance comparisons of CME against alternative strategies are made available at the following link: https://github.com/awheeler95/constrained_max_entropy_comparison. With the aging grid infrastructure showing no signs of improvement, there is a high likelihood of hurricanes causing substantial damage in the future. To evaluate the effectiveness of different storm protection methods, it is necessary to simulate hurricane effects on the power grid using historical hurricane data. This is because direct measurement of hurricane damage is impractical and extremely costly. Most current hurricane models fail to accurately depict the complex interaction between hurricane winds and power lines, which has hindered their implementation in recent years. In this paper, a new simulator is introduced that accurately simulates hurricane effects on the power grid. This is achieved by integrating advanced hurricane wind models that take into consideration the tropical storm dynamics, such as the formation of eye walls, along with parameters like storm size and forward speed. Hurricane winds are then applied to the power grid to determine which lines fail due to their maximum cross-sectional area being exceeded. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this metric, it is applied to the 69-bus and 120-bus networks, which show significant line failures that are not evident in simulations of other hurricane models. In addition to the proposed Hurricane Failure Index, the paper explores other promising applications of this metric, which could lead to the development of more resilient power grids that minimize hurricane-induced damage. This includes implementing storm protection methods that are specifically designed to save the most valuable power lines from failure, which in turn could save the grid from total collapse and restore customers quickly after a hurricane landfall. Our research introduces the Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE), an innovative model for data compression and explicit noise generation that surpasses traditional methods. By encoding data into two distinct representations, BCAE enables the separation of essential and redundant information in a compressing process. Unlike conventional convolutional autoencoders that discard information during decomposition, BCAE preserves the redundancy in the original data through a mapping function. This novel approach allows for the controlled introduction of noise into image data, making it a potential tool for semi-supervised learning and image augmentation tasks. In addition to its use as a pre-training technique, the BCAE can also be utilized as a stand-alone model for data compression, a goal that is less common in the literature. Our experiments primarily focus on the noise generation aspect of BCAE and demonstrate its superiority over existing methods in generating realistic Gaussian and adaptive noise, as well as its ability to remove existing noise from image data. In a further extension of the BCAE concept, our model can also be modified into a Multithead Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE-MT) to generate more sophisticated, spatially-adaptive and high-resolution noise, by incorporating additional processing stages for the compression of image features. In a specific application of our model, the BCAE-MT was used to remove digital artifacts resulting from the removal of glass effects in image data. Our findings show that BCAE-MT significantly outperforms other existing methods in the removal of digital artifacts, as well as in the generation of adaptive noise at a resolution of 32x32. Ultimately, our model offers an innovative approach to the compression of data while maintaining the redundancy in the original data and generating high-quality, realistic noise. The discovery of galaxy clusters has provided crucial insights into the development of the universe from its early stages to the present day. Our study examines the thermodynamic properties and phase transitions of galaxy clusters modeled as self-gravitating, interacting Bose gases. To achieve this, we employed the Gross-Pitaevskii formalism to analyze the behavior of these systems in both equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions. Our research reveals the existence of critical temperatures and densities that signify the occurrence of superfluid and Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer-like pairing phase transitions in galaxy clusters. Moreover, we find that galaxy clusters undergo a second-order phase transition when we vary their mass-to-density ratio. Additionally, we identify a non-equilibrium phase transition arising from the interplay between gravitational binding force and short-range interatomic interactions. Based on dark matter theories, we estimate that galaxy clusters are close to reaching the critical point necessary for pairing stability. Our study also predicts that galaxy clusters may undergo multiple phase transitions in response to mass growth. Finally, comparing the thermodynamic properties of galaxy clusters with those of liquid 4He droplets highlights both similarities and differences, including the distinct behavior of galaxy clusters when their mass is doubled. Our research provides a thorough understanding of galaxy clusters as quantum objects and offers a broader perspective on the connection between gravity, statistics, and the phase transitions of galaxy clusters. The findings of our study can be used to interpret future galaxy cluster observations made with space-based telescopes like the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Our knowledge of galaxy clusters' thermodynamic properties may also provide insights essential for the development and implementation of future galaxy cluster surveys. This article discusses the results of two research initiatives concerning convex geometric hypergraphs: a study on saturated problems and a examination of the extremal compressors within a fixed family of convex geometric hypergraphs. We are investigating questions like "What is the minimum number of saturated sets required for a particular set of subsets in a convex geometric hypergraph?" and "What is the maximum number of singleton sets a convex geometric hypergraph can exclude while maintaining all pair-wise sets?" The article delves into the specifics of these investigations, along with relevant examples and proof strategies. It appears there are fewer challenging cases related to extremal compressors, so the majority of the article focuses on the results of the saturated problem research, including a conclusion that concerns certain classes of convex geometric hypergraphs where the excluded sets are limited to singleton sets. We also discuss a key inequality that concerns the total number of singleton sets in a convex geometric hypergraph and demonstrate the application of this inequality to specific geometric hypergraph types, such as those that correspond to points within half-spaces and points on convex curves in a two-dimensional space. The article specifically analyzes and solves saturated problem results for the following geometric hypergraph types: points in a half-space, points on a line, points on a circle, points in a half-disc, points on a sphere, points in a ball, and a general two-dimensional convex region boundary. We provide a summary conclusion and future research suggestions based on our findings. We also include an outline of a proposed summer camp for geometric hypergraph research and provide details on how to partake in this program.

During the expedition, it collected valuable data on water conditions and made two stops at designated monitoring sites. While it was only able to collect data on the river's upper layers due to its poor visibility, the information gathered helped to reduce uncertainty about water temperature, salinity, and other factors. The collection of data was spread out over nearly four days as Trident climbed 60 meters through the water column. Immunotherapies for colon cancer have shown significant potential in enhancing patient survival rates, with immun checkpoint therapies inducing immune responses against cancer cells by releasing hidden antigens. However, many tumors evolve to evade immune detection, necessitating a combination of other treatments with immunotherapies. For instance, Doxorubicin can induce cell death that stimulates a powerful immune response, creating a conducive environment for immunotherapeutic medications. Our research leverages a preclinical mouse model to investigate the synergistic effects of Doxorubicin and Interleukin-2 on tumor regression, immune system activation, and survival rates. Our findings reveal that combining these treatments: (a) boosts T-cell and natural killer cell activity while stimulating a robust immune response; (b) enhances anti-tumor immunity and prolongs survival rates; (c) facilitates sustained anti-tumor immune memory through increased CD8 T-cell infiltration and functionality; (d) significantly increases tumor infiltration by immune cells, immune mediator production, and overall anti-tumor response compared to immunotherapy or chemotherapy alone. Therefore, combining Doxorubicin and IL-2 serves as an effective strategy for immunotherapy, offering a promising prognosis for colon cancer patients. Our findings can guide the development of combination therapies for immuncheckpoint treatments, providing valuable insights into the modulation of immunotherapy with chemotherapy agents. Moreover, our study can inspire new treatments by uncovering the immunological effects of Doxorubicin on tumor regression and the immune response. Our research has broader applications, as the principles of tumor immunology and the combinatorial therapy of IL-2 and chemotherapy can be generalized to other types of cancer and various combination therapies. The time difference between the current time and the time when the latest information was received is known as the age of information (AoI). In this paper, we explore the trade-off between throughput and AoI in a single-hop wireless communication system that uses multiple transmit antennas and has multiple users with varying data transmission requirements. We develop a novel optimization method for this wireless communication system, focusing on both time-sensitive and delay-tolerant users. Our proposed approach yields an optimal closed-form solution for time-sensitive users and an approximate solution for delay-tolerant users, with both of which demonstrate significant performance improvements. Our experimental results reveal that incorporating user specific requirements into the wireless communication system yields substantial gains in throughput and AoI compared to traditional schemes. Our findings also highlight the difficulties in achieving simultaneous maximization of throughput and AoI in this wireless communication system. We observe, however, that we can achieve optimal throughput while ensuring that the AoI for delay-tolerant users does not exceed a predetermined threshold. In contrast, we note that maximizing throughput does not necessarily ensure a bounded AoI for time-sensitive users. Moreover, we note the challenges in limiting the AoI for time-sensitive users while maximizing throughput. Our findings indicate that we can achieve a bounded AoI for both types of users by prioritizing their information update rates. Our results further show that we can ensure a bounded AoI for delay-tolerant users by limiting their information update rates. Studies of merging compact binaries detected by LIGO and Virgo have led to observations of nearly zero eccentricity among the binaries approaching detection limits. It has been proposed that this might be due to sources that, although start with significant eccentricities, are completely circularized by the time they near detection limits, unless their accretion discs are particularly thin. In contrast, this study suggests a different explanation, suggesting that merging binaries with significant eccentricities are simply not yet at detection limits. A new set of simulated findings, based on an extensive array of merging binary black holes with varying eccentricities, masses, and advancement across the universe, has been created. The results show that many merging binaries with substantial eccentricities will remain undetected by current gravitational-wave detectors, including those with significant initial eccentricities. The outcomes also show that it will take around a decade for a binary black hole with an initial eccentricity of 0.9 to be circularized, regardless of its mass ratio.
