Time-sensitive event identification in social networks, stock market fluctuations, and disease outbreaks necessitates analysis of dynamic graphs. Traditional methods, though supported by numerous studies, are hindered by several limitations, including the inability to adapt to complex scenarios and a lack of explanation for their outcomes. In response, we introduce the DyGED model, an advanced generative adversarial network designed for event detection in dynamic graphs. By employing a directed approach to generative modeling, the DyGED model captures high-dimensional graph structures, facilitating the identification of multiple events and their corresponding graphs without restriction. In addition, the model's ability to represent protocol graphs allows it to distinguish between genuine events and false positives, thereby enhancing the accuracy of its predictions. In our experiments, the DyGED model consistently outperformed existing methods on diverse datasets, and our analysis highlights the importance of adapting generative models to the representation of directional graph data. The code for the DyGED model is available at https://github.com/multinical/DyGED. Our paper, including all code, data, and experiments, can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.10397. In addition, our results are presented in detail at https://dyged.conf.pdf. In terms of future work, our research points to several potential directions, one of which involves developing generative models for the analysis of multiple related datasets, an approach that we refer to as multi-dataset generative modeling (MDGM). In this future area of study, our motivation is to significantly enhance the accuracy of event detection by taking into consideration the directional relationships between multiple graph datasets, an idea that we formally define and our results support. Our theoretical findings suggest the existence of multiple MDGM models with varying levels of adaptability and precision, and our analysis indicates that the most challenging and promising area of study involves adapting generative models to the analysis of related disease outbreak and stock market transaction datasets. In this regard, our research proposes the DyMDGED model, a sophisticated generative adversarial network designed for the accurate and explainable analysis of complex graph datasets. Our model's results demonstrate significant improvements over existing methods, and our analysis highlights the potential of MDGM in supporting the accurate and explainable detection of events in various applications. The Guderley problem is a standard test case for assessing the reliability of hydrodynamic codes, particularly those used in shock physics studies. After reviewing the current state of code validation practices, this work proposes a set of recommendations intended to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of using the Guderley problem in shock physics research. A survey of widely used hydrocodes revealed that none of these codes were found to be completely reliable in simulating the high-speed compression and shock history with acceptable precision, according to established standards. Subsequent theoretical analyses were conducted to evaluate the source of these discrepancies and to identify modifications that could improve the solutions. The outcome of this research indicates that existing hydrocodes have the potential to provide reliable results, which can serve as a more accurate benchmark for code validation. Specifically, this work demonstrates that the modified hydrocode output closely matches the experimental and previously validated numerical data for the Guderley problem, which suggests that the absolute pressure error could be reduced by approximately two orders of magnitude. A corresponding reduction in the relative pressure error is also anticipated. The numerical data generated in this research includes shock histories at higher speeds than previously reported in the literature. To facilitate code validation, this work provides access to numerical data for a range of equilibrium states spanning shock speeds from 1 to 163.2 g/cm/s. The revised standards for code validation in shock physics research are outlined in an updated table that incorporates the maximum absolute and relative deviations found in this study. The goals of this research are to contribute to the advancement of hydrocode validation best practices, promote improved accuracy in shock physics research, and encourage collaboration among code developers and researchers through the sharing of knowledge and experience. The outcomes of this research are intended to benefit the broader community through the publication of a comprehensive report that highlights existing code capabilities, outlines future research opportunities, and serves as a useful reference for code validation in shock physics research. The research specifically examines the utilization of hydrocodes in simulating high-speed compression and shock interactions within non-reacting gases. The growing importance of AI systems within high-stakes decision-making contexts has highlighted the need for their explanations. Research on making AI more explainable has primarily focused on the underlying AI methodologies rather than the broader impact on the development process. From an engineering perspective, this means that the role of requirements engineering, a crucial aspect of crafting software systems, is underutilized. To address this gap, this paper outlines current challenges in the XAI field related to requirements engineering and proposes potential solutions. These solutions are grounded in current research efforts and can be implemented in real-world projects through small-scale pilot studies. The ultimate goal is to integrate XAI practices into the standard software development process, encompassing requirements engineering, design, testing, and implementation. Only by doing so can the complexities of developing AI systems with inherent understandability be effectively tackled. The paper concludes by highlighting existing opportunities for pilot studies and research projects that can contribute to improving the explainability of AI systems by leveraging requirements engineering practices. Ultimately, this will enable the creation of more transparent, trustworthy, and understandable AI systems. To this end, three specific research areas are identified for further exploration: the integration of existing XAI approaches with traditional software development processes, the link between XAI quality attributes and requirements engineering practices and techniques, and the specific requirements and challenges associated with the role of requirements engineering in XAI projects. The paper culminates by emphasizing the need for more comprehensive evaluation of XAI solutions to assess their efficacy in addressing the unique requirements and challenges posed by the complex nature of AI systems. To this end, this involves adopting multi-faceted evaluation strategies that can harmonize diverse appraisal thresholds, promote the adoption of empirical evaluation practices within the XAI community, and foster a more collaborative relationship between the XAI and requirements engineering communities. The paper concludes by highlighting opportunities for pilot studies and research projects that can contribute to improving the explainability of AI systems by leveraging requirements engineering practices. The potential outcomes of these studies are also outlined, including process improvements and quality attribute-centric evaluations of XAI solutions. Ultimately, integrating requirements engineering practices into the development of AI systems can help ensure they are both understandable and trustworthy. By adopting a more comprehensive requirements engineering approach, developers can seamlessly integrate existing XAI solutions and create more transparent and reliable AI systems. The opportunities for pilot studies and research projects are plentiful, and it is anticipated that the integration of requirements engineering practices will yield significant improvements in the near future. The potential outcomes of these studies are also outlined, including process improvements and quality attribute-centric evaluations of XAI solutions

To evaluate the effectiveness of deep neural networks (DNNs) in identifying and ranking the severity of colorectal adenomas, researchers compared four prominent architectures in a well-established dataset. Following the success of DNNs in automatic image diagnosis, they examined the potential of adapting pre-trained models on a limited, high-quality dataset of colorectal adenomas images for use in a broader, publicly available dataset. Conversely, they also explored whether pre-trained models could be employed as a starting point and efficiently trained on a larger, non-public dataset. Ultimately, they discussed how these findings could be applied in developing reliable, adenoma severity-grade predicting systems. With such a system, they claimed the potential for reducing the workload of medical experts and improving the efficiency of hospital-scale adenoma classification processes. Experiment results demonstrated that adenoma rankings comparable to those produced by state-of-the-art models could be achieved more quickly, specifically 5-7 times faster for certain metrics. Furthermore, they found combining multiple architectures yielded better outcomes than using a single model and proposed an integrated framework capable of producing high-accuracy rankings. Additionally, they found that utilizing pre-trained models was an effective strategy for rapid development and recommended adapting models to new tasks when high-quality training datasets are available. On the other hand, when datasets are limited and non-public, they suggested developing custom models for more reliable results. The study focuses on the behavior of host stars from four systems containing validated mini-neptune planets, specifically examining the potential of these stars to support life on planet K2-22 b, known for its extreme day-night temperature fluctuations. We analyzed the X-ray emissions of these stars, which were observed by the Chandra telescope, and also investigated their radio emissions, as observed by the VLA, JMLOA, and LOFAR telescopes. The study found no significant radio emissions in three of the systems, while the system of K2-22 b showed intriguing results, as it was observed emitting radio emissions during two out of four observations, despite lacking clear X-ray emissions. We developed a model to estimate the potential impact of both X-ray and radio emissions on the atmosphere of K2-22 b. Based on our findings, we calculated the possible lifetime of K2-22 b, assuming a typical loss rate, to be around 1-100 million years, depending on the actual mass loss rate, which is significantly shorter than previously estimated timescales. We also explored the potential implications of our findings for other mini-neptune planets and found that a few of them could possibly support life, mainly those closest to their host stars. However, further observations are needed to confirm our findings and accurately determine the potential for life on these planets. Lastly, we discussed future perspectives for studying host stars and the search for life on mini-neptune planets, main-neptune planets, and other exoplanets. Additionally, we emphasized the necessity of continued funding for radial velocity surveys, space missions, and various observatories, as they are essential for understanding the diversity of planetary systems and the lives of exoplanets.

In order to cooperate with human partners effectively, a proposed collaborative assistant agent is designed to learn and think strategically. It begins by developing basic skills and instincts through interaction with a human teacher, but instead of relying on pre-built theories like most current AI systems, the assistant learns to think strategically by forming intuitive patterns. By allowing the assistant to ask its human partner questions about past experiences, the team is able to study how the assistant's thoughts and behaviors evolve over time. Initial results indicate that this approach leads to the discovery of underlying patterns in the human partner's behavior, which the assistant then uses to improve collaboration. Ultimately, this research aims to create a more natural and efficient partnership between humans and collaborative assistants. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method by presenting data from a series of studies in which an assistant agents was trained by a group of twenty participants. We found that all of the assistant agents were able to discover and utilize relevant information in order to improve collaboration, and in fact performed just as well as trained specialists in similar tests. By comparing the various approaches used by the assistant agents, we found that they developed unique strategies and perspectives, and in many cases, their performance was better than that of similar, more traditional systems. Finally, we examine how the characteristics and attitudes of the human partners affected the various approaches used by the assistant agents, and reveal interesting patterns of variation in their behavior. Overall, this research highlights a new method for creating collaborative assistants that are both effective and natural, and represents an important step towards creating more advanced collaborative assistants in the future. We hope that this work will inspire a broader group of AI researchers to utilize this approach, and in the process, create a more diverse and natural range of collaborative agents. We also hope that this study will prompt other researchers to examine the complexities of human collaboration more thoroughly.
